notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Measurements and Units
notes.body:
## MEASUREMENTS AND UNITS

(a) Length, Area and Volume

Instruments:

Metre Rule – Measures length to nearest 0.1 cm or 1mm

Vernier Calipers – Measures internal/external diameters and small lengths (accuracy: 0.01 cm or 0.1mm).

Micrometer Screw Gauge – Measures very small thickness (accuracy: 0.001 cm or 0.01mm).

The LEAST POSSIBLE ERROR = Accuracy ÷ 2

Measuring Cylinder – Measures liquid volumes.

Area: Measured by direct calculation from length and breadth, or tracing and counting squares.

Volume: For regular solids (L × B × H), for irregular solids (displacement method).

(b) Mass

Unit: Kilogram (kg).

Instrument: Simple beam balance – compares mass of object with known masses.

(c) Time

Unit: Second (s).

Devices: Stop watch/clock, pendulum clock, digital timer.

(d) Fundamental Physical Quantities

Quantities that cannot be derived from other quantities.

Examples:

1.Length (m) => L

2.Mass (kg) => M

3.Time (s) => T

4.Temperature (K) => K

5.Electric current (A) => I

6.Luminous intensity (cd) =>

7.Amount of substance (mol). => n

(e) Derived Physical Quantities and Units

Obtained from combination of fundamental quantities.

Examples:

Speed = Distance ÷ Time in m/s.

Density = Mass ÷ Volume in kg/m³.

Force = Mass × Acceleration in Newton (N).

(f) Dimensions

Definition: Expression of a physical quantity in terms of fundamental quantities.

Examples:

Velocity: [L T⁻¹]

•Acceleration: [L T⁻²]

Force: [M L T⁻²]

(g) Limitations of Experimental Measurements

Accuracy: Limited by instrument precision.

Errors:

Random error – due to observer or environment.

Systematic error – due to faulty instruments or method.

•Human error – error due to parallax, not reading vertically downward, and zero error

Significant Figures: Digits that give meaningful accuracy.

Standard Form: Writing large/small numbers in powers of 10 (e.g., 3.0 × 10⁵).

(h) Measurement, Position, Distance and Displacement

Distance: Total path covered (scalar).

Displacement: Shortest straight-line change in position (vector).

Position: Location of an object relative to a reference point.

Frame of Reference: Coordinate system used to describe motion. P(x,y)

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Scalars and Vectors
notes.body:
## SCALARS AND VECTORS

(a) Definitions

Scalar Quantity: Has magnitude only, no direction.

Vector Quantity: Has both magnitude and direction.

(b) Examples

Scalars: Mass, speed, distance, energy, temperature, time, volume. (All FUNDAMENTAL quantities)

Vectors: Displacement, velocity, force, momentum, acceleration, weight, moment, electric field, electric force, tension,friction (All FORCES) Magnetic flux or force

(c) Relative Velocity

Velocity of an object as observed from another moving object.

If two objects move in the same direction:

vAB = vA − vB

If they move in opposite directions:

vAB = vA + vB

Often solved using vector diagrams or trigonometry for 2D motion.

(d) Resolution of Vectors

Definition: Splitting a vector into two perpendicular components (usually horizontal and vertical).

If vector R makes angle θ with the horizontal:

Horizontal Component: Rx=Rcos⁡θ

Vertical Component: Ry=Rsin⁡θ

(e) Graphical Methods

Parallelogram Law – Two vectors from a point form adjacent sides; the diagonal represents their resultant.

Triangle Law – Two vectors are placed head-to-tail; the third side represents the resultant.

C

/ \n   ^   ^       AB + BC = AC

/             hence  AC is the resultant

A —>—B

Polygon Law – For more than two vectors; connect them head-to-tail, resultant is from start to end point.

If Two vectors X and Y are at right angle to each others, their resultant is  given by.

R² = X² + Y²

If Two vectors X and Y are at angle  θ to each others, their resultant is  given by.

R² = X² + Y² -2XYcos(180 – θ)

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Motion
notes.body:
## TYPES OF MOTION

Translational Motion – Movement of an object such that all parts move the same distance in the same direction.

Examples: A car moving along a straight road, a train in motion.

Oscillatory Motion – To-and-fro movement about a fixed point or equilibrium position.

Examples: Pendulum swing, vibrating string.

Rotational Motion – Motion of a body around a fixed axis.

Examples: Rotation of a fan blade, spinning wheel.

Spin Motion – Rotational motion of an object about its own axis.

Example: Earth spinning on its axis.

Random Motion – Motion without definite direction or path.

Example: Movement of pollen grains in water (Brownian motion).

(b) Relative Motion

The motion of an object as observed from another moving object.

If two objects move in the same direction, relative velocity:

V of AB = VA − VB

If in opposite directions:

V of AB = VA + VB

(c) Causes of Motion

Application of force changes the state of rest or motion.

Force may cause:

Change in speed

Change in direction

Change in shape

(d) Types of Force

Contact Force – Acts when two bodies are in physical contact.

Examples: Friction, tension, normal reaction, push/pull.

Force Field – Acts without contact over a distance.

Examples: Gravitational force, electric force, magnetic force.

(e) Linear Motion

Speed = distance / time

Velocity = displacement / time (has direction)

Acceleration = change in velocity / time

Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion:

v=u+at

s=ut+ ½at²

v² = u²+2as

Where:

u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, s = displacement, t = time.

Motion under Gravity:

Acceleration g≈9.8 m/s-²

Graphs:

Distance–time graph: slope = velocity

Velocity–time graph: slope = acceleration; area under graph = displacement

(f) Projectiles

Motion of an object thrown into air under gravity (parabolic path).

From ground:

Range = (u²sin⁡2θ)/g

Range = utcosθ

Range = u√(2H/g)

Maximum height = (u²sin⁡²θ)/2g

Time of flight = (2usin⁡θ)/g

From a height: Treat horizontal and vertical motions separately.

Applications: Ball games, water fountains, missile launching.

(g) Newton’s Laws of Motion

First Law (Inertia) – A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force.

Second Law – Force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum:

F=ma

Third Law – For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Impulse = Force × time

Momentum = mass × velocity

Conservation of Linear Momentum – Total momentum before interaction = total momentum after interaction (in absence of external force).

(h) Motion in a Circle

Angular velocity (ω/t (rad/s)

Angular acceleration = change in angular velocity / time

Centripetal force:

F = (mv²)/r

Centrifugal force – Apparent force pushing outward (experienced in rotating frame).

Applications: Car rounding a bend, planetary motion, centrifuge.

(i) Simple Harmonic Motion (S.H.M.)

Definition: Periodic to-and-fro motion where acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward a fixed point.

a ∝ −x

Examples: Pendulum, vibrating string, spring–mass system.

Terms:

Period (T) – Time for one cycle

Frequency (f) – Number of cycles per second (f=1/T)

Amplitude (A) – Maximum displacement

Velocity in S.H.M.: Maximum at mean position, zero at extremes.

Acceleration: Maximum at extremes, zero at mean position.

Energy change: Kinetic energy ↔ Potential energy exchange.

Forced vibration: External periodic force applied to a system.

Resonance: Large amplitude when forcing frequency equals natural frequency (e.g., breaking of glass by sound).

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Gravitational field
notes.body:
## GRAVITATIONAL FIELD

A region in space where a mass experiences a force due to another mass.

Source: All masses attract each other due to gravity.

(a) Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation

Every particle attracts every other particle with a force:

Where

G=6.67×10−¹¹ Nm² /kg² (universal gravitational constant)

F = (Gm1m2) / r²

​

m1m2 = interacting masses

r = distance between masses

(b) Gravitational Potential

Potential at a point: Work done in bringing unit mass from infinity to that point.

V = −GM/r

Unit: J/kg

It is negative because gravity is attractive.

(c) Conservative & Non-Conservative Fields

Conservative field: Work done moving a body between two points is path-independent.

Example: Gravitational field, electrostatic field.

Non-conservative field: Work done depends on path taken.

Example: Frictional force, air resistance.

(d) Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)

At Earth’s surface:

𝑔 = 𝐺𝑀 / 𝑅²

Where: M = mass of Earth

R = radius of Earth (~6.37×10⁶ m)

(e) Variation of g on Earth’s Surface

With altitude (h): gh = g⁰ (R/[R+h])²

With depth (d): gd = g⁰ (1− [R/d])

With latitude (φ): g decreases from poles to equator due to Earth’s rotation.

(f) Mass vs Weight

Mass: Quantity of matter; constant everywhere; measured in kg.

Weight: Force of gravity on a mass:

W=mg

Varies with g.

(g) Escape Velocity

Minimum velocity to leave a body’s gravitational field without further propulsion:

v e = √2GM/R

​For Earth:

𝑣𝑒 ≈11.2km/s.

(h) Parking Orbit (Geostationary/Geosynchronous Orbit) Satellite orbits Earth once every 24 hours, appearing stationary above a point on the equator.

Altitude ≈ 36,000km.

Uses: Communication, weather monitoring.

(i) Weightlessness

Condition where a body experiences no apparent weight because it is in free fall under gravity.

Occurs in:

Orbiting spacecraft

Falling lift (theoretical)

Deep space far from massive bodies

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Equilibrium of Forces
notes.body:
## EQUILIBRIUM OF FORCES

(a) Equilibrium of Particles

Equilibrium: A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero.

Coplanar Forces: Forces whose lines of action lie in the same plane.

Methods for Solving Equilibrium Problems:

Triangle of Forces: If three forces keep a particle in equilibrium, they can be represented in magnitude and direction by the sides of a triangle taken in order.

Polygon of Forces: For more than three forces, they can be represented by a closed polygon taken in order.

Lami’s Theorem: For three forces in equilibrium:

𝐹a/SinA = Fb/SinB = Fc/SinC

are the angles between the other two forces.

(b) Principles of Moments

Moment of a Force: Turning effect of a force about a point or axis.

Moment = Force × Perpendicular Distance from Pivot

Principle of Moments: For a body in equilibrium under parallel forces:

Sum of clockwise moments =

Sum of anticlockwise moments

Sum of clockwise moments=Sum of anticlockwise moments

Moment of a Couple (Torque):

A couple is two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide.

Torque = Force × perpendicular distance between forces.

Applications: Levers, spanners, wheel and axle, see-saw.

(c) Conditions for Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies

Parallel and Non-Parallel Forces:

Resultant force = 0 (forces balance in both horizontal and vertical directions).

Resultant moment = 0 (no net turning effect).

Resolution of Forces: Splitting a force into components (usually horizontal and vertical).

Composition of Forces: Combining two or more forces to find a single resultant.

Equilibrant: A single force equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant force.

(d) Centre of Gravity and Stability

Centre of Gravity (C.G.): The point where the entire weight of a body appears to act.

Stability Types:

Stable Equilibrium: Body returns to its original position when displaced (low C.G., wide base).

Unstable Equilibrium: Body moves further from original position when displaced (high C.G.).

Neutral Equilibrium: Body stays in new position when displaced (e.g., ball on a flat surface).

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: (a) Work, Energy and Power
notes.body:
## WORK, ENERGY, AND POWER

(a) Work, Energy, and Power

(i) Definitions

Work (W): Done when a force moves a body through a distance in the direction of the force.

W = F×d×cosθ

Unit: Joule (J)

Energy: Capacity to do work.

Power (P): Rate of doing work.

P = W/t

Unit: Watt (W)

(ii) Forms of Energy:

Mechanical: Kinetic (motion) and potential (position).

Thermal: Heat.

Chemical: Stored in chemical bonds.

Electrical: Due to moving charges.

Light (Radiant): From electromagnetic radiation.

Sound: Due to vibrations.

Nuclear: From nuclear reactions.

(iii) Conservation of Energy:

Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change from one form to another, total energy remains constant.

(iv) Qualitative Energy Conversion Examples:

Fan: Electrical => Mechanical (rotation) + Heat.

Solar panel: Solar => Electrical.

Car engine: Chemical (fuel) => Mechanical + Heat.

(v) Area under Force–Distance Curve:

Represents the work done.

(b) Energy and Society

(i) Sources of Energy:

Primary: Coal, crude oil, natural gas, solar, wind, nuclear.

Secondary: Electricity.

(ii) Renewable & Non-renewable:

Renewable: Solar, wind, hydropower, biomass.

Non-renewable: Coal, crude oil, natural gas.

(iii) Uses of Energy:

Domestic (lighting, cooking), industrial (machinery), transport, communication.

(iv) Energy & Development:

Economic growth depends on adequate, reliable, and affordable energy.

(v) Energy Diversification:

Using a variety of energy sources to reduce dependence on one.

(vi) Environmental Impact:

Global warming: Excess CO₂ trapping heat.

Greenhouse effect: Heat retention by greenhouse gases.

Oil spillage: Marine pollution.

Air pollution: From burning fossil fuels.

(vii) Energy Crises:

Shortage of energy supply, leading to economic and social challenges.

(viii) Conversion of Energy:

Electric generator: Mechanical → Electrical.

Turbine: Water/steam → Mechanical.

(ix) Devices in Energy Production:

Turbines, generators, solar panels, windmills, nuclear reactors.

(c) Dams and Energy Production

Location: Built in areas with high water flow (e.g., river valleys).

Energy production: Uses water to turn turbines in hydroelectric plants.

(d) Nuclear Energy

Produced from nuclear fission (splitting heavy nuclei) or fusion.

Advantages: Large energy output, low CO₂.

Disadvantages: Radioactive waste, high cost, accident risks.

(e) Solar Energy

Solar collector: Absorbs sunlight to produce heat (e.g., for water heating).

Solar panel (Photovoltaic): Converts sunlight directly into electricity.

Advantages: Renewable, clean.

Limitation: Dependent on sunlight availability.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Friction
notes.body:
## FRICTION

Friction is the force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.

Laws of solid friction

1. Opposes motion

2. Depend on nature of surfaces in contact

3 .Depends on normal reaction F=uR

4. Independent of relative velocity

5.  Independent of the area of surfaces in contact

NOTE = Static friction > Dynamic friction

1. Types of Friction

Static Friction: The frictional force that prevents the start of motion between two surfaces in contact.

Increases with applied force until it reaches a maximum called limiting friction.

Dynamic (Kinetic) Friction: The frictional force acting when surfaces are sliding over each other; usually less than limiting friction.

2. Coefficient of Limiting Friction (μ)

Ratio of limiting friction (Fₗ) to the normal reaction (R):

𝜇 = 𝐹/R

Determination:

Place an object on a horizontal surface.

Gradually increase pulling force until motion just starts.

Measure limiting friction and normal reaction to calculate μ.

3. Advantages of Friction

Enables walking, driving, and gripping objects.

Allows brakes to work in vehicles.

Enables writing and drawing.

4. Disadvantages of Friction

Causes wear and tear of moving parts.

Leads to energy loss as heat.

Reduces efficiency of machines.

5. Reduction of Friction

Lubrication (oil, grease).

Polishing surfaces.

Using ball bearings or rollers.

Streamlining objects to reduce air resistance.

6. Viscosity & Terminal Velocity (Qualitative)

Viscosity: A fluid’s internal resistance to flow.

Terminal Velocity: The constant speed a body attains when falling through a fluid when resistive forces balance weight.

7. Stoke’s Law

For a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid:

F=6πηrv

Where:

F = viscous drag force,

η = coefficient of viscosity,

r = radius of the sphere,

v = velocity.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Simple Machines
notes.body:
## SIMPLE MACHINE

1. Definition

A simple machine is a device that makes work easier by multiplying force, changing the direction of force, or both.

It does not create energy but helps in using energy more conveniently.

2. Types of Simple Machines

Levers – rigid bars pivoted on a fulcrum (e.g. crowbar, scissors).

There are 3 classes of lever

¶ 1st class = Fulcrum is at the middle. e.g scissors ✂️, shears, pliers

¶ 2nd class = Load is the middle e.g door 🚪, wheelbarrow

¶ 3rd class = Effort is in the middle e.g forcep, forearm Fishing rod🎣

Inclined planes – sloping surfaces for lifting loads (e.g. ramps). V.R = length of plane / height of plane = 1/sin∆ (where ∆ = angle of inclination)

Pulleys – wheels with grooves for lifting by ropes or belts. V.R = number of block

Wheel and axle – circular wheel connected to a central axle (e.g. door handle). V.R = R/r

Screws – inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. V.R = 2πa/p

Wedges – triangular tools for splitting (e.g. axe blade, knife). V.R = length of Wedge/ thickness

3. Key Terms

Mechanical Advantage (M.A.): Ratio of load to effort.

𝑀.𝐴 = Load (L) / Effort (E)

M.A.=

Effort (E)

Load (L)

Velocity Ratio (V.R.): Ratio of the distance moved by effort to the distance moved by load.

V.R.= Distance moved by load / Distance moved by effort

Efficiency (η): Measure of how well a machine converts input work to output work.

η=(M.A. / V.R) × 100%

4. Notes

Ideal Machine: One with no energy loss (Efficiency = 100%).

Real machines have friction → efficiency < 100%.

To improve efficiency: Reduce friction by lubrication, use smoother surfaces, or lighter materials.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Elasticity
notes.body:
## ELASTICITY

1. Definition

Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.

2. Key Terms

Elastic Limit: Maximum stress a material can withstand and still return to its original shape.

Yield Point: Point beyond the elastic limit where deformation becomes permanent.

Breaking Point: Stress level at which the material breaks.

Hooke’s Law:

Within the elastic limit, the extension (or compression) of a material is directly proportional to the applied force:

F∝e

F=ke

where

k = force constant.

Stress = Force per unit area : F/A

Strain = Change in length per unit length: ∆L/L

Young’s Modulus (E): Measure of stiffness of a material

𝐸 = Stress/Strain

E = (𝐹/𝐴) / Δ𝐿/𝐿

where

F = force,

A = cross-sectional area,

L = original length,

ΔL = extension.

3. The Spring Balance

A device based on Hooke’s Law used to measure force.

Force applied stretches a calibrated spring => scale reading gives force in newtons (N).

4. Work Done in Stretching

Work done per unit volume for springs and elastic strings:

W = ½ × Stress × Strain

This represents the elastic potential energy stored in the material.

5. Notes

Stiffer materials => higher Young’s modulus.

Materials with low elasticity are more likely to deform permanently.

Examples of elastic materials: steel, rubber (within limits), springs.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Pressure
notes.body:
## PRESSURE

A. Atmospheric Pressure

Definition: The force per unit area exerted by the weight of air in the Earth’s atmosphere.

S.I. Unit: Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa=1 N/m²

Standard Atmospheric Pressure: 1.013×10⁵Pa  at sea level.

Measurement of Atmospheric Pressure

Simple Mercury Barometer

Uses a column of mercury to measure pressure.

Standard height at sea level ≈ 760 mm Hg.

Aneroid Barometer

Uses a sealed, flexible metal chamber; portable.

Manometer

Measures pressure of gases in containers.

Variation of Pressure with Height

Atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in altitude due to less air above.

Barometer as Altimeter

Since pressure decreases with height, a barometer can be used to estimate altitude.

B. Pressure in Liquids

Formula:

P=ρgh

where:

ρ = density of liquid (kg/m³)

g = acceleration due to gravity (m/s²)

h = depth (m)

Key Points:

Pressure increases with depth and liquid density.

At same depth, pressure is equal in all directions.

Pascal’s Principle

Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

Applications:

Hydraulic press

Car brakes

Hydraulic lifts

Dentists’ chairs

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Liquids at Rest
notes.body:
## LIQUID AT REST

1. Determination of Density

Density (𝜌) =Mass (m) / Volume (V)

Unit : (kg/m³)

Solids:

Regular-shaped: Measure dimensions, calculate volume, weigh for mass.

Irregular-shaped: Use Archimedes’ principle or displacement method.

Liquids:

Use density bottle: Weigh empty, weigh with liquid, calculate volume.

2. Relative Density (R.D.)

Definition: Ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water.

R.D.=ρ of water / ρ of substance

No units (dimensionless).

3. Upthrust

Definition: The upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it.

Causes apparent loss of weight in liquids.

4. Archimedes’ Principle

Statement: A body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced.

Formula:

Upthrust = Upthrust=ρ of liquid × g ×V of liquid displaced

​

5. Law of Floatation

Statement: A floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats.

6. Applications

Ships: Hollow shape increases volume of water displaced, allowing heavy loads to float.

Hydrometer: Measures relative density of liquids based on depth of flotation.

Submarines: Control buoyancy by adjusting water in ballast tanks.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Temperature and Its Measurement
notes.body:
## TEMPERATURE AND ITS MEASUREMENT

1. Concept of Temperature

Definition: The degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

It is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.

Temperature determines the direction of heat flow — from higher to lower temperature.

2. Thermometric Properties

Physical properties of substances that vary uniformly with temperature and can be measured.

Examples:

Length of a mercury/alcohol column (liquid-in-glass thermometer).

Electrical resistance (resistance thermometer).

E.M.F. produced (thermocouples).

Pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume.

3. Calibration of Thermometers

Process of marking the scale of a thermometer using two fixed points:

Lower Fixed Point – melting point of ice (0 °C or 273 K).

Upper Fixed Point – boiling point of water at standard pressure (100 °C or 373 K).

Interval between points is divided into equal units.

4. Temperature Scales

Celsius Scale (°C): 0 °C – melting point of ice, 100 °C – boiling point of water.

Kelvin Scale (K): Absolute scale, 0 K is absolute zero (–273 °C).

Relationship:

T(K)=t(°C)+273T(K)

t(°C)=T(K)−273t(°C)

5. Types of Thermometers

Liquid-in-glass (mercury/alcohol).

Gas thermometers.

Resistance thermometers.

Thermocouples.

Clinical thermometers (medical use).

6. Conversion Between Temperature Scales

If two scales A and B have fixed points  LA​, UA​ and LB​, UB​:

## (XA​−LA​​)/(UA–LA) = (XAB−LA​B)/(UB–LB)

Where  XA​, XB​ are the readings on the two scales.

Example (Celsius <=> Kelvin):

## 0 °C = 273 K, 100 °C = 373 K.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Thermal Expansion
notes.body:
## THERMAL EXPANSION

1. Concept

Definition: The increase in size (length, area, or volume) of a substance when heated.

Occurs because heat increases molecular vibrations, causing them to move farther apart.

(a) Expansion in Solids

(i) Types & Definitions

Linear Expansion – Increase in length only.

Linear expansivity (α):

α = ΔL/LΔT

Where ΔL = change in length, L = original length, ΔT = temperature change.

Area Expansion – Increase in surface area.

Area expansivity (β):

β = ΔA/AΔT

Volume Expansion – Increase in total volume.

Volume expansivity (γ):

γ = ΔV/VΔT

(ii) Relationship Between Expansivities

For isotropic solids:

β≈2α,  γ≈3α

(iii) Effects & Applications

Railway lines – gaps left to prevent buckling.

Bridges/buildings – expansion joints to prevent cracks.

Bimetallic strips – used in thermostats.

Overhead cables – sag more in hot weather.

(b) Expansion in Liquids

(i) Volume Expansion

Liquids expand more than solids because of weaker molecular bonds.

Volume expansivity:

γ = ΔV/VΔT

(ii) Real & Apparent Expansivities

Real expansivity – actual expansion of the liquid.

Apparent expansivity – observed expansion when liquid is in a container that also expands.

Relationship:

γ real =γ apparent + γ container

(iii) Determination of Volume Expansivity

Measured using a dilatometers or graduated flasks to observe volume changes with temperature.

(iv) Anomalous Expansion of Water

Water contracts when heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, then expands above 4 °C.

Important in nature:

Prevents lakes from freezing solid.

Ensures survival of aquatic life in cold climates.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Gas Laws
notes.body:
## GAS LAWS

1. Boyle’s Law (Isothermal Process)

Statement: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure is inversely proportional to its volume.

P∝1V   or   PV=k

Graph:

P vs V => hyperbola

P vs 1/V => straight line

Application: Syringes, bicycle pumps.

2. Charles’ Law (Isobaric Process)

Statement: For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (K).

V∝T  or  V/T = k

Application: Hot air balloons.

3. Pressure Law (Isochoric Process)

Statement: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

P∝T   or   P/T= k

Application: Pressure cookers.

4. Absolute Zero of Temperature

Temperature at which the volume (or pressure) of an ideal gas theoretically becomes zero.

Value: −273.15°C = 0K

Basis of the Kelvin scale.

5. General Gas Equation

From combining Boyle’s, Charles’ and Pressure laws:

PV/T=constant

For two states of the same mass of gas:

## (P1V1)/T1 = (P2V2)/T2

6. Ideal Gas Equation

Formula:

PV=nRT

Where:

P = pressure (Pa)

V = volume (m³)

n = number of moles

R = universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K)

T = temperature (K)

Assumes no intermolecular forces and that gas particles have negligible volume.

7. Van der Waals Gas Equation

For real gases (corrects deviations from ideal behavior):

(P + a/V²)(V−b)=RT

Where:

a accounts for intermolecular attraction.

b accounts for finite molecular volume.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Quantity of Heat
notes.body:
## QUANTITY OF HEAT

1. Heat as a Form of Energy

Definition: Heat is a form of energy transferred between bodies due to a temperature difference.

Unit: Joule (J).

Relationship with temperature: Heat changes the internal energy of a body, raising or lowering its temperature or changing its state.

2. Heat Capacity (C)

Definition: The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K (or 1 °C).

C=Q/ΔT

Where:

Q = heat supplied (J)

ΔT= temperature change (K or °C)

Unit: J/K.

3. Specific Heat Capacity (c)

Definition: The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1 °C).

Q=mcΔT

Where:

m = mass (kg)

c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

Unit: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Typical values:

Water: 4.2×10³ J kg−¹K−¹

Copper: 3.9×10² J kg−¹K−¹

4. Determination of Heat Capacity & Specific Heat Capacity

(a) Method of Mixtures

A hot solid/liquid is mixed with a cooler liquid (usually water).

Heat lost = Heat gained (neglecting losses):

m1c1(T1−Tf) = m2c2(Tf−T2)

Where Tf is the final temperature.

(b) Electrical Method

Electrical energy converted to heat:

Q = Pt

Q = IVt

Where:

I = current (A),

V = potential difference (V),

t = time (s).

Equate to mcΔT to find c, that is Q = mcΔT = IVt

5. Newton’s Law of Cooling

Statement: The rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings, provided this difference is small.

dT/dt ∝ (T−Ts)

Where Ts is the surrounding temperature.

Applications: Cooling of hot drinks, industrial cooling processes.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Change of State
notes.body:
## CHANGE OF STATE

1. Latent Heat

Definition: The quantity of heat absorbed or released by a substance during a change of state at constant temperature.

No change in temperature occurs during the process because heat energy is used to overcome molecular forces, not to increase kinetic energy.

Unit: Joule (J).

2. Specific Latent Heat

(a) Fusion (Lf)

Heat required to convert 1 kg of a solid to liquid at its melting point without temperature change.

Formula:

Q = mLf

Example: Ice => Water at 0 °C.

(b) Vaporization (Lv)

Heat required to convert 1 kg of liquid to gas at its boiling point without temperature change.

Formula:

Q = mLv

Example: Water => Steam at 100 °C.

3. Melting, Evaporation, and Boiling

Melting: Solid => Liquid at melting point (requires latent heat of fusion).

Evaporation: Surface molecules of a liquid escape into the gas phase below boiling point; rate increases with temperature, surface area, and airflow.

Boiling: Rapid change of liquid to gas throughout the liquid at boiling point (requires latent heat of vaporization).

4. Influence of Pressure and Dissolved Substances

Pressure:

Increase in pressure → boiling point increases, melting point decreases (e.g., pressure cooker).

Decrease in pressure → boiling point decreases (e.g., boiling water at high altitude).

Dissolved Substances:

Raise boiling point (boiling point elevation).

Lower melting point (freezing point depression).

5. Applications in Appliances

Pressure cookers – faster cooking due to higher boiling point.

Refrigerators & air conditioners – use evaporation of refrigerants to absorb heat.

Ice-making machines – exploit latent heat of fusion.

Steam irons – use latent heat of vaporization to produce steam for pressing clothes.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Vapours
notes.body:
## VAPOURS

1. Unsaturated and Saturated Vapours

Unsaturated Vapour: Vapour that can still hold more vapour molecules at a given temperature before reaching equilibrium (not at maximum vapour pressure).

Saturated Vapour: Vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature; cannot hold more vapour without condensation occurring.

2. Relationship Between Saturated Vapour Pressure (S.V.P) and Boiling

S.V.P: The pressure exerted by a saturated vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.

Boiling occurs when the S.V.P of the liquid equals the external (atmospheric) pressure.

Increase in temperature → S.V.P increases.

3. Determination of S.V.P (Barometer Tube Method)

A liquid is introduced into a barometer tube containing mercury.

The liquid evaporates, and the pressure exerted by its vapour reduces the mercury column height.

S.V.P = fall in mercury column height compared to normal atmospheric pressure.

4. Formation of Dew, Mist, Fog, and Rain

Dew: Water droplets formed when air is cooled to its dew point and condenses on surfaces.

Mist/Fog: Tiny water droplets suspended in air near the ground; fog is denser.

Rain: Water vapour condenses into droplets in clouds which grow heavy and fall.

5. Dew Point, Humidity, and Relative Humidity

Dew Point: Temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.

Humidity: The amount of water vapour in the air.

Relative Humidity (RH): = (Actual water vapour content/

Saturation water vapour content at same temperature) ×100%

High RH => air feels damp; low RH => air feels dry.

6. Hygrometry

Purpose: Measurement of atmospheric humidity.

Wet and Dry Bulb Hygrometer:

Dry bulb thermometer → measures air temperature.

Wet bulb thermometer => bulb wrapped in wet cloth; evaporation cools it.

Difference in readings is used with tables to estimate relative humidity.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Structure of Matter and Kinetic Theory
notes.body:
## STRUCTURE OF MATTER AND KINETIC THEORY

(a) Molecular Nature of Matter

1. Atoms and Molecules

Atom: The smallest particle of an element that retains its chemical properties.

Molecule: The smallest particle of a substance (element or compound) that can exist independently.

Examples: O₂, H₂, H₂O, CO₂.

2. Molecular Theory

Main ideas: Matter is made of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) in constant motion.

Brownian Motion: Random, zigzag movement of particles (e.g., pollen grains in water) caused by bombardment by invisible molecules.

Diffusion: Gradual mixing of molecules from high concentration to low concentration due to random motion (e.g., smell of perfume spreading).

Surface Tension: The tendency of a liquid surface to contract and resist external force, due to cohesive forces among molecules.

Capillarity: Rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and adhesion.

Adhesion: Attraction between molecules of different substances (e.g., water on glass).

Cohesion: Attraction between molecules of the same substance (e.g., water molecules).

Angle of Contact: The angle between the liquid surface and the container wall at the point of contact.

Acute (< 90°) for water in glass (good adhesion).

Obtuse (> 90°) for mercury in glass (poor adhesion).

3. Examples and Applications

Brownian motion: Evidence of molecular motion in gases and liquids.

Diffusion: Used in the exchange of gases in lungs.

Surface tension: Used in detergents, insects walking on water.

Capillarity: Movement of water in plant xylem.

(b) Kinetic Theory of Matter

1. Assumptions of the Kinetic Theory of Gases

Gas molecules are in constant, random motion.

The volume of individual molecules is negligible compared to the container volume.

Collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic.

No intermolecular forces act except during collisions.

The average kinetic energy of molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature.

2. Explaining Phenomena with Kinetic Theory

Pressure of a gas: Caused by collisions of molecules with container walls.

Boyle’s Law: At constant temperature, decreasing volume increases collision frequency => pressure increases.

Charles’ Law: At constant pressure, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy => volume increases.

Melting & Boiling: Heat energy increases molecular motion until bonds break or particles escape into vapour phase.

Vaporization & Evaporation: Molecules at the surface with enough energy escape into vapour.

Change in temperature: Related to change in average kinetic energy of molecules.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Heat Transfer
notes.body:
## HEAT TRANSFER

(i) Modes of Heat Transfer

Conduction

Transfer of heat through a material without movement of the particles of the substance as a whole.

Occurs mainly in solids due to vibration and collision of particles.

Examples: Heating one end of a metal rod, cooking with a metal spoon.

Good conductors: Metals like copper, aluminium.

Poor conductors (insulators): Wood, rubber, plastic.

Convection

Transfer of heat by the bulk movement of fluid (liquid or gas) from one place to another.

Examples: Sea breeze, heating water in a pot, convection currents in a room.

Used in heaters, refrigerators, and ventilation systems.

Radiation

Transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves (infrared) without the need for a medium.

Can occur in vacuum.

Examples: Heat from the Sun, heat from a fire.

(ii) Temperature Gradient, Thermal Conductivity, and Heat Flux

Temperature Gradient (dT/dx): Rate of change of temperature with distance in a material.

Thermal Conductivity (k): Ability of a material to conduct heat. Higher k = better conductor.

Heat Flux (Q/t): Rate of heat flow per unit area.

Fourier’s Law: Q/t=−kA⋅(dT/dx)

where A = cross-sectional area,

dT/dx = temperature gradient.

(iii) Effect of Nature of Surface on Energy Radiated and Absorbed

Black, dull surfaces: Good absorbers and emitters of heat radiation.

Shiny, polished surfaces: Poor absorbers and emitters but good reflectors.

Applications:

Blackened kettle bottoms (absorb more heat).

Shiny teapots (reduce heat loss).

(iv) Conductivities of Common Materials

MaterialThermal Conductivity (approx., W/m·K) Silver 430,  Copper 390, Aluminium 235, Iron 80, Glass 1, Wood 0.15, Air 0.024.

(v) The Thermos Flask

Purpose: Minimize heat transfer to keep liquids hot or cold.

Design Features:

Double-walled glass container with vacuum between walls => prevents conduction and convection.

Silvery inner surfaces => reflect radiation.

Cork or plastic stopper => reduces conduction.

Support from insulating material => reduces conduction from base.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Waves
notes.body:
## WAVES

(a) Production and Propagation

Wave Motion

A disturbance that travels through a medium (or space) transferring energy without the transfer of matter.

Vibrating Systems as Sources of Waves

Sources of waves include vibrating strings, tuning forks, loudspeakers, and ripples on water.

Example: A plucked guitar string produces sound waves.

Waves as a Mode of Energy Transfer

Waves carry energy from one point to another without bulk movement of the particles of the medium.

Distinction Between Particle Motion and Wave Motion

Particle motion: Oscillation about a fixed position.

Wave motion: The disturbance moves through the medium.

Example: In water waves, water particles move in circles, but the wave pattern moves forward.

Relationship Between Frequency, Wavelength, and Wave Velocity

v=fλ

where:

v = wave speed (m/s)

f = frequency (Hz)

λ = wavelength (m)

Phase Difference

Measures how much one wave is shifted relative to another.

Measured in radians (rad) or degrees (°).

Wave Number and Wave Vector

Wave number

k = 2π/λ

​

(rad/m)

Wave vector: Direction and magnitude of propagation of the wave.

Progressive Wave Equation

For a wave moving in the positive x-direction:

y(x,t)=Asin(kx−ωt+ϕ)

where

A = amplitude,

k = wave number,

ω = angular frequency,

ϕ = phase constant.

(b) Classification

Types of Waves

Mechanical waves: Require a medium (e.g. sound, water waves).

Electromagnetic waves: Do not require a medium (e.g. light, radio waves).

Longitudinal and Transverse Waves

Longitudinal: Particles oscillate parallel to wave direction (e.g. sound).

Transverse: Particles oscillate perpendicular to wave direction (e.g. light, water ripples).

Stationary and Progressive Waves

Progressive waves: Disturbance moves through medium.

Stationary waves: Result from interference of two waves of the same frequency traveling in opposite directions.

Examples

Springs & ropes: Demonstrate transverse or longitudinal waves.

Stretched strings: Vibrations produce musical notes.

Ripple tank: Demonstrates reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference.

(c) Characteristics / Properties of Waves

Reflection

Wave bounces off a surface (e.g. echo of sound).

Refraction

Change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another due to change in speed.

Diffraction

Bending/spreading of waves around obstacles or through narrow openings.

Plane Polarization

Restricting wave vibrations to one direction (applies to transverse waves only).

Superposition of Waves

When two or more waves meet, resultant displacement is the vector sum of their individual displacements.

Interference

Constructive interference (waves reinforce) and destructive interference (waves cancel).

Beats

Periodic variation in amplitude when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere.

Beat frequency = difference between the two frequencies.

Doppler Effect (Qualitative)

Apparent change in frequency/wavelength of a wave due to relative motion between source and observer.

Example: Siren pitch changes as an ambulance passes by.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Propagation of Sound Waves
notes.body:
## PROPAGATION OF SOUND WAVES

(i) Necessity for a Material Medium

Sound waves are mechanical longitudinal waves—they require a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate.

Reason: Sound travels by causing particles of the medium to vibrate back and forth, transmitting energy from one particle to the next.

Vacuum: Cannot transmit sound because there are no particles to vibrate.

Example: Bell jar experiment—sound from a ringing bell becomes inaudible when air is removed.

(ii) Speed of Sound

The speed of sound depends on the medium and its properties (density and elasticity).

In Solids: Fastest (particles are closely packed).

Example: ~ 5000 m/s in steel.

In Liquids: Slower than in solids but faster than in gases.

Example: ~ 1500 m/s in water.

In Air: Slowest (~ 343 m/s at 20°C).

Speed in air increases with temperature:

v≈331 + 0.6Tv

where T is in °C.

(iii) Reflection of Sound

Sound waves can be reflected when they meet a surface such as a wall, cliff, or building.

Law of Reflection: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (applies to sound just like light).

Echoes

Definition: Reflection of sound that is heard distinctly after the original sound.

Condition: The reflecting surface must be far enough so that the time interval between original sound and echo is ≥ 0.1 s (human ear resolution).

Minimum distance for echo in air at 20°C:

d≈17 m

(since sound travels ~343 m/s, in 0.1 s it covers 34 m round trip).

Reverberation

Definition: Persistence of sound in a space due to multiple reflections, causing the sound to fade gradually rather than stop abruptly.

Common in empty halls, churches, and large rooms.

Applications of Echoes and Reverberations

Echo sounding: Measuring ocean depth.

Sonar: Navigation and object detection underwater.

Medical ultrasound: Imaging internal body structures.

Architectural acoustics: Designing halls for clear sound.

(iv) Disadvantages of Echoes and Reverberations

Echoes: Can cause confusion in speech perception.

Reverberations: Can make music or speech unclear in auditoriums.

Solution: Use sound-absorbing materials (e.g., curtains, carpets, acoustic panels) to minimize unwanted reflections.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Characteristics of Sound Waves
notes.body:
## CHARACTERISTICS OF SOUND WAVES

(i) Noise and Musical Notes

Noise: Unpleasant, irregular sound with no definite pattern or frequency.

Example: Traffic noise, shouting, banging.

Musical Note: Pleasant sound with a regular pattern and definite frequency.

Example: Sound from a tuned guitar or piano.

(ii) Quality, Pitch, Intensity, and Loudness

Quality (Timbre)

Distinguishes between two sounds of the same pitch and loudness.

Determined by the number and relative intensities of overtones present.

Example: Middle C on a flute vs. on a violin sounds different because of timbre.

Pitch

How high or low a sound is perceived.

Depends on the frequency of the wave:

Higher frequency => higher pitch.

Lower frequency => lower pitch.

Intensity

The power per unit area carried by a sound wave.

Measured in watts per square metre (W/m²).

Depends on the amplitude of vibration.

Loudness

How strong or soft a sound is perceived by the ear.

Related to intensity but also depends on the sensitivity of the ear and environment.

Applications to Musical Instruments:

String instruments: Pitch adjusted by string tension, length, and thickness.

Wind instruments: Pitch adjusted by length of air column.

Percussion: Loudness varied by striking force.

(iii) Overtones in Vibrating Strings and Air Columns

Fundamental: Lowest frequency produced by a vibrating system.

Overtones (Harmonics): Higher frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

Vibrating strings produce a mixture of the fundamental and overtones => richer sound.

Air columns in pipes (closed or open) also produce overtones.

(iv) Acoustic Examples of Resonance

Resonance: Large increase in amplitude when a vibrating system is forced at its natural frequency.

Examples:

Tuning fork making a nearby fork of the same frequency vibrate.

Blowing over a bottle mouth and hearing a loud note.

Singer breaking glass with sustained pitch matching glass's natural frequency.

(v) Frequency of a Note Emitted by Air Columns

Closed Pipe (one end closed, one open)

Only odd harmonics are present:

fn = nv/4L  n=1,3,5,...

Example: Clarinet.

Open Pipe (both ends open)

All harmonics are present:

fn=nv/2L,n=1,2,3,...

Example: Flute.

Where:

fn = frequency of the nth harmonic

v = speed of sound in air

L = length of air column

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Light Energy
notes.body:
## LIGHT ENERGY

(a) Sources of Light

(i) Natural and Artificial Sources

Natural Sources: Produce light without human intervention.

Examples: Sun, stars, fireflies, lightning.

Artificial Sources: Man-made sources of light.

Examples: Electric bulbs, candles, lanterns, LEDs.

(ii) Luminous and Non-Luminous Objects

Luminous Objects: Emit their own light.

Examples: Sun, torch, candle flame.

Non-Luminous Objects: Do not produce light; seen by reflecting light from luminous sources.

Examples: Moon, books, walls.

(b) Propagation of Light

(i) Speed, Frequency, and Wavelength of Light

Speed in vacuum: c=3.0×10⁸ m/s = (maximum possible speed in the universe).

Relationship:

v=fλ

Where:

v = speed of light in medium,

f = frequency,

λ = wavelength.

In denser media (like glass or water), light travels slower.

(ii) Formation of Shadows and Eclipse

Shadow: Dark region formed when an opaque object blocks light.

Umbra: Complete shadow.

Penumbra: Partial shadow.

Eclipse:

Solar Eclipse: Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth.

Lunar Eclipse: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

(iii) The Pin-Hole Camera

A simple optical device consisting of a light-proof box with a tiny hole on one side.

Working Principle: Light travels in straight lines.

Forms an inverted, real, and diminished image of an object on the opposite side.

Applications: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light and image formation.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Reflection of Light at Plane and Curved Surfaces
notes.body:
## REFLECTION OF LIGHT AT PLANE AND CURVED SURFACES

(i) Laws of Reflection

First Law: The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

Second Law: The angle of incidence i is equal to the angle of reflection r.

i = r

(ii) Applications of Reflection of Light

Plane Mirrors: Periscopes, dressing mirrors, solar cookers.

Concave Mirrors: Shaving/makeup mirrors, dentist’s mirrors, headlamps, reflecting telescopes.

Convex Mirrors: Vehicle side mirrors, security mirrors, road safety mirrors.

(iii) Formation of Images by Plane, Concave, and Convex Mirrors

Plane Mirror

Image is virtual, upright, and of same size as the object.

Appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Concave Mirror

Image type depends on the object’s distance from the mirror:

Far from the mirror: Real, inverted, smaller.

At focus: Real, inverted, highly magnified.

Between focus and mirror: Virtual, upright, magnified.

Convex Mirror

Always produces a virtual, upright, and diminished image.

(iv) The Mirror Formula

For spherical mirrors:

1/f = 1/u + 1/v

Where:

f = focal length,

u = object distance,

v = image distance.

Sign convention (Cartesian system) must be applied when solving problems.

(v) Linear Magnification

Formula:

M=Image height / Object height = v / u

M>1: Magnified image

M<1: Diminished image

M=1: Same size image

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Refraction of Light Through at Plane and Curved Surfaces
notes.body:
## REFRACTION OF LIGHT AT PLANE AND CURVED SURFACES

(i) Explanation of Refraction in Terms of Velocity of Light in the Media

Refraction: The change in direction of light as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in its speed.

Light travels faster in rarer media (e.g., air) and slower in denser media (e.g., glass, water).

Towards normal: Light slows down when entering a denser medium.

Away from normal: Light speeds up when entering a less dense medium.

(ii) Laws of Refraction

The incident ray, the refracted ray, and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence iii to the sine of the angle of refraction rrr is a constant for the same two media:

sin⁡ i° / sin⁡ r° =n

Where n is the refractive index.

(iii) Definition of Refractive Index

Refractive index nnn of a medium is the ratio of:

n=speed of light in vacuum (c) / speed of light in the medium (v)

n = c/v

It measures how much the medium slows down light.

(iv) Determination of Refractive Index Using Snell’s Law

For glass: Use a rectangular glass block and a ray box; measure iii and r, then calculate n using

n = sin⁡ i° / sin⁡ r°

For liquids: Use a pin method (real and apparent depth) or refraction tank experiments.

(v) Real and Apparent Depth

When an object is viewed from above a denser medium, it appears closer to the surface:

n = apparent depth / real depth​

(vi) Lateral Displacement

When light passes obliquely through a glass block, the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.

The lateral shift depends on the thickness of the block, the refractive index, and the angle of incidence.

(vii) Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection (TIR)

Critical Angle C: The angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°:

sin⁡C = 1/n​

TIR: Occurs when light tries to move from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence is greater than C.

Applications: Optical fibres, periscopes, binoculars, diamond sparkle.

(b) Glass Prism

(i) Minimum Deviation Formula

For a prism of refracting angle A and minimum deviation Dm:

n = sin⁡(½[A+Dm])/sin⁡½A​​​

(ii) Types of Lenses

Convex (Converging): Thicker at the center than edges; focuses parallel rays to a point.

Concave (Diverging): Thinner at the center than edges; spreads parallel rays outward.

(iii) Lens Formula

1/f = 1/u + 1/v

Where:

f = focal length,

u = object distance,

v = image distance.

(iv) Magnification in Lenses

M = Image height/Object height = v/u

M>1: Image is magnified.

M<1: Image is diminished.

M=1: Same size image.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Optical Instruments
notes.body:
## OPTICAL INSTRUMENTS

(i) Principles of Common Optical Instruments

1. Microscope

Principle: Uses two convex lenses (objective and eyepiece) to magnify very small objects.

Function: The objective lens produces a magnified real image, which is further magnified by the eyepiece to form a final virtual image.

Application: Biology labs, medical research.

2. Telescope

Principle: Uses lenses (or mirrors) to view distant objects.

Astronomical Telescope: Two convex lenses, produces an inverted final image.

Terrestrial Telescope: Uses an extra lens to produce an upright image.

Reflecting Telescope: Uses a concave mirror instead of an objective lens.

Application: Astronomy, surveillance.

3. Projector

Principle: Uses a bright light source and a converging lens to project a magnified real image of a slide/film onto a screen.

Application: Cinemas, classroom teaching.

4. Camera

Principle: A converging lens forms a real, inverted image on a photographic film or digital sensor.

Key parts: Lens, aperture, shutter, film/sensor.

Application: Photography, filming.

5. The Human Eye (basic physics only)

Principle: Functions like a camera, with the eye lens focusing light on the retina.

Focusing: Achieved by changing the curvature of the eye lens (accommodation).

Application: Vision in daily life.

(ii) Power of a Lens

Defined as:

P=100/f(in cm) or P = 1/f(in metres)

Unit: dioptre (D).

Example: A lens with f = 0.5m has P = 2D.

(iii) Angular Magnification

Definition: Ratio of the angular size of the image to that of the object when viewed with the naked eye.

For simple microscope:

M =1+ D/f

where D = least distance of distinct vision (≈ 25 cm).

(iv) Near and Far Points

Near Point: Closest distance at which an object can be seen clearly by the eye (normal value ≈ 25 cm).

Far Point: Farthest distance at which the eye can see clearly (infinite for a normal eye).

(v) Sight Defects and Corrections

Defect, Causes, and Correction

Myopia (Short-sightedness): Eye lens too strong or eyeball too long; far objects appear blurred.

Correction: Use concave (diverging) lens

Hypermetropia (Long-sightedness): Eye lens too weak or eyeball too short; near objects appear blurred

Correction: Use convex (converging) lens

Presbyopia: Loss of elasticity of eye lens due to ageing

Correction: Use bifocal lenses

Astigmatism: Uneven curvature of the cornea

Correction: lensUse cylindrical lenses

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Dispersion of light and colours
notes.body:
## DISPERSION OF LIGHT AND COLOURS

(i) Dispersion of White Light by a Triangular Prism

Dispersion: The splitting of white light into its component colours (spectrum) due to differences in refractive indices for different wavelengths.

In a prism, violet light is refracted most, and red light is refracted least.

Order of colours (VIBGYOR): Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

(ii) Production of Pure Spectrum

Achieved using a narrow slit, a collimating lens, and a prism.

A pure spectrum has clearly separated colours with no overlap.

(iii) Colour Mixing

Addition of Colours:

Primary colours of light: Red, Green, Blue.

Mixing produces:

Red + Green = Yellow

Green + Blue = Cyan

Blue + Red = Magenta

Red + Green + Blue = White light.

Subtraction of Colours:

Involves removal of certain wavelengths using filters or pigments.

Primary subtractive colours: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow.

(iv) Colour of Objects and Colour Filters

The colour of an object is the colour of light it reflects.

Example: A red object reflects red light and absorbs others.

Colour filters: Allow only their own colour to pass through and absorb the rest.

(v) Rainbow

Natural spectrum formed when sunlight is dispersed by raindrops.

Raindrops act like tiny prisms, refracting and internally reflecting light.

Always appears with red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge.

27. (b) Electromagnetic Spectrum

Definition

The complete range of electromagnetic waves arranged in order of increasing wavelength (or decreasing frequency).

Order (Shortest to Longest Wavelength)

Gamma Rays

Source: Radioactive decay, nuclear reactions.

Uses: Cancer treatment, sterilisation.

X-Rays

Source: X-ray tubes, radioactive materials.

Uses: Medical imaging, material inspection.

Ultraviolet (UV)

Source: Sun, UV lamps.

Uses: Sterilisation, detecting forged documents.

Visible Light

Source: Sun, lamps.

Uses: Vision, photography.

Infrared (IR)

Source: Hot objects, remote controls.

Uses: Night vision, heating, remote sensing.

Microwaves

Source: Electronic oscillators, radar.

Uses: Cooking, satellite communication, radar.

Radio Waves

Source: Transmitters, lightning.

Uses: Broadcasting, mobile communication.

Key Points

All EM waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum (3×10⁸ m/s).

They differ only in wavelength and frequency.

Higher frequency => more energy.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Electrostatics
notes.body:
## ELECTROSTATICS

(i) Existence of Positive and Negative Charges in Matter

All matter contains electrons (negative) and protons (positive).

Positive charge: deficiency of electrons.

Negative charge: excess of electrons.

Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

(ii) Charging a Body

By Friction

Rubbing two insulators transfers electrons from one to the other.

Example: Rubbing a plastic rod with wool makes the rod negatively charged.

By Contact

A charged body touches a neutral conductor, transferring some charge.

By Induction

A charged body brought near a neutral conductor causes redistribution of charges without contact.

(iii) Electroscope

An instrument used to detect and estimate the presence of electric charge.

Structure: Metal rod, gold leaves/foil, insulated casing.

Working: Charged body causes leaves to diverge due to repulsion.

(iv) Coulomb’s Inverse Square Law

F = kQ1Q2 / r²

Where:

F = electrostatic force

Q1,Q2= charges

r = distance between charges

k=8.99×10⁹ Nm²/C² in vacuum.

The force is directly proportional to product of charges and inversely proportional to square of their separation.

(v) Electric Field and Potential

Electric Field: Region around a charge where it exerts force on another charge.

Electric Field Intensity (E): Force per unit positive charge (E = F/q). Unit: N/C.

Electric Potential (V): Work done to bring unit positive charge from infinity to a point.

(vi) Electric Potential Difference

Work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to another in an electric field.

Measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter.

(vii) Electric Discharge and Lightning

Electric discharge: Sudden flow of electric charges through a medium.

Lightning: A natural electric discharge between clouds or between cloud and earth due to charge separation in thunderclouds.

Lightning arresters protect buildings by providing a safe discharge path.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Capacitors
notes.body:
## CAPACITORS

Capacitors are devices for storing electric charges

(i) Types and Functions of Capacitors

Types

Fixed capacitors – e.g. ceramic, electrolytic, mica.

Variable capacitors – capacitance can be adjusted (e.g. in radio tuning).

Electrolytic capacitors – high capacitance, used in DC circuits.

Functions

Storing electrical energy.

Blocking direct current (DC) while allowing alternating current (AC) to pass.

Smoothing voltage in power supplies.

Tuning circuits (e.g. radio receivers).

(ii) Parallel Plate Capacitors

Consist of two large conductive plates separated by an insulator (dielectric).

When connected to a battery, opposite charges accumulate on the plates.

(iii) Capacitance of a Capacitor

Definition: The ability of a capacitor to store charge per unit potential difference.

C=Q/V

Where:

C = capacitance (farads, F)

Q = charge stored (coulombs, C)

V = potential difference (volts, V).

(iv) Relationship Between Capacitance, Plate Area, Separation, and Medium

For a parallel plate capacitor:

C=εA/d

Where:

A = area of plates (m²)

d = distance between plates (m)

ε = permittivity of the dielectric (ε = ε0 × εr​)

ε0 = 8.85×10−¹² F/m (permittivity of free space)

εr​ = relative permittivity of the dielectric material.

Implications:

Larger plate area =>  higher capacitance.

Smaller separation =>  higher capacitance.

Higher permittivity => higher capacitance.

(v) Capacitors in Series and Parallel

Series:  1/CT = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3+…

Parallel:  CT = C1 + C2 + C3 +…

Series connection => decreases total capacitance.

Parallel connection => increases total capacitance.

(vi) Energy Stored in a Capacitor

E=½CV²

Where E is in joules (J).

This energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Electric Cells
notes.body:
## ELECTRIC CELLS

(i) Simple Voltaic Cell and Its Defects

Simple Voltaic Cell:

Consists of a copper plate and a zinc plate dipped in dilute sulphuric acid.

Working: Zinc acts as the negative electrode, copper as the positive electrode. Chemical action produces a potential difference.

Defects:

Polarization – build-up of hydrogen gas on the copper electrode increases internal resistance.

Remedy: Use a depolarizer (e.g. manganese dioxide or potassium dichromate).

Local Action – impure zinc causes continuous discharge even when not connected.

Remedy: Use amalgamated zinc (coated with mercury).

(ii) Daniel Cell, Leclanché Cell (Wet and Dry)

Daniel Cell:

Copper vessel with copper sulphate solution.

Porous pot containing zinc in dilute sulphuric acid.

Gives steady current; used in laboratories.

Leclanché Wet Cell:

Zinc rod (negative) and carbon rod surrounded by manganese dioxide (positive) in ammonium chloride solution.

Used for intermittent work (e.g. bells).

Leclanché Dry Cell:

Paste of ammonium chloride as electrolyte.

Portable and convenient for torches, radios, clocks.

(iii) Lead-Acid Accumulator and Nickel-Iron (NiFe), Lithium-Iron, Mercury-Cadmium

Lead-Acid Accumulator:

Plates of lead and lead dioxide in dilute sulphuric acid.

Rechargeable; used in cars, UPS systems.

Nickel-Iron (NiFe) Cell:

Nickel(III) oxide-hydroxide positive plate, iron negative plate, electrolyte is potassium hydroxide.

Durable, used in trains, mines.

Lithium-Iron Cell:

Lithium compound as positive electrode, iron or graphite as negative.

High energy density; used in electronics.

Mercury-Cadmium Cell:

Compact, stable voltage; used in hearing aids, watches.

(iv) Maintenance of Cells and Batteries

Keep terminals clean and tight.

Avoid complete discharge in rechargeable cells.

Maintain correct electrolyte level (for wet cells).

Store in cool, dry places.

Avoid short-circuiting.

(v) Arrangement of Cells

Series:

Voltages add up: Vtotal = V1 + V2 + …V

Used when higher voltage is required.

Parallel:

Voltage remains the same, current capacity increases.

Used when longer-lasting supply is needed.

Series-Parallel Combination:

For both higher voltage and capacity.

(vi) Efficiency of a Cell

Voltage Efficiency:

ηv = (Terminal Voltage / EMF) × 100

Energy Efficiency:

Ratio of electrical energy output to chemical energy supplied.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Current Electricity
notes.body:
## CURRENT ELECTRICITY

(i) Electromotive Force (EMF), Potential Difference (P.D.), Current, Internal Resistance and Lost Volt

Electromotive Force (EMF):

The total energy supplied by a cell per unit charge to drive electrons around a circuit.

Unit: volt (V).

E = Work done / Charge​

Potential Difference (P.D.):

Energy used per unit charge between two points in a circuit.

V = Work done / Charge

Current (I):

Rate of flow of electric charge.

I = Q/t

Unit: ampere (A).

Internal Resistance (r):

Resistance inside the cell that reduces the terminal voltage.

Relationship: E=V+Ir

Lost Volt:

The voltage drop inside the cell due to internal resistance.

Lost Volt = Ir

(ii) Ohm’s Law

States that: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant.

Mathematical form:

V=IR

Where R is resistance in ohms (Ω).

(iii) Measurement of Resistance

Using Ammeter and Voltmeter:

Measure V and I, then R = V/I

Using Wheatstone Bridge or Meter Bridge:

Based on the principle of balancing ratios of resistances.

(iv) Meter Bridge

Consists of a wire of uniform cross-section mounted on a meter scale.

Unknown resistance X is found using the balance length lll:

## (X / R) = (L /100−L)

where RRR is known resistance.

(v) Resistance in Series and Parallel

Series:    RT = R1 + R2 + R3 +…

Current is the same, voltage divides.

Parallel:   1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2 +....

Voltage is the same, current divides.

Combination:

Apply series and parallel formulas as required.

(vi) Potentiometer Method of Measuring EMF, Current and Internal Resistance

Principle:

Uses a uniform resistance wire to compare potential differences without drawing current from the source.

Measuring EMF: Balance length gives ratio of EMFs.

Measuring Internal Resistance: Compare balance lengths with and without load connected.

(vii) Electrical Networks

Analysis of complex circuits using:

Kirchhoff’s First Law (Current Law): Sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving.

Kirchhoff’s Second Law (Voltage Law): Sum of potential differences in a closed loop is zero.

Used for solving circuits with multiple loops and junctions.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Electrical Energy and Power
notes.body:
## ELECTRICAL ENERGY AND POWER

(i) Concepts of Electrical Energy and Power

Electrical Energy:

The work done by an electric current in moving charge through a circuit.

Formula: W=V⋅I⋅t

Unit: joule (J).

1J=1V×1A×1s

Electric Power:

The rate at which electrical energy is converted to other forms (heat, light, motion, etc.).

Formula:

P = W/t =V×I

Unit: watt (W).

(ii) Commercial Unit of Electric Energy

Kilowatt-hour (kWh):

Energy consumed when a 1 kW device runs for 1 hour.

1 kWh = 1000 W×3600s=3.6×10⁶ J

Electricity bills are calculated in kWh

(iii) Electric Power Transmission

Principle:

To reduce energy loss in long-distance transmission, electricity is sent at high voltage and low current using transformers.

Reason:

Power loss in transmission lines is:

Power loss=I²R

Lowering III greatly reduces the loss.

(iv) Heating Effects of Electric Current

Described by Joule’s Law:

The heat produced by a current I in a resistor R for time t is:

H=I²Rt

Applications:

Electric heaters

Electric cookers

Electric irons

Electric bulbs.

(v) Electrical Wiring of Houses

Types:

Radial system: Each circuit connected separately to the main supply.

Ring system: Wires form a loop with outlets along the way.

Components:

Live wire (brown or red) — carries current from the supply.

Neutral wire (blue or black) — completes the circuit.

Earth wire (green/yellow) — safety path to ground.

(vi) Use of Fuses

Fuse: A safety device made of a wire that melts when current exceeds a safe limit, breaking the circuit.

Prevents damage to appliances and risk of fire.

Circuit breakers serve a similar function but can be reset.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Magnets and Magnetic Fields
notes.body:
## MAGNETS AND MAGNETIC FIELDS

(i) Natural and Artificial Magnets

Natural magnets: Found in nature, e.g., lodestone (magnetite), which can attract iron.

Artificial magnets: Made from magnetic materials (e.g., steel) by magnetization.

(ii) Magnetic Properties of Soft Iron and Steel

Soft iron:

Easily magnetized and demagnetized.

Used for temporary magnets, electromagnet cores, transformer cores.

Steel:

Hard to magnetize but retains magnetism longer.

Used for permanent magnets, magnetic tools.

(iii) Methods of Making Magnets and Demagnetization

Making magnets:

Single-touch method: Stroking with one pole of a magnet.

Double-touch method: Stroking from the centre to the ends with opposite poles.

Electrical method: Passing current through a coil around the material. (fastest)

Demagnetization:

Heating above Curie temperature.

Hammering in random positions.

Using alternating current in a solenoid.

(iv) Concept of Magnetic Field

The region around a magnet where magnetic force can be felt.

Represented by magnetic field lines — always from north to south outside the magnet.

(v) Magnetic Field of a Permanent Magnet

Strongest at poles.

Field pattern can be shown by iron filings or a compass needle.

(vi) Magnetic Field Around Current-Carrying Conductors

Straight conductor: Circular field lines around it (right-hand grip rule).

Circular coil: Field is similar to a bar magnet’s field pattern.

Solenoid: Field inside is uniform, similar to that of a bar magnet.

(vii) Properties of the Earth’s Magnetic Field

Magnetic poles: North-seeking (N) and south-seeking (S) poles.

Magnetic meridian: Vertical plane containing magnetic axis.

Angle of dip: Angle between magnetic field and horizontal plane.

Angle of declination: Angle between magnetic meridian and geographic meridian.

(viii) Flux and Flux Density

Magnetic flux (ΦhiΦ): Total magnetic field passing through a surface (unit: Weber, Wb).

Flux density (B): Magnetic flux per unit area:

B = Φ / A

Unit: Tesla (T).

(ix) Variation of Magnetic Field Intensity Over the Earth’s Surface

Strongest near poles.

Weakest near the magnetic equator.

(x) Applications

Navigation: Magnetic compass for direction finding.

Mineral exploration: Detecting variations in Earth’s magnetic field caused by mineral deposits.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field
notes.body:
## FORCE ON A CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR IN A MAGNETIC FIELD

(i) Quantitative Treatment of Force Between Two Parallel Current-Carrying Conductors

When two parallel conductors carry currents:

Currents in same direction → conductors attract each other.

Currents in opposite direction → conductors repel each other.

Force per unit length between them:

F/L = (μ⁰×I×I)/2πd

where:

F = force (N)

L = length (m)

I, I = currents in conductors (A)

d = distance between conductors (m)

μ⁰ = 4π ×1 0−⁷H/m (permeability of free space)

(ii) Force on a Charge Moving in a Magnetic Field

A moving charge qqq with velocity vvv in a magnetic field BBB experiences a force:

F=qvBsin⁡θ

θ is the angle between velocity and magnetic field.

Direction given by Right-hand rule.

(iii) The D.C. Motor

Principle: Current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.

Parts: Armature, commutator, brushes, field magnets.

Operation:

Current flows through armature coils => force rotates coil.

Commutator reverses current every half turn => continuous rotation.

Use: Converts electrical energy to mechanical energy.

(iv) Electromagnets

Made by winding insulated wire around a soft iron core and passing current.

Advantages: Can be switched on/off, strength can be varied.

Uses: Lifting magnets, relays, electric bells, magnetic separation.

(v) Carbon Microphone

Principle: Sound waves vary the resistance of carbon granules.

Operation:

Diaphragm vibrates with sound → pressure on carbon granules changes.

Changes resistance → causes variation in current in the circuit.

Use: In telephones, sound recording.

(vi) Moving Coil and Moving Iron Instruments

Moving Coil:

Measures DC quantities.

Coil in magnetic field rotates in proportion to current.

Moving Iron:

Measures AC and DC quantities.

Soft iron piece moves in magnetic field generated by coil.

(vii) Conversion of Galvanometers

To Ammeter: Connect shunt resistor in parallel to bypass most current.

To Voltmeter: Connect multiplier resistor in series to limit current.

(viii) Sensitivity of a Galvanometer

Current sensitivity: Deflection per unit current.

Voltage sensitivity: Deflection per unit voltage.

Increased by:

Stronger magnetic field.

Lighter coil.

More turns in coil.

Lower suspension torque.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Electromagnetic Induction
notes.body:
## ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION

(i) Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction

First Law: An electromotive force (emf) is induced in a conductor whenever the magnetic flux linking it changes.

Second Law: The magnitude of the induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux:

emf = −N (Δt/ΔΦ​)

where:

N = number of turns in the coil

Φ = magnetic flux

Negative sign from Lenz’s law.

(ii) Factors Affecting Induced EMF

Speed or velocity of motion between conductor and magnetic field.

Strength of magnetic field.

Number of turns in coil.

Angle between conductor and magnetic field lines.

(iii) Lenz’s Law and Conservation of Energy

Lenz’s Law: The direction of induced current opposes the change that produces it.

This ensures conservation of energy: work done to move conductor is converted into electrical energy.

(iv) A.C. and D.C. Generators

Principle: Rotating coil in magnetic field induces emf.

AC Generator:

Slip rings used.

Output alternates direction (sinusoidal).

DC Generator:

Split-ring commutator used.

Output is unidirectional (pulsating).

(v) Transformers

Principle: Mutual induction.

Types:

Step-up: increases voltage, decreases current.

Step-down: decreases voltage, increases current.

Equation:

( Vp / Vs ) = ( Np / Ns )​​

where VpV_pVp​ and VsV_sVs​ are primary and secondary voltages.

Uses: Power transmission, electrical appliances.

(vi) Induction Coil

Device producing high voltage from low voltage DC using a transformer and interrupter.

Use: Ignition systems in petrol engines.

(b) Inductance

(i) Explanation of Inductance

Self-Inductance: Property of a coil to oppose change in current in itself.

Mutual Inductance: Induction of emf in one coil due to changing current in another coil.

(ii) Unit of Inductance

Henry (H): An inductor has inductance of 1 H if a current changing at 1 A/s induces emf of 1 V.

(iii) Energy Stored in an Inductor

E =½LI²

where:

L = inductance (H)

I = current (A)

(iv) Applications/Uses of Inductors

Filtering in power supplies.

Energy storage in magnetic field.

Tuning radio and TV circuits.

Chokes in fluorescent lamps.

35. (c) Eddy Current

(i) Reduction of Eddy Current

Laminating magnetic cores.

Using insulated sheets of iron.

Using ferrite cores.

(ii) Applications of Eddy Current

Induction heating.

Braking systems in trains.

Energy meters.

Magnetic damping in instruments.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Simple A. C. Circuits
notes.body:
## SIMPLE A.C. CIRCUITS

(i) Explanation of A.C. Current and Voltage

Alternating Current (A.C.): Current whose magnitude and direction vary periodically with time.

Alternating Voltage: Voltage that changes polarity and magnitude with time.

Usually follows a sinusoidal waveform:

I = I⁰sin⁡(ωt),

V = V⁰sin⁡(ωt)

where:

I⁰, V⁰  = peak current / voltage

ω = angular frequency (ω=2πf)

(ii) Peak and R.M.S. Values

Peak Value (I0I_0I0​, V0V_0V0​): Maximum value of current or voltage.

Root Mean Square (RMS) Value:

I rms = I⁰ / √2,

Vrms=V⁰ / √2

RMS value gives the equivalent DC value that would produce the same heating effect.

(iii) A.C. Source Connected to a Resistor

Current and voltage are in phase (no phase difference).

Ohm’s law applies:

I = V/R

(iv) A.C. Source Connected to a Capacitor — Capacitive Reactance

Capacitive Reactance (XC) is opposition offered by a capacitor to AC:

XC = 1/ωC = 1/(2πfC)

Current leads voltage by 90°

(v) A.C. Source Connected to an Inductor — Inductive Reactance

Inductive Reactance (XL​) is opposition offered by an inductor to AC:

XL = ωL = 2πfLX

Current lags voltage by 90°

(vi) Series R-L-C Circuits

Contains a Resistor (R), Inductor (L), and Capacitor (C) in series.

Impedance (Z):

## Z² = R² + (XL−XC)²

Current:

I = V / Z

(vii) Vector Diagram, Phase Angle, and Power Factor

Phase Angle (ϕ):

tan⁡ϕ = (XL−XC) / R

Power Factor:

p.f.=cos⁡ϕ

Power factor indicates efficiency of power usage.

(viii) Resistance and Impedance

Resistance (R): Opposition to current in a resistor (independent of frequency).

Impedance (Z): Total opposition to AC, combining resistance and reactance.

(ix) Effective Voltage in an R-L-C Circuit

Effective voltage is the RMS value of voltage across the combination:

V rms = I rms × Z

(x) Resonance and Resonance Frequency

Resonance occurs when:

## XL​=XC​

Impedance is minimum (Z = R) and current is maximum.

Resonance Frequency:

f⁰ = 1/(2π√[LC])

Used in tuning radio and TV receivers.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Conduction of Electricity
notes.body:
## CONDUCTION OF ELECTRICITY THROUGH

(a) Liquids

(i) Electrolytes and Non-Electrolytes

Electrolytes: Liquids that conduct electricity due to the movement of ions when dissolved in water or molten.

Examples: acids (H₂SO₄), bases (NaOH), salts (NaCl solution).

Non-Electrolytes: Liquids that do not conduct electricity because they have no free ions.

Examples: pure water, sugar solution, kerosene.

(ii) Concept of Electrolysis

Electrolysis: The chemical decomposition of an electrolyte by passing electric current through it.

Involves:

Anode: Positive electrode (attracts negative ions/anions).

Cathode: Negative electrode (attracts positive ions/cations).

(iii) Faraday’s Laws of Electrolysis

First Law: The mass (m) of substance liberated/deposited during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity (Q) passed:

m ∝ Q    ⇒   m  = ZIt

where Z = electrochemical equivalent, I = current, t = time.

Second Law: When the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses deposited are proportional to their chemical equivalents.

(iv) Applications of Electrolysis

Electroplating: Coating an object with a thin layer of metal to improve appearance or prevent corrosion.

Purification of metals: e.g., refining copper.

Extraction of metals: e.g., sodium from molten NaCl.

Calibration of ammeters: Using electrolysis to measure exact current by relating mass deposited to charge passed.

Production of chemicals: e.g., chlorine, hydrogen, sodium hydroxide.

(b) Gases

(i) Discharge Through Gases (Qualitative Treatment)

At low pressure and high voltage, gases become ionized and conduct electricity.

Ionization produces positive ions and free electrons.

Phenomena observed:

Glow discharge: Faint glow due to electron collisions.

Spark discharge: Sudden ionization causing a spark.

Corona discharge: Glow around a conductor due to partial ionization of surrounding gas.

(ii) Applications of Conduction of Electricity Through Gases

Fluorescent lamps and neon signs (glow discharge).

Spark plugs in engines (spark discharge).

Gas discharge tubes in voltage regulators.

X-ray tubes (electron acceleration in a vacuum).

Particle detectors (e.g., Geiger-Müller tube).

## CATHODE RAYS

Definition: Streams of fast-moving electrons emitted from the cathode in a vacuum tube when a high voltage is applied.

Production: Formed in a discharge tube at low pressure and high potential difference.

Properties:

Travel in straight lines in a vacuum.

Cast sharp shadows of objects placed in their path.

Cause certain materials to fluoresce.

Can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

Possess momentum and can turn a light paddle wheel.

Produce heat when striking a target.

Applications:

In Cathode Ray Tubes (CRT) for televisions and oscilloscopes.

In X-ray production (when striking a metal target).

In studying atomic structure.

## X-RAYS

Definition: High-energy electromagnetic waves with very short wavelengths, produced when high-speed electrons strike a heavy metal target.

Production: In an X-ray tube, cathode rays are accelerated and directed onto a metal target (e.g. tungsten).

Properties:

Travel in straight lines at the speed of light.

Highly penetrating (penetration depends on energy).

Cause fluorescence in certain substances.

Affect photographic plates.

Ionize gases.

Not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

Applications:

Medical imaging (radiography).

Detection of cracks in metals.

Security scanning at airports.

Cancer treatment (radiotherapy).

Hazards: Prolonged exposure can damage living tissues — use shielding (lead screens).

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Elementary Modern Physics
notes.body:
## ELEMENTARY MODERN PHYSICS

(i) Models of the Atom and Limitations

Dalton: Atom indivisible => failed to explain subatomic particles.

Thomson (Plum pudding): Electrons embedded in a positive sphere => failed to explain nucleus.

Rutherford: Small dense positively charged nucleus => failed to explain electron stability.

Bohr: Electrons in quantized orbits => worked for hydrogen but not complex atoms.

(ii) Elementary Structure of the Atom

Nucleus: Contains protons (+) and neutrons (neutral).
