Electrons: Negatively charged, in energy levels around the nucleus.

(iii) Energy Levels and Spectra

Electrons occupy discrete energy levels.

Movement between levels => emission or absorption of photons => produces line spectra.

(iv) Thermionic and Photoelectric Emissions

Thermionic: Emission of electrons from a heated metal.

Photoelectric: Emission of electrons when light of sufficient frequency falls on a surface.

(v) Einstein’s Photoelectric Equation

hf = ϕ + ½mv²

Where hf = photon energy,

ϕ = work function,

½mv² = max kinetic energy.

Stopping potential: Minimum p.d. to stop emitted electrons.

(vi) Applications

Thermionic emission: Cathode ray tubes, valves, electron microscopes.

Photoelectric effect: Light meters, automatic doors, solar panels.

(vii) Production of X-rays

High-speed electrons strike a heavy metal target in an X-ray tube → X-rays produced.

Types of X-rays

X-rays are classified based on their energy (wavelength) and method of production:

1. Soft X-rays

Low energy (longer wavelength, ≈ 10⁻⁸ m to 10⁻¹⁰ m).

Produced when electrons decelerate slightly in the target material.

Uses: Studying crystal structures, imaging soft tissues in medicine, detecting cracks in materials.

Limitation: Low penetration; easily absorbed.

2. Hard X-rays

High energy (shorter wavelength, ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m to 10⁻¹² m).

Produced when electrons strike the target at very high speed, causing strong deceleration.

Uses: Medical imaging of bones, security scanning, industrial radiography, cancer treatment.

Advantage: High penetration power.

3. Continuous (Bremsstrahlung) X-rays

Produced when high-speed electrons are decelerated by the nuclei of the target atoms.

Energy is spread over a range => continuous spectrum.

4. Characteristic X-rays

Produced when high-speed electrons knock out inner-shell electrons of target atoms, and higher-level electrons fall into the vacant shell.

Energy is fixed (characteristic of the target element) => sharp lines in the X-ray spectrum.

(viii) Properties and Applications of Alpha, Beta, Gamma Rays

Alpha (α): Helium nuclei, low penetration, high ionization → smoke detectors.

Beta (β): Electrons/positrons, medium penetration → thickness measurement.

Gamma (γ): High-energy photons, high penetration, low ionization → cancer treatment, sterilization.

(xiii) Half-Life and Decay Constant

Half-life (T₁/₂): Time for half of radioactive nuclei to decay.

Decay constant (λ): Probability of decay per unit time.

N = N⁰e−λt

(xiv) Nuclear Energy Production

Fission: Splitting of heavy nuclei (e.g. U-235) => nuclear reactors.

Fusion: Joining of light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen) => sun’s energy source.

(xv) Binding Energy & Mass Defect

Mass defect: Difference between mass of nucleus and sum of individual nucleons.

Binding energy: Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.

E = mc²

(xvi) Wave-Particle Duality

Matter (especially electrons) shows both wave and particle properties.

(xvii) Electron Diffraction

Electrons diffract when passed through crystals, confirming their wave nature.

(xviii) Uncertainty Principle

Heisenberg: Cannot simultaneously know exact position and momentum of a particle.

Δx⋅Δp ≥ h/4π

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Physics: Introductory Electronics
notes.body:
## INTRODUCTORY ELECTRONICS

(i) Distinction between Metals, Semiconductors, and Insulators

Metals: Have very small or no band gap; electrons flow easily => good conductors.

Example: Copper, Aluminium.

Semiconductors: Have a small band gap (~1 eV); conductivity can be increased by temperature or doping.

Example: Silicon, Germanium.

Insulators: Have a large band gap (>3 eV); electrons cannot move freely.

Example: Rubber, Glass.

(ii) Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors

Intrinsic: Pure semiconductor without impurities; conduction is due to electrons excited across the band gap.

Extrinsic: Semiconductor doped with impurities to improve conductivity.

n-type: Doped with pentavalent atoms (e.g. phosphorus) => more electrons as majority carriers.

p-type: Doped with trivalent atoms (e.g. boron) => more holes as majority carriers.

(iii) Uses of Semiconductors and Diodes in Rectification; Transistors in Amplification

Diodes: Allow current in one direction only → used in rectification (converting AC to DC).

Transistors: Used in amplification (increasing signal strength) and switching circuits.

(iv) n-type and p-type Semiconductors

n-type: Electrons = majority carriers; holes = minority carriers.

p-type: Holes = majority carriers; electrons = minority carriers.

(v) Elementary Knowledge of Diodes and Transistors

Diode: A two-terminal semiconductor device; conducts when forward-biased, blocks when reverse-biased.

Transistor: A three-terminal device (e.g. NPN or PNP) used for amplification and switching.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Separation of mixtures and purification of chemical substances
notes.body:
## SEPARATION TECHNIQUES

## COMMON CHEMISTRY LABORATORY APPARATUS AND THEIR FUNCTIONS:

Beaker – Holds, mixes, and heats liquids.

Test Tube – Used for small-scale reactions and heating substances.

Conical Flask (Erlenmeyer Flask) – Ideal for mixing and swirling liquids without spillage.

Measuring Cylinder – Measures the volume of liquids accurately.

Burette – Delivers variable, measured volumes of liquid accurately during titration.

Pipette – Transfers a fixed volume of liquid accurately.

Volumetric Flask – Prepares standard solutions with precise volume.

Funnel – Helps in transferring liquids and for filtration when used with filter paper.

Watch Glass – Holds small amounts of substances, often for evaporation or observation.

Evaporating Dish – Evaporates excess solvents, usually water, from a solution.

Crucible – Heats substances to very high temperatures.

Tripod Stand – Supports containers during heating.

Wire Gauze – Placed on a tripod to support beakers/flasks while heating evenly.

Bunsen Burner – Provides a flame for heating substances.

Test Tube Rack – Holds multiple test tubes upright.

Test Tube Holder – Holds a test tube while heating or handling.

Tongs – Picks up hot apparatus like crucibles.

Mortar and Pestle – Grinds solid chemicals into powder.

Spatula – Transfers small quantities of solid substances.

Dropper (Pasteur Pipette) – Transfers small drops of liquid.

Thermometer – Measures temperature.

Reagent Bottle – Stores chemicals, especially liquid reagents.

Distillation Flask – Used in distillation to separate mixtures based on boiling points.

Condenser – Cools and condenses vapors into liquid during distillation.

Separating Funnel – Separates immiscible liquids based on density differences.

Kipp’s Apparatus: To produce gas intermittently e.g. CO₂ and H₂ and hydrogen sulfide

Dessicator – To keep salt dry (to keep deliquescent or hygroscopic substances)

Liebig Condenser – Converts vapours into liquid.

Hoffman Voltameter – To determine volumetric compositions of water

Standard Volumetric flask: To prepare standard solutions

## SEPARATION OF MIXTURES AND PURIFICATION OF CHEMICAL SUBSTANCES

(a) Pure and Impure Substances:

Pure substances have fixed boiling and melting points and consist of only one type of particle (e.g., distilled water, NaCl).

Impure substances (mixtures) have variable composition and do not boil or melt sharply.

(b) Boiling and Melting Points:

Used to determine purity. Pure substances melt and boil at constant temperatures, while impurities cause deviation.

(c) Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures:

Element: A substance made of one type of atom (e.g., O₂).

Compound: A chemical combination of elements in fixed ratio (e.g., H₂O).

Mixture: A physical combination of two or more substances (e.g., air, saltwater).

(d) Chemical and Physical Changes:

Chemical change: New substances are formed (e.g., rusting, burning).

Physical change: No new substance is formed (e.g., melting, dissolving).

(e) Separation Processes:

Evaporation: Removes liquid from solution (e.g., salt from seawater).

Simple Distillation: Separates liquid from non-volatile solute or two liquids with large boiling point difference.

Fractional Distillation: Separates miscible liquids with close boiling points (e.g., ethanol and water).

Sublimation: Separates substances that sublime (e.g., iodine, ammonium chloride).

Filtration: Separates insoluble solids from liquids.

Crystallization: Purifies solid by forming crystals from solution.

Paper/Column Chromatography: Separates components based on solubility and adsorption.

Simple/Fractional Crystallization: Separates solid mixtures based on solubility differences.

Magnetization: Uses magnets to separate magnetic materials.

Decantation: Separates immiscible liquids or sediments from liquids by pouring.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Chemical combination
notes.body:
## CHEMICAL COMBINATION AND RELATED CONCEPTS

Stoichiometry

Involves the calculation of reactants and products in chemical reactions using balanced chemical equations.

Laws of Chemical Combination

Law of Definite Proportions: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed ratio by mass.

Law of Multiple Proportions: When two elements form more than one compound, the mass of one element that combines with a fixed mass of the other is in simple whole number ratios.

Law of Conservation of Matter: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.

Gay-Lussac’s Law of Combining Volumes: Gases react in simple whole number volume ratios under the same temperature and pressure.

Avogadro’s Law: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.

Chemical Symbols and Formulae

Symbols represent elements (e.g., H for hydrogen).

Formulae represent compounds and show the types and number of atoms (e.g., H₂O for water).

Chemical Equations

Show the reactants and products in a reaction. They must be balanced to obey the law of conservation of matter.

Relative Atomic Mass (RAM)

The average mass of an atom of an element compared to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

The Mole Concept and Avogadro’s Number

Mole is the SI unit for amount of substance.

Avogadro’s Number = 6.022×10²³ particles per mole.

Used to relate mass, number of particles, and volume of gases.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Kinetic theory of matter and Gas Laws
notes.body:
## KINETIC THEORY OF MATTER AND GAS LAWS

(a) Kinetic Theory of Matter

Basic Idea: All matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) in constant motion. The state (solid, liquid, or gas) depends on the energy and arrangement of these particles.

Changes of State (Explained by Molecular Motion):

Melting: Solid to liquid. Particles gain energy, vibrate faster, and overcome strong forces holding them in place.

Vapourization (includes boiling and evaporation): Liquid to gas. Particles gain enough energy to escape into the air.

Boiling: Rapid vapourization at the boiling point, occurring throughout the liquid.

Freezing: Liquid to solid. Particles lose energy and become fixed in position.

Condensation: Gas to liquid. Particles lose energy and move closer together.

Brownian Movement: Random movement of particles suspended in a fluid, showing the motion of molecules and supporting the kinetic theory.

(b) Gas Laws

(i) Basic Gas Laws:

Boyle’s Law:

𝑃 ∝1/𝑉

​

(at constant T). Pressure increases as volume decreases.

Charles’ Law:

V∝T (at constant P). Volume increases as temperature increases.

Graham’s Law of Diffusion: The rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass.

## T1R1√M1 = T2R2√M2

Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures: The total pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of individual gases.

P total = P1 + P2 + P3 + Pn

Other Gas Concepts:

Combined Gas Law:

(𝑃1𝑉1)/𝑇1 = (𝑃2𝑉2)/𝑇2

Molar Volume: Volume occupied by 1 mole of a gas at STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure) = 22.4 dm³.

Atomicity of Gases: Number of atoms in one molecule of a gas (e.g., O₂ is diatomic, atomicity = 2).

(ii) Ideal Gas Equation:

PV=nRT

Where:

P = pressure,

V = volume,

n = number of moles,

R = gas constant (8.314 Jmol⁻¹K⁻¹),

T = temperature in Kelvin.

(iii) Vapour Density and Relative Molecular Mass:

Vapour Density (VD) is half the Relative Molecular Mass (Mr):

𝑀𝑟 = 2 × Vapour Density

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Atomic structure and bonding
notes.body:
## ATOMIC STRUCTURE AND BONDING

(a) Concepts and Atomic Structure

(i) Atoms, Molecules, and Ions

Atoms: Smallest particle of elements that can take part in chemical reaction

Molecules: Two or more atoms bonded together (e.g., O₂, H₂O).

Ions: Charged species formed by loss (cation) or gain (anion) of electrons.

Key Scientists and Their Contributions:

Dalton: Proposed the first atomic theory — atoms are indivisible and combine in simple ratios.

Thomson: Discovered the electron; proposed the “plum pudding” model.

Rutherford: Discovered the nucleus and proposed a nuclear model of the atom.

Millikan: Measured the charge of the electron via the oil-drop experiment.

Moseley: Showed that atomic number (not mass) determines element identity.

Bohr: Proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels.

(ii) Atomic Structure, Electron Configuration, Atomic and Mass Numbers, Isotopes

Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons in the nucleus (e.g., Hydrogen = 1).

Mass Number (A): Total number of protons + neutrons.

Isotopes: Atoms with the same Z but different A (e.g., ¹²C and ¹⁴C).

Electron Configuration (Z = 1–20):

H (Z = 1): 1s¹

He (Z = 2): 1s²

Na (Z = 11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹

Ca (Z = 20): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²

(iii) Orbital Shapes

s-orbitals: Spherical.

p-orbitals: Dumbbell-shaped (x, y, z directions).

(b) Periodic Table and Periodicity

Arranged in increasing atomic number.

Elements grouped into:

Alkali metals (Group 1): e.g., Na, K

Halogens (Group 17): e.g., Cl, F

Noble gases (Group 18): e.g., Ne, Ar

Transition metals: d-block elements e.g., Fe, Cu

Periodic Trends:

Ionization Energy: Increases across a period, decreases down a group.

Ionic Radii: Decreases across a period, increases down a group.

Electron Affinity: Generally increases across a period.

Electronegativity: Increases across a period, decreases down a group.

(c) Chemical Bonding

Electrovalent (Ionic) Bonding: Complete transfer of electrons (e.g., NaCl).

Covalent Bonding: Sharing of electrons (e.g., H₂O, Cl₂).

Metallic Bonding: Delocalized electrons shared among metal atoms (e.g., Cu).

Hydrogen Bonding: Weak bond between H and electronegative atoms (e.g., in H₂O).

Coordinate (Dative) Bonding: Both electrons in a shared pair come from one atom (e.g., NH₄⁺).

Bonding is influenced by electron configuration, as atoms tend to attain the noble gas configuration (octet/duplet rule).

Atoms bond to attain noble gas configuration (stable octet/duplet).

(d) Shapes of Simple Molecules

Linear: H₂, O₂, Cl₂, HCl, CO₂

Non-linear (Bent): H₂O

Tetrahedral: CH₄

Pyramidal: NH₃

(e) Nuclear Chemistry

(i) Radioactivity

Radioactivity: Spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei.

Types of Radiation:

Alpha (α): Helium nuclei, low penetration, +2 charge.

Beta (β): High-speed electrons, more penetrating than alpha, -1 charge.

Gamma (γ): Electromagnetic radiation, highly penetrating, no charge/mass.

Alpha (α): He nuclei; heavy and slow.

Beta (β): High-speed electrons; lighter than alpha.

Gamma (γ): High-energy electromagnetic waves; no mass or charge.

(ii) Nuclear Reactions

Involve changes in the atomic nucleus (e.g., nuclear fission and fusion).

Represented by nuclear equations:

¹⁴C6 ---> ¹⁴N7 + β −

Applications:

Medical diagnosis and treatment (e.g., cancer therapy),

Carbon dating,

Energy production in nuclear reactors.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Air
notes.body:
🌬️💨 AIR  💨🌬️

(a) Natural Gaseous Constituents and Their Proportions

📌 Air is a mixture of gases, primarily composed of:

🚀Gas Approximate Percentage by Volume

Nitrogen (N₂) = 78%

Oxygen (O₂) =  21%

Argon (Ar)  = 0.93%

Carbon(IV) oxide (CO₂) = 0.03%

Water vapour (H₂O) Varies = (0.1 – 4%) depending on weather

Other noble gases (e.g., Neon) Trace amounts

🎯 Nitrogen: Inert; dilutes oxygen to prevent rapid combustion.

Oxygen: Supports respiration and combustion.

Water Vapour: Regulates weather and humidity.

Carbon(IV) Oxide: Used by plants during photosynthesis.

Noble Gases: Present in trace amounts (e.g., argon, neon).

(b) Air as a Mixture and Uses of Noble Gases

Why Air is a Mixture:

Its components retain individual properties.

Gases can be physically separated (e.g., by fractional distillation of liquid air).

No fixed composition — varies slightly with location and conditions.

Uses of Noble Gases:

Helium Filling balloons, cooling superconductors, and deep-sea diving mixtures.

Neon Neon signs (advertising lights).

Argon Filling electric bulbs, welding (prevents oxidation).

Krypton/Xenon High-intensity lamps, laser technology.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Water
notes.body:
## WATER AND INTERACTION OF SUBSTANCES WITH ATMOSPHERE

(a) Water as a Product of Hydrogen Combustion and Its Composition by Volume

Water is formed when hydrogen burns in oxygen:

2𝐻2(𝑔) + 𝑂2(𝑔) ––> 2𝐻2𝑂(𝑙)

Composition by volume:

Hydrogen: 2 parts

Oxygen: 1 part

Hence, water is 2:1 by volume of H₂ to O₂

(b) Water as a Solvent and Dissolved Atmospheric Gases

Water is a universal solvent: it dissolves many substances, especially salts and gases.

Atmospheric gases dissolved in water:

Oxygen (O₂): Used by aquatic animals for respiration.

Carbon(IV) oxide (CO₂): Used by aquatic plants for photosynthesis; helps maintain pH by forming carbonic acid.

Nitrogen (N₂): Mostly inert, but small amounts help in nitrogen cycle.

Biological significance:

Sustains aquatic life.

Enables nutrient transport in organisms.

Medium for biochemical reactions.

(c) Hard and Soft Water

Soft water: Easily lathers with soap (no dissolved calcium or magnesium salts).

Hard water: Does not lather easily due to dissolved Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺ ions.

Types of Hardness:

Temporary hardness: Caused by bicarbonates (e.g., Ca(HCO₃)₂); removed by boiling.

Permanent hardness: Caused by chlorides and sulfates (e.g., CaSO₄); not removed by boiling.

Methods of Softening Hard Water:

Boiling – removes temporary hardness.

Addition of washing soda (Na₂CO₃) – removes both types.

Ion-exchange resins – replace Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ with Na⁺.

Distillation – removes all dissolved solids (most expensive).

(d) Treatment of Water for Town Supply

Steps in water treatment:

Screening – removes large debris.

Sedimentation – allows particles to settle.

Coagulation and Flocculation – chemicals like alum added to clump fine particles.

Filtration – removes suspended impurities.

Chlorination – kills germs using chlorine.

Storage and Distribution – for use in homes and industries.

(e) Water of Crystallization, Efflorescence, Deliquescence, and Hygroscopy

Water of Crystallization : Fixed water molecules chemically bound in a salt’s crystal structure. CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol) Gives crystals their shape and colour.

Efflorescence Loss of water of crystallization on exposure to air. Na₂CO₃·10H₂O Appears powdery when exposed to air.

Deliquescence Absorbs moisture from air and dissolves in it. CaCl₂, NaOH pellets Used as drying agents (desiccants).

Hygroscopy Absorbs moisture but does not dissolve. CuO, conc. H₂SO₄ Used in drying gases.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Solubility
notes.body:
## SOLUBILITY

(a) Unsaturated, Saturated and Supersaturated Solutions:

Unsaturated Solution: A solution that can dissolve more solute at a given temperature.

Saturated Solution: A solution that holds the maximum amount of solute at a given temperature.

Supersaturated Solution: Contains more solute than the saturated solution at the same temperature, usually unstable.

Solubility: The amount of solute (in moles) that can dissolve in 1 dm³ of solvent at a specific temperature to form a saturated solution.

Unit: mol/dm³

Solubility Curves: Graphs showing how solubility changes with temperature.

Deductions:

Increase in temperature generally increases solubility of solids.

Comparing solubilities of different substances at a specific temperature.

Determining if a solution is saturated, unsaturated, or supersaturated.

Simple Calculations: Finding solubility from given mass or moles of solute and volume of solvent.

(b) Solvents for Fats, Oil and Paints:

Common Solvents:

Fats & Oils: Alcohol, ether, benzene.

Paints: Turpentine, acetone, kerosene.

Use: These solvents help in removing stains of oil, grease, paint, etc., from clothes, surfaces, or skin.

(c) False Solutions (Suspensions and Colloids):

Suspensions: Mixtures where solid particles are visible and settle on standing.

Examples: Harmattan haze, water paint.

Colloids: Intermediate between true solutions and suspensions; particles do not settle.

Properties: Scatters light (Tyndall effect), stable, cannot be filtered.

Examples:

Fog (liquid in gas)

Milk (liquid in liquid – emulsion)

Aerosol spray (solid/liquid in gas)

Emulsion paints

Rubber solution

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Environmental Pollution
notes.body:
## ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION

Environmental Pollution

Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances (called pollutants) into the environment, causing adverse changes to air, water, or soil. Pollution harms living organisms and disturbs natural processes.

(a) Sources and Effects of Pollutants

Sources of pollutants include:

Industrial activities (factories releasing chemicals and smoke)

Vehicle emissions

Domestic waste (refuse, sewage)

Agricultural activities (use of fertilizers, pesticides)

Oil spillage and mining

Effects of pollutants:

Harm to human health (e.g. respiratory problems, cancers)

Damage to ecosystems (killing of aquatic life, destruction of plants)

Acid rain formation

Ozone layer depletion

Global warming and climate change

(b) Air Pollution

Air pollution occurs when harmful gases and particles are released into the atmosphere.

Examples of air pollutants and their effects:

Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) – Has a foul smell and is toxic; it affects the respiratory system.

Carbon monoxide (CO) – A colorless, odorless gas that interferes with oxygen transport in the blood.

Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) – Causes acid rain, which corrodes buildings and harms plant life.

Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO₂) – Also contribute to acid rain and photochemical smog.

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) – Cause depletion of the ozone layer, increasing UV radiation.

Dust and particulate matter – Can cause lung diseases and reduce visibility.

(c) Water Pollution

Water pollution results from the discharge of harmful substances into water bodies like rivers, lakes, and oceans.

Examples of water pollutants:

Sewage – Contains harmful microorganisms that cause waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

Oil pollution – Comes from oil spills and leaks; it coats aquatic animals and plants, suffocating them.

Industrial waste – Often contains heavy metals and toxic chemicals.

Fertilizers and pesticides – Lead to eutrophication, where excess nutrients cause algae overgrowth and oxygen depletion.

(d) Soil Pollution

Soil pollution occurs when the soil is contaminated with harmful substances.

Sources and examples:

Oil spillage – Destroys soil structure, reducing fertility and killing soil organisms.

Biodegradable pollutants – Can be broken down by natural processes. Examples: food waste, paper, human excreta.

Non-biodegradable pollutants – Cannot be easily broken down and remain in the environment for a long time. Examples: plastics, glass, polythene bags, metals.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Acids, bases and salts
notes.body:
(a) General Characteristics and Properties

Acids

Definition: An acid is a substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions (hydronium ions) or acts as a proton (H⁺) donor.

Properties:

Sour taste

Turns blue litmus paper red

Reacts with metals to produce hydrogen gas

Reacts with bases to form salts and water (neutralization)

Examples:

Strong acids: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃

Weak acids: CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid), H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid)

Naturally occurring organic acids:

Ethanoic acid – in vinegar

Citric acid – in citrus fruits

Tartaric acid – in grapes and tamarind

Bases

Definition: A base is a substance that furnishes OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution or accepts protons.

Properties:

Bitter taste and slippery feel

Turns red litmus paper blue

Neutralizes acids

Examples:

Strong bases: NaOH, KOH

Weak bases: NH₄OH, Ca(OH)₂

Salts

Definition: Compounds formed when the hydrogen ion of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

Types:

Normal salts – all replaceable H⁺ ions are substituted. (e.g. NaCl, KNO₃)

Acid salts – contain replaceable H⁺ ions. (e.g. NaHSO₄, NaHCO₃)

Basic salts – contain replaceable OH⁻ or O²⁻. (e.g. Zn(OH)Cl)

Double salts – contain two different cations. (e.g. Alums like KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O)

Acid/Base Indicators

Used to detect the presence of an acid or base by a color change.

Indicator In Acid In Base

Litmus Red Blue

Methyl orange Red Yellow

Phenolphthalein Colorless Pink

Preparation of Salts

Neutralization: Acid + Base → Salt + Water

E.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

Precipitation: Mixing solutions to form an insoluble salt

E.g. BaCl₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2HCl

Action of Acids on Metals:

E.g. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑

Oxides and Trioxocarbonate(IV) Salts

Metal oxides (e.g., Na₂O, CaO) are basic.

Non-metal oxides (e.g., CO₂, SO₂) are acidic.

Trioxocarbonates(IV) are salts of carbonic acid.

E.g. Na₂CO₃, CaCO₃

(b) Conductance of Acids and Bases

Strong acids/bases: Ionize completely → high conductance

Examples: HCl, NaOH

Weak acids/bases: Ionize partially → low conductance

Examples: CH₃COOH, NH₄OH

Conductance is directly related to the number of ions present in solution.

(c) pH and pOH Scale

pH = –log[H⁺] → Measures acidity

pOH = –log[OH⁻] → Measures alkalinity

pH + pOH = 14 (at 25°C)

pH Value Nature

0 – 6 Acidic

7 Neutral

8 – 14 Basic/Alkaline

Example Calculation:

If [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, then

pH = –log(10⁻³) = 3

(d) Acid/Base Titrations

Titrations determine the concentration of an unknown solution using a standard solution.

Common pairs:

Strong acid vs strong base: HCl vs NaOH

Weak acid vs strong base: CH₃COOH vs NaOH

Indicators used:

Phenolphthalein (for strong base)

Methyl orange (for strong acid)

(e) Hydrolysis of Salts

Hydrolysis is the reaction of salt with water to form an acidic or basic solution.

Examples:

NH₄Cl (Ammonium chloride) – Weak base + strong acid → Acidic solution

AlCl₃ (Aluminium chloride) – Weak base + strong acid → Acidic solution

Na₂CO₃ (Sodium carbonate) – Strong base + weak acid → Basic solution

CH₃COONa (Sodium ethanoate) – Strong base + weak acid → Basic solution

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Oxidation and reduction
notes.body:
Oxidation and Reduction

(a) Oxidation (Addition of Oxygen / Removal of Hydrogen)

Oxidation: A chemical process in which oxygen is added to a substance or hydrogen is removed.

Example:

2𝑀𝑔+ 𝑂2 ===> 2MgO (Magnesium oxidized to magnesium oxide)

𝐻2S ===> 2H+ + S- (Hydrogen removed from hydrogen sulphide).

(b) Reduction (Removal of Oxygen / Addition of Hydrogen)

Reduction: A process in which oxygen is removed from a substance or hydrogen is added.

Example:

𝐶𝑢𝑂 + 𝐻2 ===>𝐶𝑢+ + 𝐻2𝑂  (Oxygen removed from copper(II) oxide)

## N2 +3H2 ===> 2NH3

​

(Hydrogen added to nitrogen).

(c) Electron Transfer Definition

Oxidation: Loss of electrons (LEO – Loss of Electrons is Oxidation).

Reduction: Gain of electrons (GER – Gain of Electrons is Reduction).

Example:

𝑁𝑎 ===> Na+ + e−  (Oxidation)

𝐶𝑙2 +2e− ===> 2Cl−  (Reduction).

(d) Use of Oxidation Numbers

Oxidation Number: The apparent charge on an atom in a compound or ion.

Oxidation: Increase in oxidation number.

Reduction: Decrease in oxidation number.

Balancing Equations: Adjust oxidation and reduction half-reactions so total electrons lost = electrons gained.

(e) IUPAC Nomenclature Using Oxidation Number

Oxidation number written in Roman numerals after the element.

Examples:

FeCl2 (Iron(II) chloride).

FeCl3 (Iron(III) chloride).

𝐶𝑢2O (Copper(I) oxide).

𝐶𝑢𝑂 (Copper(II) oxide).

(f) Tests for Oxidizing and Reducing Agents

Oxidizing Agents: Substances that cause oxidation by accepting electrons (reduced themselves).

Examples:

𝐾𝑀𝑛𝑂4 , 𝐾𝐾2𝐶𝑟2𝑂7 , 𝐶𝑙2 , 𝑂3.

Reducing Agents: Substances that cause reduction by donating electrons (oxidized themselves).

Examples:

𝐻2𝑆 , 𝑆𝑂2 , metals like Zn and Fe.

Test: Decolourises acidified KMnO4 or turns acidified 𝐾2𝐶𝑟2𝑂7 from orange to green.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Electrolysis
notes.body:
ELECTROLYSIS write more on type of cell with their electrolyte, diff betw electrolytic and electrochemical, ECS

Definition: The chemical decomposition of a substance (electrolyte) by passing an electric current through its molten form or aqueous solution.

(a) Electrolytes and Non-Electrolytes

Electrolytes: Substances that conduct electricity in molten or aqueous form, undergoing chemical decomposition.

Examples: NaCl solution, H₂SO₄, CuSO₄.

Non-Electrolytes: Substances that do not conduct electricity in solution or molten state.

Examples: Sugar solution, petrol.

Faraday’s Laws of Electrolysis:

First Law: The mass of substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.

m=ZIt

where m= mass, Z = electrochemical equivalent, I = current, t = time.

Second Law: When the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses deposited are proportional to their chemical equivalent masses.

(b) Electrolysis Examples

(i) Selected Electrolysis Reactions:

Dilute H₂SO₄:

Anode (+): 4OH- ===> O2 + 2H2O + 4e−

Cathode (-): 2H+ + 2e- ===> H2

Aqueous CuSO₄ (with inert electrodes):

Anode: 4OH- ===> O2 + 2H2O + 4e−

Cathode: Cu²+ + 2e- ===> Cu

Aqueous CuCl₂:

Anode: 2Cl− ===> Cl2 + 2e−

Cathode: Cu²+ + 2e− ===> Cu

Dilute NaCl:

Products: Hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode.

Concentrated NaCl (brine):

Products: Hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode, NaOH in solution.

Fused NaCl:

Anode: 2Cl− ===> Cl2 + 2e−

Cathode: Na+ + e− ===> Na

(ii) Factors Affecting Discharge of Ions:

Position in electrochemical series (cations lower down discharge more easily; anions with lower discharge potential are preferred).

Concentration of ions.

Nature of electrode (inert or active).

(c) Uses of Electrolysis

Purification of metals: e.g., copper.

Extraction/production of elements:

Aluminium from bauxite (Al2O3​)

Sodium from fused NaCl

Chlorine and NaOH from brine

Oxygen from water electrolysis.

Electroplating: Coating metals for protection or decoration.

(d) Electrochemical Cells

Devices producing electricity from redox reactions.

Redox Series (in order of decreasing reactivity):

K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au.

Half-Cell Reactions: Oxidation at anode, reduction at cathode.

Electrode Potentials: Quantitative measure of tendency to gain/lose electrons.

Simple calculations: E cell = E cathode − E anode

(e) Corrosion and Prevention

Corrosion: Gradual destruction of metals (e.g., rusting of iron) by environmental reactions; an electrolytic process involving oxygen and water.

Prevention:

Cathodic protection: Connecting to a more reactive metal (sacrificial anode).

Painting, electroplating, greasing/oiling to block moisture and air.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Energy changes
notes.body:
## ENERGY CHANGE

(a) Enthalpy Changes (ΔH) in Physical and Chemical Processes

Enthalpy Change (ΔH): Heat absorbed or released during a process at constant pressure.

Exothermic Reactions (ΔH < 0): Heat is released; temperature of surroundings increases.

Examples:

Dissolution of NaOH in water

Reaction of Na or K with water

Combustion of fuels.

Endothermic Reactions (ΔH > 0): Heat is absorbed; temperature of surroundings decreases.

Examples:

Dissolution of NH₄Cl in water

Thermal decomposition of CaCO₃.

Illustrations:

Na + H₂O  violent exothermic reaction producing NaOH and H₂.

NH₄Cl + H₂O  absorbs heat, solution feels cold.

(b) Entropy (S) – Order/Disorder Concept

Entropy: Measure of disorder or randomness in a system.

High Entropy: Greater disorder (e.g., gases, solutions).

Low Entropy: Greater order (e.g., solids).

Examples:

Mixing of gases: Entropy increases.

Dissolution of salts (e.g., NaCl in water): Solids become dispersed as ions; entropy increases.

(c) Spontaneity of Reactions and Gibbs Free Energy

Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG): Predicts spontaneity of a reaction.

## ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

where T = temperature in kelvin.

Criteria:

ΔG < 0  Spontaneous reaction (occurs naturally).

ΔG > 0  Non-spontaneous reaction.

ΔG = 0  System at equilibrium.

Examples:

Rusting of iron (ΔG < 0) – spontaneous.

Electrolysis of water (ΔG > 0) – requires external energy.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Rates of Chemical Reaction
notes.body:
## RATES OF CHEMICAL REACTION

Definition: The speed at which reactants are converted to products, usually measured by the change in concentration of a substance per unit time.

(a) Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction

(i) Temperature

Increasing temperature increases particle kinetic energy → more frequent and energetic collisions.

Examples:

Reaction between HCl and Na₂S₂O₃ occurs faster at higher temperatures.

Reaction between Mg and HCl releases H₂ faster when heated.

(ii) Concentration (or Pressure for gases)

Higher concentration = more particles in a given volume → higher collision frequency.

Examples:

HCl + Na₂S₂O₃ reaction becomes faster with more concentrated acid.

HCl + marble chips reaction speeds up with higher acid concentration.

Iodine clock reaction time decreases with higher reactant concentration.

For gases, higher pressure increases effective concentration.

(iii) Surface Area

Greater surface area = more exposed particles and faster reaction.

Example:

Marble powder reacts with HCl much faster than marble lumps of the same mass.

(iv) Catalyst

Speeds up reaction without being consumed by lowering activation energy.

Examples:

Decomposition of H₂O₂ is faster with MnO₂.

*V2O5 in contact process to produce H2SO4

* Impregnated iron catalyst ( Fe + Al2O3) in haber process to produce Ammonia

KClO₃ decomposes more rapidly with MnO₂.

* Pt, Rh, Ni and Pa for cracking

* Nickel for the hydrogenation of oil to form margarine

(b) Reaction Rate Curves

Graph of concentration or volume of product vs. time.

Steeper slope = faster reaction rate.

Rate decreases as reactants are used up.

(c) Activation Energy (Eₐ)

Minimum energy required for particles to react.

Arrhenius’ Law:

k=Ae−Ea/RT where Ink and InA are the intercept on y and x axis respectfully

where k = rate constant, A = frequency factor, R = gas constant, T = temperature (K).

Increasing temperature or adding a catalyst lowers Eₐ, increasing reaction rate.

Collision Theory

Reaction rate depends on:

Frequency of collisions.

Proper orientation of particles.

Sufficient energy (≥ Eₐ) during collisions.

Effect of Light on Reactions

Some reactions are photochemical (initiated or accelerated by light).

Example: Halogenation of alkanes (e.g., CH₄ + Cl₂) proceeds faster under UV light.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Chemical equilibrium
notes.body:
## CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM

Reversible Reactions

Definition: Reactions that occur in both forward and backward directions under the same conditions.

## A+B⇌C+D

Examples:

Action of steam on iron:

3Fe + 4H2O(g)⇌Fe3O4 + 4H2

Dissociation of nitrogen(IV) oxide:

N2O4(g)⇌2NO2(g)

Dynamic Equilibrium

State in a reversible reaction where forward and backward reaction rates are equal.

Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but not zero).

Factors Governing Equilibrium Position (Le Chatelier’s Principle)

Principle: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that opposes the disturbance.

Change in Concentration

Increasing reactants shifts equilibrium to products (forward direction).

Increasing products shifts it backward.

Change in Temperature

Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction.

Decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction.

Example: N2O4⇌2NO2

Change in Pressure (for gases)

Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas.

Decreasing pressure favours the side with more moles.

Catalyst

Speeds up both forward and backward reactions equally.

No effect on equilibrium position—only helps it reach equilibrium faster.

Equilibrium Constant (K)

Expression relating concentrations of products and reactants at equilibrium.

For aA+bB⇌cC+dD

K=[C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b

K is constant at a given temperature; changes only when temperature changes.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Non-metals and their compounds
notes.body:
## NON-METALS AND THEIR COMPOUNDS

(a) Hydrogen

Commercial Production:

From water gas (CO + H₂) via water-gas shift reaction.

From cracking petroleum fractions.

Laboratory Preparation:

Reaction of metals (e.g., Zn) with dilute acids.

HNO3 does not produce hydrogen gas but H20

Metals below hydrogen does not displace hydrogen in an acid

Zn + H2SO4 ==> ZnSO4 + H2

Properties: Colourless, odourless, insoluble in water, lightest gas, burns with a pale blue flame.

Uses: Ammonia production, hydrogenation of oils, oxy-hydrogen flame, rocket fuel.

Test: Burns with a ‘pop’ sound.

(b) Halogens – Chlorine as Example

Laboratory Preparation: MnO₂ + conc. HCl ==> Cl₂.

Industrial Production: Electrolysis of brine.

Properties: Greenish-yellow gas, pungent smell, soluble in water, turn litmus red then bleach it strong oxidizing agent.

Chlorine bleach by oxidation while SO2 bleach by reduction

Uses: Water sterilization, bleaching, manufacture of HCl, plastics (PVC), insecticides.

Hydrogen Chloride (HCl): Prepared by heating NaCl with conc. H₂SO₄; dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid.

Chlorides: Test with AgNO₃ – white precipitate of AgCl.

(c) Oxygen and Sulphur

Oxygen

Lab Preparation: Thermal decomposition of KClO₃ with MnO₂ catalyst.

Commercial Production: Fractional distillation of liquid air.

Uses: Respiration, welding, steelmaking.

Oxides:

Acidic (SO₂), Basic (Na₂O), Amphoteric (Al₂O₃), Neutral (CO).

Ozone (O₃): Allotrope of oxygen; protects Earth from UV radiation.

Sulphur

Uses: Manufacture of H₂SO₄, vulcanization of rubber, fungicides.

SO₂: Prepared by burning sulphur in air; reacts with alkalis to form sulphites.

H₂SO₃ and salts: Acids decompose salts to release SO₂ gas.

H₂SO₄ (Conc.):

Preparation: Contact process (SO₂ => SO₃ => H₂SO₄).

Properties: Dilute – strong acid; Conc. – oxidizing & dehydrating agent.

Uses: Fertilizers, detergents, battery acid.

H₂S: Prepared from FeS + acid; weak acid, strong reducing agent, forms metal sulphide precipitates.

Test for S²⁻: Pb²⁺ or other heavy metal ions give coloured precipitates.

(d) Nitrogen

Nitrogen Gas

Lab Preparation: From heating NH₄Cl + NaNO₂.

Commercial: Fractional distillation of liquid air.

Ammonia (NH₃)

Lab: Heating NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂.

Industrial: Haber Process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Fe catalyst).

Uses: Fertilizers, cleaning agents, explosives.

Test for NH₄⁺: Warm with alkali – NH₃ evolved turns red litmus blue.

Oxidation: NH₃ => NO => NO₂ => HNO₃.

HNO₃

Lab: From NaNO₃ + H₂SO₄.

Uses: Explosives, fertilizers, dyes.

Nitrates: On heating, give NO₂, O₂, or nitrites depending on metal.

Test for NO₃⁻: Brown ring test.

Oxides of Nitrogen: NO, NO₂ – acidic, contribute to acid rain.

Nitrogen Cycle: Movement of nitrogen through atmosphere, soil, and living organisms.

(e) Carbon

Allotropes:

Diamond – hard, non-conductor; cutting tools.

Graphite – conductor; lubricants, electrodes.

Amorphous – charcoal, coke.

The purest form of charcoal is sugar charcoal obtained by dehydrating sugar using conc H2SO4

CO₂

Lab: CaCO₃ + acid → CO₂.

Uses: Fire extinguishers, refrigeration, fizzy drinks.

Test: Turns limewater milky.

Thermal Decomposition: Carbonates → oxides + CO₂.

CO

Lab: Dehydration of formic acid over conc. H₂SO₄.

Properties: Colourless, odourless, poisonous (forms carboxyhaemoglobin).

Sources: Incomplete combustion (charcoal fires, exhaust fumes).

Coal: Anthracite, bituminous, lignite, peat.

Products from Destructive Distillation: Coke, coal tar, ammonia liquor, coal gas.

Coke: Carbon-rich fuel; used in steelmaking, as reducing agent.

Synthetic Gas (Water Gas): CO + H₂; used as fuel and in chemical synthesis.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Metals and their compounds
notes.body:
## METALS AND THEIR COMPOUNDS

(a) General Properties of Metals

Good conductors of heat and electricity.

Malleable and ductile.

Lustrous and sonorous.

Form basic oxides and positive ions in reactions.

(b) Alkali Metals – Sodium

(i) Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH)

Production: Electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution).

Reactions:

Precipitates hydroxides from solutions of Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, Pb²⁺.

Uses: Soap making, paper manufacture, water treatment.

(ii) Sodium Trioxocarbonate(IV) (Na₂CO₃) & Sodium Hydrogen Trioxocarbonate(IV) (NaHCO₃)

Production: Solvay process.

Uses:

Na₂CO₃ in glass manufacture, detergents.

NaHCO₃ in baking powder, fire extinguishers.

(iii) Sodium Chloride (NaCl)

Occurrence: Abundant in sea water.

Economic importance of sea water: Source of NaCl, Mg, Br₂, fishery.

Uses: Food seasoning, raw material for chemicals.

(c) Alkaline-Earth Metals – Calcium

Compounds:

Calcium Oxide (CaO): Produced from heating sea shells; used in cement manufacture.

Calcium Hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂): Used in neutralizing acids, making mortar.

Calcium Trioxocarbonate(IV) (CaCO₃): Raw material in cement, glass manufacture.

Test for Ca²⁺: Brick-red flame test.

(d) Aluminium

Extraction: Purification of bauxite and electrolytic reduction (Hall-Héroult process).

Properties: Light, strong, corrosion-resistant.

Uses: Aircraft, cooking utensils, cables.

Test for Al³⁺: White gelatinous precipitate with NaOH, soluble in excess.

(e) Tin

Extraction: From cassiterite (SnO₂) by reduction.

Uses: Plating, alloys (bronze, solder).

(f) First Transition Series Metals

Properties:

Variable oxidation states.

Formation of coloured ions.

Formation of complex ions.

Act as catalysts.

Partially filled d-orbitals in electron configuration.

(g) Iron

Extraction: From haematite (Fe₂O₃) or FeS ores in blast furnace.

Forms:

Wrought iron (pure, malleable).

Cast iron (hard, brittle).

Steel (strong, less corrosive than iron).

Test:

Fe²⁺ – Green precipitate with NaOH.

Fe³⁺ – Brown precipitate with NaOH.

(h) Copper

Extraction: From sulphide ores (CuFeS₂) or oxide ores by roasting and reduction.

Uses: Electrical wires, coins, alloys.

Preparation: CuSO₄ from copper + H₂SO₄.

Test: Blue precipitate with NaOH.

(i) Alloys (Constituents & Uses)

Steel: Iron + carbon – Construction.

Stainless steel: Fe + Cr + Ni – Cutlery, surgical tools.

Brass: Cu + Zn – Musical instruments.

Bronze: Cu + Sn – Medals, statues.

Type metal: Pb + Sb + Sn – Printing.

Duralumin: Al + Cu + Mg + Mn – Aircraft.

Soft solder: Pb + Sn – Joining metals.

Permalloy: Ni + Fe – Magnetic cores.

Alnico: Al + Ni + Co + Fe – Permanent magnets.

Extraction Details of Selected Metals

Aluminium (Al)

¶ Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O)

¶ Hall–Héroult Cell

¶ Electrolysis of molten alumina

¶ Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) to lower melting point and increase conductivity

¶ Carbon (graphite)Carbon (graphite) anode and cathode.

¶ Molten aluminium Al2O3.

¶ Bayer process purify the ore

Tin (Sn)Cassiterite (SnO₂)

¶ Furnace smelting

¶ Reduction

¶ Carbon (as coke) used as reducing agent—

¶ (not electrolytic)— Reduction

¶ Molten tin (collected at bottom of furnace)CO₂ from carbon combustion

Iron (Fe)

¶ Haematite (Fe₂O₃) or Magnetite (Fe₃O₄)

¶ Blast Furnace

¶ Reduction

¶ Limestone (CaCO₃) to remove impurities as slag— (Slag = CaSiO3)

¶ Reduction (not electrolytic)—

¶ Molten iron (pig iron)CO₂ from reduction with coke

Copper (Cu)

¶ From oxide oreCopper(II)oxide ores (e.g. cuprite, Cu₂O)— (smelting) ¶ Reduction using Carbon (as coke) used for reduction——Copper metal

Notes for Each Metal:

1. Aluminium

Bauxite is purified to obtain alumina (Al₂O₃).

Cryolite reduces melting point from ~2000°C to ~950°C.

Molten aluminium sinks to bottom; CO₂ is released at anode due to oxidation of carbon.

2. Tin

Ore roasted to remove sulphur/arsenic, then reduced with carbon.

Impurities removed as slag.

Collected molten tin cooled and cast.

3. Iron

Coke reduces iron oxide to iron.

Limestone decomposes to CaO, which reacts with silica impurities to form calcium silicate slag.

Molten iron (pig iron) tapped from bottom.

4. Copper (oxide ores)

Reduced with carbon.

For high purity, electrolysis is done after smelting.

5. Copper (sulphide ores)

Roasted to convert sulphide to oxide, then reduced.

Electrolytic refining in CuSO₄ + H₂SO₄ gives 99.9% pure copper.

Anode mud contains precious metals like Ag and Au.

Some metals like Gold, Silver, Platinum exist naturally in their pure state hence they are referred to as Nobel metals (since they don't react with earthy impurities to form ore)

Metals which has been known to Man for long are called NATIVE METALS e.g Copper, Gold, Silver

Gangue is the ore of an element from which it can not be extracted e.g Silicon can not be extracted from sand hence sand is the gangue of silicon.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Organic Compounds
notes.body:
## HYDROCARBON AND ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

Carbon tetravalency that is carbon forms 4 covalent bonds, allowing a variety of structures (chains, rings, branched).

General formula & IUPAC nomenclature → Naming based on longest carbon chain, functional group, and substituents.

Empirical formula → Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

(a) Aliphatic Hydrocarbons

(i) Alkanes

General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂

Homologous series: Members differ by –CH₂– group; gradual change in physical properties.

Reactions: Mainly substitution with halogens under UV light.

Uses of halogenated products: Refrigerants, solvents.

Isomerism: Structural only (up to 6 carbons). For straight chain use 2ⁿ-⁴ +1.  e.g Petane has 2⁵-⁴ + 1 = 2¹ + 1 = 3 isomers

Petroleum: A dark viscous liquid.

Nigeria petroleum is the best as it contains low or no sulphur impurity

Composition: Mixture of hydrocarbons.

Fractional distillation: Produces LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, bitumen.

Cracking : Convert heavy fractions into lighter (This increases quantity)

Types : Thermal and Catalystic

Conditions for cracking: Suitable catalyst (e.g Pt, Pa and Rh) and heat

Reforming : Conversion of straight chain hydrocarbon into branched or Cyclo. (This increases quality of fuel). e.g n octane with octane rating of ZERO can be reformed into 2,2,4 trimethylpentane with octane rating of 100%

Petrochemicals: Feedstock for plastics, detergents, alcohols.

Octane number: Measure of petrol’s resistance to knocking.

(ii) Alkenes

General formula: CₙH₂ₙ

Isomerism: Structural and geometric (cis/trans).

Reactions: Addition (H₂, halogens, HX), polymerization.

Products: Polythene (plastic), synthetic rubber (vulcanized for tyres).

(iii) Alkynes

General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂

Example: Ethyne (C₂H₂) from water + calcium carbide.

Reactions: Addition of halogens, hydrogen, and HX.

(b) Aromatic Hydrocarbons

Example: Benzene – C₆H₆ (planar, delocalized π-electrons).

Properties: Substitution with halogens/nitro group.

Uses: Solvents, starting material for drugs, dyes.

(c) Alkanols (Alcohols)

Types: Primary, secondary, tertiary.

Ethanol production:

Fermentation: Glucose → ethanol + CO₂ (yeast).

Petroleum by-product: Hydration of ethene.

Local examples: Gin from palm wine.

Polyhydric alcohol: Glycerol (in cosmetics, explosives).

Test for type: Oxidation & Lucas test.  LUCAS REAGENT = HCl + Zn

This is used to test for the degree of Alkanols whether monohydric, dihydric or polyhydric.   It gives more turbidity with Polyhydric Alkanols because of the presence of more OH– functional group

(d) Alkanals & Alkanones

Aldehydes vs Ketones:

Aldehyde test: Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent => silver mirror or red ppt.

Ammoniacal silver nitrate or Ammoniacal copper (i) chloride

Ketones: No reaction with these reagents.

(e) Alkanoic Acids

Reactions: Neutralization, esterification.

Examples:

Oxalic acid (ethanedioic) – dicarboxylic.

Benzoic acid – aromatic.

(f) Alkanoates (Esters)

Formation: Alkanoic acid + alcohol → ester + water.

Examples:

Fats/oils = natural esters.

Saponification: Alkali hydrolysis → soap + glycerol.

Margarine production: Hydrogenation of unsaturated oils.

Soaps vs detergents: Soaps form scum in hard water, detergents do not.

(g) Amines (Alkanamines)

Types: Primary, secondary, tertiary.

Uses: Dyes, drugs.

(h) Carbohydrates

Classes:

Monosaccharides (glucose),

Disaccharides (sucrose),

Polysaccharides (starch, cellulose).

Tests: Benedict’s/Fehling’s (reducing sugars), reaction with conc. H₂SO₄ (dehydration).

Hydrolysis: Starch → glucose (enzymes/acids).

Uses: Alcoholic beverages, pharmaceuticals, textiles.

(i) Proteins

Structure: Amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

Tests: Ninhydrin, Biuret, Millon’s, xanthoproteic.

Enzymes: Biological catalysts.

(j) Polymers

Natural: Rubber, cellulose.

Synthetic: Nylon, PVC, Bakelite.

Polymerization:

Addition (monomers with double bonds).

Condensation (loss of small molecule).

Plastics: Thermoplastics (soften on heating) & thermosetting (do not soften).

1. ALKANES (CnH₂n+₂)

¶Preparation: From crude oil (fractional distillation), hydrogenation of alkenes.

MAJOR PREP = Soda lime (NaOH/CaO) and sodium alkanoates.

¶Type: Saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons.

¶Chemical Properties: Substitution reactions with halogens (UV light), combustion, cracking.

¶Physical Properties: Non-polar, insoluble in water, low melting/boiling points increase with molecular mass.

¶Uses: Fuels (petrol, kerosene), lubricants, paraffin wax.

Test: No specific lab test; inert to most reagents.

2. ALKENES (CnH₂n)

¶Preparation: Dehydration of alkanols, cracking of alkanes.

¶Type: Unsaturated hydrocarbons (double bond).

¶Chemical Properties: Addition reactions (H₂, halogens, HX, polymerization), oxidation.

¶Physical Properties: Non-polar, insoluble in water, more reactive than alkanes.

¶Uses: Manufacture of plastics, synthetic alcohols, detergents.

¶Test: Decolourises bromine water.

3. ALKYNES (CnH₂n−₂)

¶Preparation: Hydrolysis of calcium carbide (CaC₂ + H₂O → ethyne).

¶Type: Unsaturated hydrocarbons (triple bond).

¶Chemical Properties: Addition reactions, combustion, polymerization.

¶Physical Properties: Insoluble in water, reactive triple bond.

¶Uses: Welding (oxy-acetylene flame), organic synthesis.

¶Test: Decolourises bromine water, forms white precipitate with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂.

4. ALKANOLS (CnH₂n+₁OH)

¶Preparation: Fermentation of sugars, hydration of alkenes.

¶Type: Alcohols – primary, secondary, tertiary.

¶Chemical Properties: Oxidation, esterification, dehydration.

¶Physical Properties: Soluble in water (low mass), boiling point increases with mass, polar.

¶Uses: Solvents, fuels, beverages, antiseptics.

¶Test: Sodium metal test (effervescence), Lucas test for classification.

5. ALKANOIC ACIDS (CnH₂nO₂)

¶Preparation: Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes.

¶Type: Carboxylic acids – mono- or dicarboxylic.

¶Chemical Properties: Neutralization, esterification, reactions with metals and carbonates.

¶Physical Properties: Sharp smell, acidic taste, soluble in water (small chain).

¶Uses: Food preservation, soap manufacture, plastics.

¶Test: Turns blue litmus red, effervescence with carbonates.

## 6. ALKANOATES (ESTERS) (RCOOR’)

¶Preparation: Esterification of carboxylic acids with alcohols.

¶Type: Esters – derivatives of carboxylic acids.

¶Chemical Properties: Hydrolysis, saponification.

¶Physical Properties: Sweet smell, insoluble in water, low boiling point.

¶Uses: Flavourings, perfumes, soaps, margarine.

¶Test: Pleasant fruity smell; hydrolysis yields acid and alcohol.

## 7. ALKANALS (ALDEHYDES) (RCHO)

¶Preparation: Partial oxidation of primary alcohols.

¶Type: Carbonyl compounds with terminal –CHO group.

¶Chemical Properties: Oxidation to acids, addition reactions.

¶Physical Properties: Sharp odour, soluble in water (small chain).

¶Uses: Manufacture of plastics, dyes, perfumes.

¶Test: Fehling’s solution (red precipitate), Tollens’ reagent (silver mirror).

## 8. ALKANONES (KETONES) (RCOR’)

¶Preparation: Oxidation of secondary alcohols.

¶Type: Carbonyl compounds with internal C=O.

¶Chemical Properties: Do not oxidize easily, addition reactions.

¶Physical Properties: Sweet odour, soluble in water (small chain).

¶Uses: Solvents, manufacture of explosives.

¶Test: No reaction with Fehling’s or Tollens’; reacts with 2,4-DNP (orange ppt).

## 9. ETHERS (R–O–R’)

¶Preparation: Dehydration of alcohols under controlled conditions.

¶Type: Oxygen-containing organic compounds.

¶Chemical Properties: Generally inert, cleavage by strong acids.

¶Physical Properties: Low boiling points, volatile, insoluble in water.

¶Uses: Solvents, anaesthetics.

¶Test: No specific simple test; identified by IR spectra.

## 10. AMINES (R–NH₂, R₂NH, R₃N)

¶Preparation: Reduction of nitro compounds, ammonolysis of alkyl halides.

¶Type: Primary, secondary, tertiary.

¶Chemical Properties: Basic, react with acids to form salts, acylation.

¶Physical Properties: Fishy odour, soluble in water (low mass).

¶Uses: Dyes, drugs, corrosion inhibitors.

¶Test: Turns red litmus blue, reacts with nitrous acid (primary amines evolve N₂).

## 11. AMIDES (R–CONH₂)

¶Preparation: Reaction of acid chlorides with ammonia, from ammonium salts.

¶Type: Derivatives of carboxylic acids.

¶Chemical Properties: Hydrolysis in acid or base, dehydration.

¶Physical Properties: High melting point, often crystalline. They smell like mice

¶Uses: Nylon production, pharmaceuticals.

¶Test: Hydrolysis yields ammonia and acid.

## 12. PROTEINS

¶Preparation: Naturally occurring polymers of amino acids.

¶Type: Natural polymers – polypeptides.

¶Chemical Properties: Hydrolysis to amino acids, denaturation.

¶Physical Properties: High molecular mass, colloidal.

¶Uses: Food, enzymes, hormones.

¶Test: Biuret (violet colour), Millon’s, Xanthoproteic.

## 13. CARBOHYDRATES

¶Preparation: Photosynthesis in plants.

¶Type: Monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides.

¶Chemical Properties: Hydrolysis, fermentation.

¶Physical Properties: Sweet (simple sugars), soluble in water (mono/di).

¶Uses: Food, fermentation products, textiles.

¶Test: Benedict’s or Fehling’s (red ppt for reducing sugars), iodine (blue-black for starch).

## 14. POLYMERIZATION

¶Preparation: Addition or condensation reactions of monomers.

¶Type: Natural (rubber, cellulose) and synthetic (nylon, polythene).

¶Chemical Properties: Often inert; may depolymerize under extreme conditions.

¶Physical Properties: Vary from flexible to rigid, high molecular mass.

¶Uses: Plastics, fibres, elastomers.

¶Test: No simple chemical test; identified by physical properties.

## SOAP AND DETERGENTS

1. Preparation

Soap: Prepared by saponification – boiling fats or oils with aqueous sodium hydroxide (NaOH) or potassium hydroxide (KOH), followed by salting out with NaCl.

Detergents: Prepared from petrochemicals (long-chain hydrocarbons) treated with concentrated H₂SO₄, then neutralized with NaOH to form sodium alkyl sulphate or sodium alkyl benzene sulphonate.

2. Types

Soap: Sodium salts of fatty acids (hard soap) or potassium salts (soft soap).

Detergents:

Anionic – e.g. sodium alkyl sulphates.

Cationic – e.g. quaternary ammonium compounds.

Non-ionic – no charge, used in mild cleaning.

3. Chemical Properties

Soaps react with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in hard water to form scum.

Detergents do not form scum in hard water.

4. Physical Properties

Soap: Solid or semi-solid, soluble in water (except in hard water), lathers in soft water.

Detergent: Powder or liquid, readily soluble in water, lathers in both soft and hard water.

5. Uses

Soap: Domestic and industrial cleaning, textile processing.

Detergent: Cleaning in hard water areas, shampoos, dishwashing liquids, industrial degreasers.

6. Test

Soap: Shake with water → forms lather in soft water but forms scum in hard water.

Detergent: Shake with water → lathers in both soft and hard water.

## FATS AND OILS

1. Preparation

Extracted from animal tissues (fats) or seeds/fruits (oils) by pressing, rendering, or solvent extraction.

Purified by filtration and sometimes bleaching.

2. Types

Fats: Solid at room temperature, mainly from animals (e.g. tallow, butter).

Oils: Liquid at room temperature, mainly from plants (e.g. palm oil, groundnut oil).

3. Chemical Properties

Hydrolysis: Produces glycerol and fatty acids (in presence of enzymes or alkali).

Hydrogenation: Converts oils to fats (used in margarine production).

Saponification: Reaction with NaOH/KOH to form soap and glycerol.

Rancidity: Oxidation or hydrolysis causing bad smell/taste.

4. Physical Properties

Fats: Solid, higher melting points, less unsaturated.

Oils: Liquid, lower melting points, more unsaturated.

Both: Insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

5. Uses

Food (energy source), soap production, margarine, cosmetics, lubricants, biodiesel.

6. Test

Grease test: Leaves translucent spot on paper.

Unsaturation test: Decolorizes bromine water or acidified KMnO₄ if unsaturated.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Chemistry: Chemistry and Industry
notes.body:
## CHEMISTRY AND INDUSTRY

1. Chemical Industries

Industries where raw materials undergo chemical processes to produce useful products.

Types and Examples

Petrochemical Industry – Uses crude oil and natural gas to produce fuels, plastics, synthetic fibres, detergents.

Cement Industry – Uses limestone, clay, and gypsum to produce cement for construction.

Fertilizer Industry – Uses ammonia, phosphates, and potassium salts to produce nitrogenous, phosphatic, and potassic fertilizers.

Soap and Detergent Industry – Uses fats/oils, NaOH/KOH, sulphuric acid, and alkyl benzene to produce soaps and detergents.

Food and Beverage Industry – Uses agricultural produce (sugarcane, grains, fruits) to produce sugar, drinks, and processed foods.

Textile Industry – Uses cotton, wool, silk, or synthetic fibres to produce fabrics.

2. Raw Materials and Their Sources

Minerals: e.g. limestone, bauxite, iron ore.

Agricultural Products: e.g. palm oil, cassava, maize.

Fossil Fuels: e.g. crude oil, natural gas, coal.

Air & Water: e.g. nitrogen from air, water as solvent/coolant.

3. Relevance of Chemical Industries

Provide employment.

Support other industries (construction, agriculture, transport).

Contribute to GDP.

Improve standard of living through availability of products.

Encourage technological advancement.

4. Biotechnology

The use of living organisms or their products to make useful materials or carry out industrial processes.

Applications

Food production: Bread (yeast fermentation), cheese, yoghurt.

Beverage industry: Alcoholic drinks from yeast fermentation.

Medicine: Production of antibiotics, vaccines, insulin.

Agriculture: Genetically modified crops, biofertilizers.

Waste management: Microbial breakdown of waste.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Variety of Organisms
notes.body:
## VARIETY OF LIVING THINGS

1. Living Organisms

Living organisms are organisms that show all the characteristics of life, such as feeding, respiration, growth, reproduction, movement, excretion, irritability, and death.

(a) Characteristics of Living Things

Movement – Ability to change position or part of the body (e.g. animals walking, plants bending towards light).

Respiration – Breaking down of food to release energy.

Nutrition – Obtaining food for energy and growth (e.g. autotrophs and heterotrophs).

Growth – Permanent increase in size and dry mass.

Excretion – Removal of metabolic waste products (e.g. CO₂, urea).

Reproduction – Production of new individuals of the same species.

Sensitivity/Irritability – Ability to detect and respond to stimuli.

Death – End of all life processes.

(b) Cell Structure and Functions of Cell Components

Cell wall: (plants)Provides support and protection.

Cell membrane: Controls movement of substances in and out.

Cytoplasm: Site of most chemical reactions.

Nucleus: Controls activities of the cell, contains genetic material.

Mitochondria: Site of aerobic respiration, energy production.

Chloroplasts (plants): Site of photosynthesis.VacuoleStores food, water, and waste.

(c) Levels of Organisation

Living organisms show increasing complexity from cells => tissues => organs => systems => whole organism.

Cell – Basic structural and functional unit of life.

Examples:

Euglena – unicellular, both autotrophic & heterotrophic.

Paramecium – unicellular, heterotrophic, moves with cilia.

Tissue – A group of similar cells performing a common function.

Examples:

Epithelial tissue – covers body surfaces and lines organs.

Hydra – has simple tissues for body covering and digestion.

Organ – A structure made of different tissues working together.

Example: Onion bulb – storage organ made of scale leaves and stem.

System – A group of organs working together for a specific function.

Examples:

Reproductive system – production of gametes and offspring.

Digestive system – breakdown and absorption of food.

Secretory system – production of substances like hormones, enzymes.

Organism – A complete living individual capable of independent life.

Example: Chlamydomonas – unicellular green alga.

## OTHER CELL ORGANELLES AND THEIR FUNCTIONS

1. Tonoplast

Description: Semi-permeable membrane surrounding the vacuole in plant cells.

Function:

Regulates movement of water, ions, and molecules in and out of the vacuole.

Maintains turgor pressure in plant cells.

2. Lysosome

Description: Membrane-bound sac containing digestive enzymes (found mostly in animal cells).

Function:

Breaks down waste materials, old organelles, and foreign substances.

Involved in cell self-destruction (autolysis) when necessary.

3. Ribosome

Description: Small, non-membranous structures made of RNA and protein, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum.

Function:

Site of protein synthesis.

4. Protoplasm

Description: The living content of the cell, including cytoplasm and nucleus.

Function:

Serves as the site for all life processes of the cell.

Houses all organelles and provides a medium for biochemical reactions.

5. Golgi Body (Golgi Apparatus)

Description: Stack of flattened, membrane-bound sacs.

Function:

Modifies, packages, and transports proteins and lipids.

Forms lysosomes.

Produces secretory vesicles.

6. Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

Description: Network of membranous tubules and sacs; two types:

Rough ER (RER) – has ribosomes on surface.

Smooth ER (SER) – lacks ribosomes.

Function:

RER: Protein synthesis and transport.

SER: Lipid synthesis, detoxification of harmful substances.

7. Cytoplasm

Description: Jelly-like fluid between the cell membrane and nucleus.

Function:

Medium in which organelles are suspended.

Site of many metabolic reactions.

8. Nucleolus

Description: Dense structure inside the nucleus.

Function:

Produces ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

Assembles ribosome subunits.

9. Chromosomes

Description: Thread-like structures made of DNA and proteins (chromatin when uncoiled).

Function:

Carry genetic information that controls cell activities.

Pass hereditary traits from parent to offspring.

10. Peroxisome : Detoxification of harmful materials. e.g conversion of H2O2 into H2O

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Classification of Living Organisms
notes.body:
## EVOLUTION AMONG MAJOR GROUPS OF ORGANISMS

Evolution refers to the gradual change and diversification of living organisms over long periods of time, resulting in the variety of life seen today. The different groups show a progression from simple to complex forms, both structurally and functionally.

A. Monera (Prokaryotes)

Examples: Bacteria, Blue-green algae (Cyanobacteria).

Features:

Unicellular, prokaryotic (no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles).

Reproduce mostly by binary fission.

Earliest and simplest life forms.

Evolutionary Note: Represent the first stage of life on Earth, capable of photosynthesis (blue-green algae) or chemosynthesis.

B. Protista (Protozoans and Protophyta)

Examples: Amoeba, Euglena, Paramecium.

Features:

Unicellular eukaryotes (have a true nucleus and organelles).

Show animal-like (protozoa) or plant-like (protophyta) characteristics.

Some, like Euglena, are mixotrophic (both autotrophic and heterotrophic).

Evolutionary Note: Bridge between prokaryotes and multicellular eukaryotes.

C. Fungi

Examples: Mushroom, Rhizopus (bread mould).

Features:

Non-green, eukaryotic organisms; cell walls contain chitin.

Absorb nutrients from decaying matter (saprophytic) or live as parasites.

Evolutionary Note: Likely evolved from protists; important in decomposition and nutrient cycling.

D. Plantae (Plants)

1. Thallophyta

Example: Spirogyra.

Features:

Simple, non-vascular, body not differentiated into root, stem, and leaves.

Mostly aquatic.

2. Bryophyta

Examples: Mosses (Brachymenium), Liverworts (Marchantia).

Features:

Non-vascular; have simple leaves and stems, but no roots (have rhizoids instead).

Depend on water for reproduction.

3. Pteridophyta

Example: Dryopteris (fern).

Features:

Vascular plants without seeds; reproduce by spores.

4. Spermatophyta (Seed plants)

Gymnosperms: Cycads, Conifers — produce naked seeds.

Angiosperms: Flowering plants;

Monocots: Maize — one cotyledon, parallel leaf venation.

Dicots: Water leaf — two cotyledons, net-like venation.

Evolutionary Note: Shows a progression from non-vascular to vascular plants, from spores to seeds, and finally to flowers and fruits.

E. Animalia (Animals)

1. Invertebrates (No backbone)

Coelenterata: Hydra — body has a single opening; radial symmetry.

Platyhelminthes: Flatworms (Taenia) — bilaterally symmetrical, acoelomate.

Nematoda: Roundworms — cylindrical, unsegmented body.

Annelida: Earthworm — segmented body, true coelom.

Arthropoda: Mosquito, Cockroach, Housefly, Bee, Butterfly — segmented, jointed appendages, exoskeleton.

Mollusca: Snails — soft-bodied, usually with a shell.

2. Vertebrates (Backbone present)

Pisces: Cartilaginous fish (sharks), bony fish (tilapia).

Amphibia: Frogs, Toads — live on land and water; moist skin.

Reptilia: Lizards, Snakes, Turtles — dry, scaly skin; lay eggs on land.

Aves: Birds — feathers, wings, lay hard-shelled eggs.

Mammalia: Humans, Goats — hair or fur, produce milk, give birth to live young (mostly).

✅ Evolutionary Pattern:

From unicellular prokaryotes => unicellular eukaryotes => simple multicellular => complex multicellular => invertebrates => vertebrates, showing increased complexity, specialization, and adaptation to different environments.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Adaptation
notes.body:
## ADAPTATION: STRUCTURAL & BEHAVIORAL

Organisms possess various features and behaviours that enable them to survive in their specific environments. These adaptations may be structural (physical form), functional (physiological processes), or behavioural (actions and responses).

A. Adaptive Colouration and Its Functions

Adaptive colouration is the development of colours or patterns on an organism’s body that enhance its survival.

Types & Functions:

Camouflage (Cryptic colouration) –

Blending with the surroundings to avoid predators or sneak up on prey.

Example: Chameleon, stick insect, leaf insect.

Warning colouration (Aposematism) –

Bright colours that warn predators of toxicity or bad taste.

Example: Poison dart frog, wasp, monarch butterfly.

Mimicry –

Resembling another organism for protection or advantage.

Example: Viceroy butterfly mimics the monarch; harmless hoverfly mimics wasp.

Seasonal colour change –

Changing body colour according to the season for better concealment.

Example: Arctic fox and snowshoe hare (brown in summer, white in winter).

B. Behavioural Adaptations in Social Animals

These are specific patterns of behaviour that improve survival and reproduction in animals that live in groups.

Examples:

Division of labour – In insect societies like ants, bees, and termites (workers, soldiers, queen).

Cooperative hunting – Lions hunting in groups to catch large prey.

Food storage – Squirrels storing nuts; ants storing seeds.

Communication – Bees using waggle dance to show food location.

Care for young – Elephants protecting calves, birds feeding chicks.

Warning signals – Meerkats giving alarm calls when predators approach.

C. Structural Adaptations in Organisms

Physical features that enhance survival in a particular environment.

Examples:

Plants in dry areas (Xerophytes) –

Thick cuticle (cactus).

Sunken stomata (oleander).

Fleshy stems/leaves for water storage (succulents).

Plants in water (Hydrophytes) –

Broad leaves with stomata on upper surface (water lily).

Air spaces for buoyancy (lotus).

Animals in cold regions –

Thick fur/blubber (polar bear, seal).

Small extremities to reduce heat loss (Arctic fox).

Animals in hot/dry regions –

Long legs and eyelashes (camel).

Ability to store fat in humps (camel).

Predatory animals –

Sharp claws and teeth (lion, eagle).

Forward-facing eyes for depth perception (owl).

Key JAMB Point:

Adaptations (structural, functional, and behavioural) enable organisms to cope with environmental conditions, avoid predators, obtain food, and reproduce successfully.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Form and Functions
notes.body:
## FORM AND FUNCTIONS OF ORGANISMS

1. Internal Structure of a Flowering Plant

(i) Root

Function: Anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, stores food.

Internal Structure:

Epidermis – Outer layer, may have root hairs for absorption.

Cortex – Parenchyma cells for storage and transport.

Endodermis – Inner layer controlling movement of water to xylem.

Xylem – Transports water and minerals from root to stem.

Phloem – Transports food (sugars) from leaves to other parts.

Pericycle – Gives rise to lateral roots.

(ii) Stem

Function: Supports leaves and flowers, transports water, minerals, and food, stores food.

Internal Structure:

Epidermis – Protective outer layer.

Cortex – Stores food and sometimes contains chloroplasts.

Vascular bundles – Xylem (upward transport of water/minerals) and Phloem (downward transport of food).

Pith – Central region, mainly for storage.

(iii) Leaf

Function: Photosynthesis, transpiration, and gas exchange.

Internal Structure:

Epidermis – Upper and lower layers; lower may have stomata for gas exchange.

Mesophyll –

Palisade layer: Dense chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

Spongy layer: Loosely arranged for gas circulation.

Veins (Vascular bundles) – Xylem and Phloem for transport of water, minerals, and food.

Cuticle – Waxy layer to reduce water loss.

2. Internal Structure of a Mammal (Example: Human)

Function: Structural support, protection, movement, and internal processes like digestion, circulation, and respiration.

Major Internal Structures and Functions:

Skeletal system – Supports the body, protects organs, enables movement.

Muscular system – Allows movement and maintains posture.

Circulatory system – Heart and blood vessels transport nutrients, gases, and wastes.

Respiratory system – Lungs for oxygen intake and carbon dioxide removal.

Digestive system – Mouth, stomach, intestines; breaks down food and absorbs nutrients.

Excretory system – Kidneys and urinary system remove metabolic wastes.

Nervous system – Brain, spinal cord, and nerves control and coordinate body activities.

Reproductive system – Produces gametes and supports reproduction.

Endocrine system – Glands secrete hormones for regulation of growth and metabolism.

Key JAMB Point:

In plants, roots, stems, and leaves have specialized structures for absorption, support, transport, and photosynthesis. In mammals, organs are organized into systems performing specific functions essential for survival.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Nutrition
notes.body:
## NUTRITION

Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food for growth, repair, and energy.

(A) Modes of Nutrition

Autotrophic Nutrition – Organisms make their own food from inorganic substances.

Example: Green plants (photosynthesis).

Heterotrophic Nutrition – Organisms obtain food from other living organisms.

Example: Animals, fungi, most bacteria.

(B) Types of Nutrition

Photosynthetic – Using sunlight to make food (plants, algae).

Holozoic – Ingesting solid or liquid food (most animals).

Saprophytic – Feeding on dead organic matter (fungi, bacteria).

Parasitic – Feeding on living hosts (tapeworm, mistletoe).

Relationship (+ and –)

This is similar to Predation

Symbiotic/Mutualism – Two organisms benefiting each other (lichens: fungi + algae).

Relationship (+ and +)

•Comensalism: – One organism benefits from a host without causing harm.

Relationship (+ and 0)

(C) Plant Nutrition

(i) Photosynthesis

Definition: Process by which green plants convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using sunlight and chlorophyll.

Equation:

sunlight, chlorophyll

## 6CO2 + 6H2O =================>C6H12O6 + 6O2​

Importance: Produces food and oxygen for other organisms.

(ii) Mineral Requirements

Macronutrients (needed in large amounts): N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S

Example: Nitrogen – leaf growth, Phosphorus – root and seed formation.

Micronutrients (needed in trace amounts): Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, Cl

Example: Iron – chlorophyll formation, Zinc – enzyme activation.

(D) Animal Nutrition

(i) Classes of Food Substances

Carbohydrates – Energy source (starch, sugar).

Proteins – Growth and repair (meat, legumes).

Fats and Oils – Energy storage and insulation.

Vitamins – Regulation of body processes (A, D, E, K, B, C).

Mineral Salts – Body functions and structure (Ca, Fe, Na, K).

Water – Solvent, transport, temperature regulation.

(ii) Food Tests

🥪🍜 Food Test🍛🍨

📌Starch

Test: Iodine

Result: Blue-black

📌Reducing sugar

Test: Benedict’s

Result: Brick-red precipitate

📌Protein

Test: Biuret

Result: Violet/purple

📌Fat/Oil

Test: Sudan III or grease spot

Result: Red-stained layer / translucent spot

(iii) Mammalian Tooth

Structure: Crown, neck, root, enamel, dentine, pulp, cementum.

Types & Functions:

Incisors – cutting

Canines – tearing

Premolars – grinding

Molars – crushing

(iv) Mammalian Alimentary Canal

Main Parts: Mouth => Oesophagus  Stomach => Small intestine => Large intestine => Rectum => Anus.

Use MOSDJICRA to remember the movement D = Duodenum (small intestine). JIC = large intestine

C = colon there are 4 colon (DATS)

Function: Breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, eliminates waste.

(v) Nutrition Processes

Ingestion – Taking in food (mouth).

Digestion – Breakdown of food into simpler substances (mechanical & chemical).

Absorption – Nutrients pass into the blood or lymph (small intestine).

Assimilation – Nutrients used for energy, growth, and repair.

Key JAMB Point:

Nutrition involves the intake, breakdown, absorption, and use of food. Plants are mostly autotrophic (photosynthetic), while animals are heterotrophic. Food substances are tested for nutrients, and the mammalian digestive system is specialized for processing varied diets.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Transport System
notes.body:
## TRANSPORT

Transport in Organisms

Transport is the movement of substances within an organism to maintain life processes and homeostasis.

(A) Need for Transportation

To supply nutrients and oxygen to all cells.

To remove wastes and carbon dioxide.

To distribute hormones and other regulatory substances.

To maintain homeostasis (internal balance).

(B) Materials for Transportation

Excretory products: Urea, ammonia, salts.

Gases: Oxygen (O₂) for respiration; Carbon dioxide (CO₂) for excretion.

Manufactured food: Glucose, amino acids, and other nutrients from leaves.

Digested food: From intestines to body cells.

Nutrients: Minerals and vitamins.

Water: For hydration and metabolic reactions.

Hormones: Chemical messengers for growth, metabolism, and reproduction.

(C) Channels for Transportation

(i) Mammalian Circulatory System

Heart: Muscular organ that pumps blood through the body.

Arteries: Carry blood away from the heart (usually oxygenated).

Veins: Carry blood toward the heart (usually deoxygenated).

Capillaries: Thin-walled vessels where exchange of materials occurs between blood and tissues.

Key Note: Blood transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and wastes.

(ii) Plant Vascular System

Xylem: Transports water and mineral salts from roots to leaves; provides mechanical support.

Phloem: Transports manufactured food (mainly sugars) from leaves to other parts of the plant.

(D) Media and Processes/Mechanisms of Transportation

In Animals (Blood)

Media: Blood plasma, red blood cells, and other formed elements.

Processes:

Diffusion: Movement of substances from high to low concentration.

Osmosis: Water movement across membranes.

Active transport: Energy-requiring transport of ions or molecules.

Circulation: Pumped by heart through vessels.

In Plants

Media: Water, minerals, and sap.

Processes:

Transpiration pull: Water moves upward due to evaporation from leaves.

Root pressure: Upward push of water from roots.

Capillarity: Rise of water in narrow tubes (xylem vessels).

Mass flow (translocation): Movement of sugars in phloem from source (leaves) to sink (roots/fruits).

Key Point:

Transport is essential for survival. Animals use a circulatory system to move blood and nutrients, while plants use xylem and phloem to move water, minerals, and food. Mechanisms include diffusion, osmosis, active transport, transpiration pull, and mass flow.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Respiration
notes.body:
## RESPIRATION

Respiration is the process by which living organisms release energy from food to power life activities.

(A) Respiratory Organs and Surfaces

Organs and surfaces are specialized for gas exchange:

Plants: Stomata, lenticels, root hairs.

Animals: Lungs (mammals), gills (fish), tracheae (insects), skin (amphibians).

Characteristics of good respiratory surfaces: Thin, moist, large surface area, and well-supplied with blood vessels.

(B) Mechanism of Gaseous Exchange

(i) In Plants

Stomata: Open to allow CO₂ in for photosynthesis and O₂ out from respiration.

Lenticels (woody stems): Permit gas exchange in stems.

Diffusion: Gases move passively from high to low concentration.

(ii) In Mammals

Lungs are the primary respiratory organs.

Process:

Inhalation: Diaphragm contracts ==> thoracic cavity expands ==> air enters lungs.

Gas exchange: Oxygen diffuses into blood at alveoli; carbon dioxide diffuses out.

Exhalation: Diaphragm relaxes ==> thoracic cavity reduces ==> air leaves lungs.

(C) Aerobic Respiration
