Definition: Breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.

Equation:

C6​H12​O6​ + 6O2​======> 6CO2​ + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

Importance: Provides large amounts of energy for growth, repair, movement, and other life processes.

(D) Anaerobic Respiration

Definition: Breakdown of glucose without oxygen, releasing less energy.

Equations:

In animals:

C6​H12​O6 =====> 2C3​H6​O3​ + energy (ATP)

In plants (fermentation):

C6​H12​O6​ ====> 2C2​H5​OH + 2CO2​ + energy (ATP)

Importance: Allows survival in oxygen-deficient conditions.

Key Point:

Respiration releases energy from food. Gaseous exchange occurs through specialized surfaces: stomata in plants, lungs in mammals. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases more energy, while anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases less energy.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Excretion
notes.body:
Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes from the body to maintain internal balance (homeostasis).

(A) Types of Excretory Structures

Structure, Organism/Location and  Function

Contractile vacuole

Organism:  Protozoans (e.g., Amoeba)

Collects and expels excess water and wastes

Flame cell

Organism: Flatworms (e.g., Planaria)

Function: Filters and removes waste liquids

Nephridium

Organism: Earthworms, molluscs

Function: Excretes nitrogenous wastes from coelomic fluid

Malpighian tubule

Organism: Insects (e.g., grasshopper)

Function: Removes nitrogenous wastes and regulates salts

Kidney

Organism: Mammals

Function: Filters blood to remove urea, excess salts, water

Stoma

Organism: Plants

Function: Gas exchange and minor water vapor removal

Lenticel

Organism: Woody plants

Function: Facilitates gaseous exchange and excretion of some wastes

(B) Excretory Mechanisms

(i) Kidneys (Mammals)

Structure: Cortex, medulla, nephron (functional unit).

Function: Filters blood, reabsorbs useful substances, excretes urea, salts, and water as urine.

(ii) Lungs

Function: Remove carbon dioxide (CO₂) and some water vapor during breathing.

(iii) Skin

Function: Sweat glands excrete water, salts, and small amounts of urea.

Importance: Helps regulate body temperature (thermoregulation).

(C) Excretory Products of Plants

Oxygen: Produced during photosynthesis and released via stomata.

Water vapor: Lost through transpiration.

Resins, gums, and tannins: Stored in vacuoles or secreted externally.

Carbon dioxide: From respiration, released via stomata and lenticels.

Key Point:

Excretion removes metabolic wastes to maintain homeostasis. Animals use specialized organs like kidneys, lungs, and skin, while plants excrete via stomata, lenticels, and by storing secondary metabolites.

## KIDNEY – PARTS AND FUNCTIONS

Cortex: Outer layer; contains nephrons for filtration of blood

Medulla: Inner layer; contains loops of Henle and collecting ducts; concentrates urine

Pelvis (renal pelvis): Funnel-shaped cavity; collects urine from medulla and sends it to ureter

Ureter: Transports urine from kidney to bladder

Renal artery: Brings oxygenated blood and waste products to the kidney

Renal vein: Carries filtered blood away from the kidney

## 2. NEPHRON – PARTS AND FUNCTIONS

Bowman’s capsule (glomerular capsule): Surrounds glomerulus; collects filtrate from blood

Glomerulus: Network of capillaries; filters water, salts, and small molecules from blood

Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): Reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts, and water into blood

Loop of Henle: Concentrates urine by reabsorbing water (descending limb) and salts (ascending limb)

Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): Regulates salts and pH; fine-tunes urine composition

Collecting duct: Collects urine from several nephrons; transports it to renal pelvis

## 3. SKIN – PARTS AND FUNCTIONS

Epidermis: Outer protective layer; prevents entry of pathogens; contains melanocytes for pigmentation

Dermis: Inner layer; contains blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, and sweat glands

Hypodermis (subcutaneous layer): Stores fat; insulates the body; cushions internal organs

Sweat glands: Secrete sweat for excretion and thermoregulation

Sebaceous glands: Produce oil (sebum) to lubricate skin and hair

Hair follicles: Protects against UV, dust, and minor injuries

Nerve endings: Detect touch, pressure, pain, and temperature

Blood vessels: Supply nutrients and help regulate temperature through dilation/constriction

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Support and Movement
notes.body:
## TISSUE AND SUPPORTIVE SYSTEM

(A) Movements in Plants

Type, Description, Example

Tropic: Growth towards or away from a stimulus (directional) it involves Phototropism – growth towards light and Geotropism – growth towards gravity

Tactic: Movement of whole organism toward/away from stimulus (non-growth)Euglena moving toward light (positive phototaxis)

Nastic: Non-directional response to stimulus, independent of stimulus direction (Closing of Mimosa pudica leaves)

Sleep (Nyctinastic): Daily folding/unfolding of leaves or flowers in response to light and Dark Legume leaves folding at night

(B) Supporting Tissues in Animals

Tissue, Function.

Cartilage: Flexible support and shock absorption (ears, nose, joints)

Bone: Rigid support, protection, mineral storage, movement

Ligaments: Connect bones to bones; stabilize joints

Tendons: Connect muscles to bones; transmit force for movement

(C) Skeletons in Animals

Type, Description, Examples.

Exoskeleton: Hard outer covering; provides protection and support

•Found in Insects, crabs

Endoskeleton: Internal skeleton; provides support and attachment for muscles

Found in Humans, vertebrates

Functions of Skeleton in Animals:

Provides support and shape

Protects internal organs

Enables movement (with muscles)

Stores minerals (Ca, P)

Produces blood cells (bone marrow)

(D) Vertebrae in Humans

Region, Number, Characteristics, •Function.

Cervical: 7, Small, flexible; transverse foramen

•Function: Supports head, allows neck movement

Thoracic:12, Articulate with ribs; long spinous processesProtects thoracic organs, supports ribcage

Lumbar: 5, Large, strong, thick

•Function: Supports body weight, movement

Sacral: 5, (fused)

•Fused to form sacrum

•Connects spine to pelvis

Coccygeal: 4, (fused)

•Forms tailbone

•Minor support and attachment for ligaments

Ribs and Joints

Structure, Type, Location

Ribs

True: (1–7),

False:  (8–12),

Floating: (11–12)

Protect thoracic organs; assist in breathing

Joints

Fibrous – immovable (skull bones)

Cartilaginous – slightly movable (vertebrae)

Synovial – freely movable (elbow, knee)Allow movement and flexibility

Supporting Tissues in Plants

Parenchyma: Storage, photosynthesis, wound healing

Location: Throughout plant; cortex, pith, mesophyll

Collenchyma: Flexible support, allows growth

Location: Under epidermis of stems and leaves

Sclerenchyma: Rigid support and protection

Location: Fibres in stems, hard seed coats, stone cells in fruits

Transport Tissues in Plants

Xylem: Transports water and minerals from roots to leaves

Location: Vascular bundles of roots, stems, leaves

Phloem: Transports manufactured food from leaves to other parts

Location: Vascular bundles of roots, stems, leaves

Single Definitions (Function, Description, Location)

Pith: Stores food and water

Location: Central soft tissue of stem

•Center of stem

Vascular bundle: Transports water, minerals, and food

Location: Xylem + Phloem arranged together

•Stems, roots, leaves

Cambium: Produces new xylem and phloem

Location: Meristematic layer,

•Between xylem and phloem

Piliferous layer: Absorption of water and minerals

Location: root epidermal layer with root hairs and outer layer of root

Cortex: Storage, support, transport

Location: Parenchymatous layer under epidermis.

•Between epidermis and vascular bundles in root/stem

Vertebra Structures

Neural canal: This is the hollow passage in a vertebra through which the spinal cord runs.

Neural spine (spinous process): A projection from the vertebra for the attachment of muscles and ligaments; it helps in movement.

Transverse processes: Lateral projections on each side of a vertebra that serve as attachment points for muscles and for articulation with ribs.

Centrum (vertebral body): The thick, cylindrical part of the vertebra that bears most of the body’s weight.

Facet: A smooth surface on the vertebra that allows articulation with adjacent vertebrae or ribs.

Zygapophysis (articular process): Projections that connect one vertebra to the next, providing stability.

Prezygapophysis: The anterior-facing articular process that joins with the preceding vertebra.

Types of Joints and Locations

Suture: An immovable fibrous joint found between the bones of the skull.

Ball and socket joint: A joint where a rounded head fits into a cup-shaped cavity, allowing movement in multiple directions. Examples include the shoulder (humerus and scapula) and hip (femur and pelvis).

Hinge joint: Allows movement in one plane, primarily flexion and extension. Found in the elbow, knee, and fingers.

Gliding (plane) joint: Flat surfaces slide over each other, allowing limited movement. Located in the wrist (carpals) and ankle (tarsals).

Pivot joint: A joint where a rounded end rotates within a ring of bone or ligament. Examples are the atlas-axis joint in the neck (allowing head rotation) and the proximal radioulnar joint of the forearm.

## FACT ABOUT THE SKELETON 🦴

1. Each halves of the pelvis are called INNOMINATE BONES

2. The INNOMINATE BONES are separated by PUBIC SYMPHYSIS

3. The longest, closest, strongest bone is FEMUR

4. The skull is also known as BRAINS BOX

5. LONG TRANSVERSE PROCESSES is common to Thoracic Vertebrae (it has long neural spine)

6. ODONTOID PROCESS is common to AXIS ( CERVICAL)

7. CERVICAL = Axis and Atlas

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Reproduction
notes.body:
## REPRODUCTION

Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms produce new individuals of the same kind. It may be asexual or sexual.

(A) Asexual Reproduction

Fission – The organism splits into two or more identical individuals.

Example: Paramecium divides by binary fission.

Budding – A new individual grows from a small outgrowth (bud) of the parent.

Example: Yeast, Hydra.

Natural Vegetative Propagation – New plants develop from specialized parts of the parent without gametes.

Examples: Runners in strawberry, tubers in potato, bulbs in onion.

Artificial Vegetative Propagation – Humans use plant parts to produce new plants.

Examples: Grafting, cutting, tissue culture.

(B) Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

Floral Parts and Functions:

Sepals: Protect the flower bud.

Petals: Attract pollinators.

Stamens (male): Produce pollen grains containing male gametes.

Carpels/Pistil (female): Consists of ovary, style, and stigma; produces ovules containing female gametes.

Pollination and Fertilization:

Pollination: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma (can be self or cross-pollination).

Fertilization: Fusion of male gamete (from pollen) with female gamete (ovule) to form a zygote.

Products of Sexual Reproduction:

Zygote: Develops into an embryo.

Seed: Contains the embryo and food reserves.

Fruit: Develops from the ovary to protect seeds.

(C) Reproduction in Mammals

Male Reproductive Structures and Functions:

Testes: Produce sperm and testosterone.

Epididymis: Stores and matures sperm.

Vas deferens: Transports sperm from testes to urethra.

Urethra: Conducts sperm during ejaculation.

Penis: Delivers sperm into female reproductive tract.

Female Reproductive Structures and Functions:

Ovaries: Produce ova (eggs) and hormones (estrogen, progesterone).

Oviduct/Fallopian tube: Site of fertilization; transports ovum to uterus.

Uterus: Houses and nourishes developing embryo.

Cervix: Opening of uterus; controls entry and exit.

Vagina: Receives sperm; birth canal during delivery.

Fertilization and Development:

Fertilization: Fusion of sperm and ovum to form a zygote.

Development: Zygote divides and develops into an embryo, then fetus, and eventually a baby.

Key Point:

Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring; sexual reproduction produces genetically varied offspring. Flowering plants and mammals have specialized structures to ensure successful reproduction, fertilization, and development.

Types of Fruits

Simple fruits: Develop from a single ovary of one flower.

Examples: Mango, tomato, guava.

Compound (Aggregate) fruits: Develop from many ovaries of one flower.

Examples: Pawpaw, raspberry.

Multiple (Composite) fruits: Develop from inflorescence (many flowers together).

Examples: Pineapple, jackfruit.

Dehiscent fruits: Split open at maturity to release seeds.

Examples: Beans, cotton.

Indehiscent fruits: Do not split at maturity.

Examples: Coconut, cashew.

Types of Flowers

Complete flowers: Have all four whorls – sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels.

Example: Hibiscus.

Incomplete flowers: Lack one or more whorls.

Example: Grasses (no petals).

Perfect (bisexual) flowers: Contain both stamens and carpels.

Example: Tomato, hibiscus.

Imperfect (unisexual) flowers: Have either stamens or carpels only.

Example: Maize, papaya.

Types of Seeds

Monocotyledonous (monocot) seeds: Single cotyledon.

Example: Maize, rice.

Dicotyledonous (dicot) seeds: Two cotyledons.

Example: Beans, groundnut.

Endospermic seeds: Contain endosperm for food storage.

Example: Maize, wheat.

Non-endospermic seeds: Cotyledons store food; endosperm absent.

Example: Beans, groundnut.

Agents of Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.

Abiotic agents: Wind (anemophily), water (hydrophily).

Biotic agents: Animals (zoophily) including insects, birds, and bats.

Agents of Seed Dispersal

Wind (anemochory): Seeds carried by wind.

Example: Dandelion, cotton.

Water (hydrochory): Seeds float on water.

Example: Coconut, water lily.

Animals (zoochory): Seeds carried externally (burrs) or ingested and passed out.

Example: Mango, dates, Xanthium.

Explosion (auto-chory): Fruits burst open, ejecting seeds.

Example: Castor, pea.

Types of Placentation

Axile: Ovules attached to a central column in a compound ovary.

Example: Tomato, lemon.

Parietal: Ovules attached to the ovary wall.

Example: Cucumber, mustard.

Free central: Ovules attached to a central column with no septa.

Example: Dianthus, primrose.

Basal: Ovules attached at the base of the ovary.

Example: Sunflower.

Marginal: Ovules attached along the margin of a single carpel.

Example: Pea, bean.

Fragmentation

Definition: A form of asexual reproduction where the body of an organism breaks into two or more fragments, each of which develops into a complete individual.

Example: Some filamentous algae (Spirogyra), flatworms.

Key Point: Each fragment regenerates missing parts to form a whole organism.

Schizogony

Definition: A type of asexual reproduction by multiple fission, in which the nucleus divides repeatedly before the cell divides into many daughter cells.

Example: Plasmodium (malaria parasite) in liver and red blood cells.

Key Point: Produces many offspring simultaneously from a single parent cell.

Sporogony (Spore Formation)

Definition: Asexual reproduction in which spores are produced, usually after sexual fertilization or directly from the parent, capable of developing into new individuals.

Example: Plasmodium, fungi like rusts and mildews.

Key Point: Spores are resistant structures that survive harsh conditions and aid dispersal.

## TYPES OF REPRODUCTION IN ANIMALS

Oviparous

Definition: Animals that lay eggs outside the body, where development occurs.

Examples: Birds, most reptiles, amphibians, fish.

Viviparous

Definition: Animals that give birth to live young; development occurs inside the mother.

Examples: Humans, most mammals.

Ovoviviparous

Definition: Animals that produce eggs which hatch inside the mother’s body; young are born alive.

Examples: Some snakes, sharks.

Parts of an Egg and Their Functions

Chalaza: Twisted strands of protein that keep the yolk centered in the egg.

Embryo: The developing young organism inside the egg.

Allantois: Membrane that stores metabolic waste and helps in respiration.

Amniotic sac: Protective membrane surrounding the embryo; contains amniotic fluid.

Amniotic fluid: Cushions the embryo, preventing mechanical shocks and dehydration.

Yolk: Stores food (proteins, fats, vitamins) for the developing embryo.

Shell: Hard, protective outer covering; allows gas exchange through pores.

Air space: Provides oxygen for the developing embryo before hatching.

Cell membrane (vitelline membrane): Surrounds the yolk and egg contents; acts as a selective barrier.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Growth
notes.body:
## GROWTH

(A) Meaning of Growth

Definition: Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass of an organism or part of an organism.

Key Point: Growth involves cell division, cell enlargement, and differentiation.

(B) Germination of Seeds

Definition: Germination is the process by which a seed resumes metabolic activity and develops into a seedling.

Conditions necessary for germination:

Water: Activates enzymes and softens the seed coat.

Oxygen: Needed for aerobic respiration to release energy.

Suitable temperature: Ensures proper enzyme activity.

Sometimes light: Required for some seeds (photoblastic seeds).

Stages Involved in Mitosis

Mitosis is the process of nuclear division producing two genetically identical nuclei.

Prophase: Chromosomes condense and become visible; nuclear membrane begins to break down; spindle fibers form.

Metaphase: Chromosomes align at the equatorial plane of the cell (metaphase plate).

Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.

Telophase: Chromatids reach poles, nuclear membrane reforms, chromosomes decondense.

Cytokinesis: Division of cytoplasm (often overlaps with telophase), producing two daughter cells.

Key Point:

Growth is permanent increase in size and mass, often involving cell division (mitosis). Seed germination requires water, oxygen, suitable temperature, and sometimes light. Mitosis ensures genetic continuity in growth and repair.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Co-ordination and control
notes.body:
## NERVOUS COORDINATION

(i) Central Nervous System (CNS)

The central nervous system consists of the brain and the spinal cord.

Brain: The brain is divided into major parts:

Cerebrum: Controls voluntary actions, thinking, memory, learning, emotions, and intelligence.

Cerebellum: Maintains balance, posture, and coordinates muscular activities.

Medulla oblongata: Controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing, swallowing, sneezing, and digestion.

Olfactory lobe: Processes information about smell and sends it to the cerebrum.

Spinal Cord: Serves as a pathway for transmitting impulses to and from the brain. It also coordinates reflex actions.

(ii) Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

This consists of all the nerves outside the CNS. It includes sensory nerves, which carry impulses from sense organs to the CNS, and motor nerves, which carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands. The PNS connects the CNS to all parts of the body, ensuring communication between them.

(iii) Mechanism of Transmission of Nerve Impulses

Nerve impulses travel along neurons in the following order: dendrites receive the stimulus and pass it to the cell body, which sends it through the axon to the synapse. At the synapse (the junction between two neurons), chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, such as acetylcholine, carry the impulse to the next neuron or directly to an effector organ.

(iv) Reflex Action

Reflex action is a rapid, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus. For example, pulling the hand away from a hot object. The pathway of a reflex action is: stimulus ==> receptor ==> sensory neuron ==> spinal cord (CNS) ==> motor neuron ==> effector ==> response.

(b) Sense Organs

THE SKIN is the tactile organ. It detects pressure, pain, temperature, and touch through specialized nerve endings.

THE NOSE is the olfactory organ. It detects smells through olfactory receptors that send signals to the olfactory lobe in the brain.

THE TONGUE is the organ of taste. It has taste buds that detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami sensations.

Tip of the tongue: Detects sweet taste.

Sides of the tongue (front sides): Detect salty taste.

Sides of the tongue (middle sides): Detect sour taste.

Back of the tongue: Detects bitter taste.

All over the tongue: Detects umami (savory) taste, e.g. glutamate.

THE EYE is the organ of sight. It detects light, shapes, and colours using photoreceptor cells (rods for dim light, cones for colour vision) in the retina.

THE EAR is the auditory organ. It detects sound through the cochlea and maintains balance using the semicircular canals.

(c) Hormonal Control

(i) Animal Hormonal System

Pituitary gland: Secretes growth hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and others. It is called the master gland because it regulates the activity of other glands.

Thyroid gland: Produces thyroxine which regulates metabolism, growth, and development.

Parathyroid gland: Produces parathormone which regulates calcium and phosphate levels in the blood.

Adrenal gland: Produces adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response and cortisol for metabolism and stress management.

Pancreas: Produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose levels.

Gonads (ovaries and testes): Produce sex hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone which control reproduction and secondary sexual characteristics.

(ii) Plant Hormones (Phytohormones)

Auxins: Promote cell elongation and root growth.

Gibberellins: Stimulate stem elongation and seed germination.

Cytokinins: Promote cell division and delay leaf aging.

Ethylene: Promotes ripening of fruits and leaf fall.

Abscisic Acid: Inhibits growth and promotes dormancy.

(d) Homeostasis

(i) Body Temperature Regulation

The body maintains a constant temperature of about 37°C for optimum enzyme activity. When the body is too hot, mechanisms such as sweating and vasodilation (widening of blood vessels) help cool it down. When it is too cold, shivering and vasoconstriction (narrowing of blood vessels) help conserve heat.

(ii) Salt and Water Regulation

Salt and water balance, also called osmoregulation, is controlled mainly by the kidneys, skin, and lungs. Excess water and salts are removed in urine and sweat. Hormones such as antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increase water reabsorption in the kidneys, while aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption..

1. Parts of the Ear and Functions

Pinna (auricle): Collects sound waves.

Auditory canal: Channels sound to the eardrum.

Eardrum (tympanum): Vibrates to sound waves.

Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes): Amplify and transmit vibrations.

Eustachian tube: Balances air pressure.

Cochlea: Converts vibrations into nerve impulses.

Semicircular canals: Maintain balance.

Auditory nerve: Sends impulses to the brain.

2. Mechanism of Hearing

Sound waves are collected by the pinna and directed into the auditory canal.

The eardrum vibrates with sound waves.

Vibrations are amplified by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).

The oval window passes vibrations into the cochlea.

The cochlea contains fluid and sensory hair cells that convert vibrations into electrical impulses.

Impulses are carried by the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound.

3. Parts of the Eye (Outer and Inner) and Functions

Outer parts:

Sclera: White layer, protects the eye.

Cornea: Transparent front part, refracts light.

Conjunctiva: Thin membrane, lubricates and protects.

Iris: Controls size of pupil and light entry.

Pupil: Opening through which light enters.

Inner parts:

Lens: Focuses light rays onto the retina.

Ciliary body & suspensory ligament: Change lens shape for focusing.

Retina: Contains rods (dim light) and cones (color vision).

Choroid: Dark layer, absorbs stray light and nourishes retina.

Aqueous humor & vitreous humor: Maintain shape and refract light.

Optic nerve: Transmits impulses to the brain.

4. Parts of the Human Skin, Layers and Functions

Epidermis: Outermost protective layer; prevents entry of germs and reduces water loss.

Dermis: Contains sweat glands, sebaceous glands, nerve endings, and blood vessels; controls sensation and temperature regulation.

Hypodermis (subcutaneous layer): Stores fat for insulation and energy.

Functions of the skin: Protection, temperature regulation, sensation, excretion, fat storage, and vitamin D synthesis.

5. Parts of a Nerve Cell (Neuron) and Functions

Cell body (soma): Contains nucleus; controls cell activities.

Dendrites: Receive impulses and transmit them to the cell body.

Axon: Carries impulses away from the cell body.

Myelin sheath: Insulates axon; speeds up transmission.

Node of Ranvier: Gaps in myelin; allow faster saltatory conduction.

Axon terminal (synaptic knob): Releases neurotransmitters to the next neuron or effector.

Nucleus: Directs cell metabolism and functions.

## DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE NERVOUS SYSTEM AND THE HORMONAL SYSTEM.

1. The nervous system uses electrical impulses for communication, while the hormonal system uses chemical messengers (hormones).

2. Nervous impulses are transmitted through neurons, whereas hormones are transported through the bloodstream.

3. Nervous responses are usually very fast (milliseconds), while hormonal responses are generally slower (seconds to days).

4. Nervous control is often short-lived, but hormonal control is usually long-lasting.

5. Nervous system effects are  localized to specific effectors (like muscles and glands), whereas hormonal effects are often widespread throughout the body.

6. The nervous system mainly controls immediate actions (movement, reflexes, sensation), while the hormonal system regulates long-term processes (growth, metabolism, reproduction).

7. The nervous system works by direct connections (synapses between neurons), while the hormonal system works by secretion into body fluids that travel to target organs.

## FACT

1. The brain consume 20% of Oxygen taken into the body

2. The size of the human brain is from 1.2kg to 1.4kg

3. It is made up of 3 layers namely INNER (PIA MATER), MIDDLE (ARACHNOID) and OUTER (DURA MATER).

4. It is divided into two lobes (Hemisphere) by the MEDIAN FISSURE

5. The group of Gland that produces INSULIN are known as ISLET OF LANGERHANS

6. HYPOTHALAMUS serves as the link between the nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Ecology
notes.body:
## ECOLOGY

Ecology is the study of organisms, their environment, and the interactions between them.

1. Factors Affecting the Distribution of Organisms

(i) Abiotic Factors (non-living components):

Light: Affects photosynthesis, plant growth, and animal activities.

Temperature: Determines survival of organisms; some thrive in cold regions, others in hot climates.

Water availability: Influences distribution of plants and animals; deserts vs. rainforests.

Soil type: Affects plant growth and determines the kinds of animals present.

pH (acidity/alkalinity): Determines what plants and aquatic organisms can survive.

Topography (landform): Influences drainage, vegetation, and animal habitats.

(ii) Biotic Factors (living components):

Competition: Struggle among organisms for resources (e.g., food, light, space).

Predation: One organism (predator) feeds on another (prey).

Parasitism: One organism (parasite) lives on or in another (host), harming it.

Symbiosis (mutualism): Both organisms benefit (e.g., bees and flowers).

Human activities: Deforestation, farming, urbanization affect distribution of organisms.

2. Symbiotic Interactions of Plants and Animals

Mutualism: Both organisms benefit (e.g., lichens = algae + fungi).

Commensalism: One benefits, the other is unaffected (e.g., barnacles on whales).

Parasitism: Parasite benefits while host is harmed (e.g., tapeworm in humans).

(a) Energy Flow in the Ecosystem

Energy flows in a one-way direction from the sun ==> producers ==> consumers ==> decomposers.

Food chain: Simple sequence showing energy transfer (e.g., grass ==> grasshopper ==> lizard ==> hawk).

Food web: Complex interconnection of food chains in an ecosystem.

Trophic levels: Feeding levels in a food chain: producers (plants), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), tertiary consumers (top carnivores), and decomposers (fungi, bacteria).

(b) Nutrient Cycling in Nature

(i) Carbon Cycle

Plants absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis.

Animals obtain carbon by feeding on plants.

Respiration, decay, and combustion return CO₂ to the atmosphere.

(ii) Water Cycle

Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and plants (transpiration).

Water vapor condenses to form clouds.

Precipitation (rainfall) returns water to the earth.

Water flows back into oceans and groundwater, repeating the cycle.

(iii) Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen gas in air is fixed by lightning and nitrogen-fixing bacteria into nitrates.

Plants absorb nitrates and use them to form proteins.

Animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants.

Decomposers break down dead organisms, releasing ammonium compounds.

Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrates.

Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas, completing the cycle.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Natural Habitat
notes.body:
## HABITATS

(a) Aquatic Habitats

These are water-based environments where organisms live either permanently or temporarily. Examples include ponds, streams, lakes, seashores, and mangrove swamps.

Ponds: Small bodies of standing freshwater. Organisms include algae, plankton, snails, tadpoles, fish, and frogs.

Streams: Flowing freshwater habitats. Organisms must adapt to moving water, e.g. water snails, fish (like tilapia), crabs, aquatic insects.

Lakes: Large bodies of standing freshwater with zones (surface, middle, deep). Contain plants, fish, mollusks, and water birds.

Seashores: Where land meets the sea. Organisms include crabs, mollusks, barnacles, and shore birds.

Mangrove swamps: Coastal wetlands with mangrove trees. Rich in fish, crabs, shrimps, and birds. They act as breeding grounds for many aquatic organisms.

(b) Terrestrial/Arboreal Habitats

These are land-based habitats, which may include tree tops, grasslands, burrows, and man-influenced areas.

Tree-tops (arboreal): Found in trees such as oil palm. Animals like monkeys, birds, squirrels, and insects live here. They adapt by climbing, gliding, or flying.

Abandoned farmland: Provides a habitat for grasses, shrubs, rodents, snakes, insects, and small carnivores. It usually undergoes succession (gradual replacement of plant species).

Dry grassy field (savanna): Dominated by grasses with scattered trees. Home to herbivores (antelopes, grasshoppers, zebras) and carnivores (lions, leopards).

Burrows or holes: Underground habitats used by rabbits, rats, earthworms, snakes, and some insects. They provide shelter and protection from predators and extreme weather.

2. Adaptive Features of Organisms in Different Habitats

(A) Animals

Forest habitat:

Monkeys have grasping limbs and tails for climbing trees.

Birds have strong wings and beaks for feeding on fruits and insects.

Insects show camouflage to blend with vegetation.

Aquatic (water) habitat:

Fish have gills for breathing dissolved oxygen.

Webbed feet in ducks and frogs for swimming.

Streamlined body in fish and dolphins for easy movement in water.

Fins for movement and balance.

Desert habitat:

Camels store fat in humps for energy.

Ability to withstand long periods without water.

Nocturnal lifestyle to avoid daytime heat.

Lizards and snakes burrow to escape heat.

Savannah habitat:

Herbivores like antelopes have long legs for running from predators.

Lions and leopards have strong claws and teeth for hunting.

Animals often migrate or burrow to escape seasonal droughts.

Mangrove swamp habitat:

Crabs and mudskippers tolerate changes in salinity.

Mudskippers use modified fins to move on mud.

Periwinkles and oysters attach to roots and withstand tides.

Fiddler crabs burrow to avoid predators and survive low tides.

(B) Plants

Forest habitat:

Tall trees with broad leaves to capture sunlight.

Buttress roots for support.

Epiphytes (plants growing on trees) to reach sunlight.

Aquatic (water) habitat:

Floating leaves with waxy surfaces (e.g., water lily).

Aerenchyma (air spaces) in stems for buoyancy.

Roots poorly developed since water is abundant.

Desert habitat:

Succulent stems for water storage (e.g., cactus).

Reduced leaves (spines) to reduce water loss.

Deep tap roots to reach underground water.

Thick cuticle to reduce transpiration.

Savannah habitat:

Grasses with narrow leaves to reduce water loss.

Fire-resistant plants and underground stems for regeneration.

Trees with thick bark to withstand drought and fire.

Mangrove swamp habitat:

Stilt roots and pneumatophores (breathing roots) for support and respiration in waterlogged soil.

Salt excretion through leaves.

Seeds capable of germinating while still attached to parent plant (vivipary).

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Local (Nigerian Biomes)
notes.body:
## LOCAL (NIGERIAN BIOMES)

Nigeria has a wide range of biomes (vegetation zones) due to variations in rainfall, temperature, and soil. These biomes support different plants, animals, and human activities.

(a) Tropical Rainforest

Location: Southern Nigeria (e.g., Cross River, Ondo, parts of Delta, Edo, Imo, and Rivers States).

Climate: Heavy rainfall (over 2000 mm annually), high temperature (25–28°C), high humidity.

Vegetation: Tall evergreen trees forming canopy, undergrowth of shrubs and climbers, epiphytes (plants growing on trees).

Animals: Monkeys, chimpanzees, parrots, hornbills, forest elephants, snakes, insects.

Human activities: Timber production, crop farming (yam, cocoa, palm oil, rubber, cassava), hunting, bushmeat trade.

(b) Guinea Savanna

Location: Middle Belt of Nigeria. Southern Guinea Savanna is around Kwara, Kogi, Benue, and parts of Niger; Northern Guinea Savanna stretches into Kaduna, Taraba, Bauchi, and Adamawa.

Climate: Rainfall 1000–1500 mm annually, distinct wet and dry seasons, moderate temperature.

Vegetation: Mixture of grasses and scattered trees (parkland appearance). Trees shed leaves during dry season.

Animals: Antelopes, grasscutters, lions, leopards, snakes, birds like guinea fowl and weaver birds.

Human activities: Farming (maize, yam, millet, sorghum, rice, groundnut), cattle rearing, hunting, settlement building.

(c) Sudan Savanna

Location: Northern Nigeria (e.g., Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, Borno, Jigawa, Yobe States).

Climate: Rainfall 500–1000 mm annually, long dry season, high temperature.

Vegetation: Short grasses and scattered drought-resistant trees (baobab, acacia, date palm, neem).

Animals: Cattle, goats, sheep, camels, ground squirrels, vultures, snakes, termites.

Human activities: Cattle rearing, cultivation of millet, sorghum, groundnut, cotton; trading.

(d) Desert (Sahel Region)

Location: Extreme northeastern Nigeria (parts of Borno, Yobe, Sokoto near the border with Niger Republic).

Climate: Rainfall less than 500 mm annually, very long dry season, high evaporation, hot days and cold nights.

Vegetation: Very sparse, mostly thorny shrubs, scattered grasses, and drought-resistant plants.

Animals: Camels, donkeys, goats, desert foxes, scorpions, snakes.

Human activities: Nomadic pastoralism, irrigation farming (oasis farming), trading (salt, livestock).

(e) Highlands of Montane Forests and Grasslands

Location: High altitudes such as Obudu Plateau (Cross River State), Jos Plateau (Plateau State), and Mambilla Plateau (Taraba State).

Climate: Cooler temperatures due to altitude, moderate to high rainfall.

Vegetation: Montane grasslands mixed with patches of forests, shrubs, and unique highland plants.

Animals: Monkeys, antelopes, grazing cattle, unique bird species.

Human activities: Cattle grazing, crop farming (tea, coffee, Irish potatoes, maize), tourism (Obudu Cattle Ranch, Mambilla Plateau).

✅ These local Nigerian biomes show the country’s rich ecological diversity, ranging from thick rainforests in the south to semi-desert areas in the far north.

1. National Parks (for conservation of wildlife and natural resources)

Yankari National Park – Bauchi State (famous for elephants, baboons, and hot springs).

Kainji Lake National Park – Niger and Kwara States (hippopotamus, lions, crocodiles, antelopes).

Cross River National Park – Cross River State (gorillas, chimpanzees, drills, rainforests).

Gashaka-Gumti National Park – Taraba and Adamawa States (largest national park, home to chimpanzees, leopards, buffalo).

Old Oyo National Park – Oyo State (antelope, bushbuck, hyenas, monkeys).

Okomu National Park – Edo State (forest elephants, white-throated monkeys, rainforest species).

Chad Basin National Park – Borno and Yobe States (rare water birds, antelopes, crocodiles).

2. Game Reserves

Borgu Game Reserve – Niger/Kwara States (part of Kainji Lake National Park).

Lame Burra Game Reserve – Bauchi State.

Kamuku Game Reserve – Kaduna State.

Falgore Game Reserve – Kano State.

Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary – Cross River State (home of drill monkeys and gorillas).

3. Conservation & Wildlife Sanctuaries

Lekki Conservation Centre – Lagos State (famous for canopy walk, monkeys, peacocks).

Ogbunike Caves Conservation Area – Anambra State.

Okomu Forest Reserve – Edo State.

Nguru Lake Wetlands – Yobe State (important bird conservation site).

Oluwa Forest Reserve – Ondo State.

Olujimi Forest Reserve – Ekiti State.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Ecology of Populations
notes.body:
## THE ECOLOGY OF POPULATIONS

A population is a group of organisms of the same species living together in a given area at a particular time. The study of populations helps us understand how organisms interact with each other and with their environment.

(a) Population Density and Overcrowding

Population density refers to the number of individuals of a species per unit area or volume of habitat.

Overcrowding occurs when the number of individuals becomes too high for the available resources, leading to competition, stress, disease spread, and sometimes migration or death.

(b) Adaptation for Survival

(i) Factors that Bring About Competition

Limited food supply

Lack of space (shelter, nesting sites, territory)

Mating opportunities

Light (in plants)

Water and minerals (in plants and animals)

(ii) Intra- and Inter-Specific Competition

Intraspecific competition: Occurs between members of the same species (e.g. two lions fighting for territory or two maize plants competing for sunlight).

Interspecific competition: Occurs between different species (e.g. goats and cattle grazing the same field, or trees shading undergrowth).

(iii) Relationship Between Competition and Succession

Competition influences succession, which is the gradual replacement of one community by another.

As new species colonize an area, they outcompete the weaker species, leading to changes in the composition of the community.

(c) Factors Affecting Population Sizes

(i) Biotic Factors

Food availability – more food increases population.

Predation – predators reduce prey population.

Pests and diseases – reduce survival rates.

Competition – limits population growth.

Reproductive ability – species with high reproductive rates (e.g. rabbits, insects) grow faster.

(ii) Abiotic Factors

Temperature – extremes may reduce survival.

Space – overcrowding limits growth.

Light – affects plant photosynthesis.

Rainfall – determines water availability.

Topography – land features may limit distribution.

Pressure – affects organisms at different altitudes or depths.

pH – affects soil fertility and aquatic life.

(d) Ecological Succession

Succession is the gradual and sequential replacement of one community of organisms by another until a stable climax community is established.

(i) Primary Succession

Occurs in areas that have never previously supported life (e.g. bare rocks, volcanic islands).

Pioneer species like lichens and mosses colonize first, followed by grasses, shrubs, and trees until a climax community forms.

(ii) Secondary Succession

Occurs in areas where a community previously existed but was disturbed (e.g. abandoned farmland, burnt forest).

Soil is already present, so succession is faster than primary succession.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Soil
notes.body:
## SOIL

Soil is the uppermost layer of the earth’s surface that supports plant growth. It is formed from the weathering of rocks and decomposition of organic matter.

(i) Characteristics of Different Types of Soil

## SANDY SOIL

Contains large particles with big spaces between them.

Drains water quickly but holds little moisture.

Poor in nutrients.

Easy to cultivate and well-aerated.

## CLAY SOIL

Very small particles packed closely together.

Poorly aerated and drains water slowly.

Sticky when wet, hard when dry.

Rich in nutrients but difficult to work with.

## LOAMY SOIL

A balanced mixture of sand, clay, and humus.

Retains enough water while allowing excess to drain.

Well-aerated and fertile.

Best soil for farming.

(ii) Soil Structure

Soil structure refers to the way soil particles (sand, silt, clay, and humus) are arranged into aggregates or clumps. Good soil structure improves water retention, aeration, and root penetration.

(iii) Porosity, Capillarity and Humus Content

Porosity: The proportion of spaces (pores) between soil particles, determining how much water and air the soil can hold.

Capillarity: The ability of soil to draw water upward through tiny pores. Clay has high capillarity; sand has low.

Humus Content: The amount of decomposed organic matter present in the soil, which improves fertility, water retention, and soil structure.

(iv) Components of the Soil

Soil is made up of:

Inorganic components (minerals like sand, silt, clay).

Organic components (decayed plants and animals, humus).

Living organisms (earthworms, termites, bacteria, fungi).

Soil air (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen).

Soil water (in form of moisture and solution).

(v) Inorganic Components

These include mineral particles such as sand, silt, and clay derived from weathered rocks. They give soil its texture and influence aeration and drainage.

(vi) Organic Components

These are mainly humus formed from decomposed plants and animals. They enrich the soil with nutrients and improve its fertility.

(vii) Soil Organisms

Living things in the soil include:

Animals: Earthworms, termites, ants, rodents.

Microorganisms: Bacteria, fungi, protozoa, actinomycetes.

Functions: They decompose organic matter, aerate the soil, and recycle nutrients.

(viii) Soil Air

Air fills the spaces between soil particles. Oxygen in soil air is essential for root respiration and the activities of soil organisms.

(ix) Soil Water

Water exists in soil in different forms:

Gravitational water – drains quickly, not available to plants.

Capillary water – held between soil particles, available to plants.

Hygroscopic water – thin film tightly bound to particles, not available to plants.

(x) Soil Fertility

Soil fertility refers to the ability of soil to supply essential nutrients to plants in sufficient quantity.

Loss of Soil Fertility

Continuous cropping without replenishment

Soil erosion

Leaching (washing away of nutrients)

Bush burning

Overgrazing

Renewal and Maintenance of Soil Fertility

Application of fertilizers (organic and inorganic)

Crop rotation

Mixed cropping

Use of compost and manure

Cover cropping

Irrigation and mulching

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Human and Environment
notes.body:
## HUMANS AND ENVIRONMENT

Human health and well-being are greatly influenced by the interaction between people and their environment. This relationship involves diseases, pollution, sanitation, conservation of resources, and preservation of biodiversity.

(a) Diseases

(i) Common and Endemic Diseases

Common diseases: Malaria, typhoid, influenza, measles, chickenpox.

Endemic diseases: These are diseases that occur regularly in a particular region. In Nigeria and other tropical regions, malaria, yellow fever, river blindness (onchocerciasis), and guinea worm disease are examples.

(ii) Easily Transmissible Diseases and Disease Syndromes

Poliomyelitis (Polio)

Viral disease causing paralysis of limbs.

Transmitted by contaminated food, water, or direct contact.

Preventable by polio vaccine.

Cholera

Caused by Vibrio cholerae bacteria.

Spread through contaminated water or food.

Symptoms include severe diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration.

Prevented by proper sanitation, clean water, and hygiene.

Tuberculosis (TB)

Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Attacks lungs, leading to chronic cough with blood, weight loss, and fever.

Spread by inhaling droplets from infected persons.

Prevented by BCG vaccination and good ventilation.

Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)

Gonorrhea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, leads to painful urination and discharge.

Syphilis: Caused by Treponema pallidum, progresses in stages with sores, rashes, and if untreated, organ damage.

AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome): Caused by HIV, weakens the immune system, making the body prone to infections. Transmitted through sexual contact, blood transfusion, sharing needles, and from mother to child. Prevented by safe sex practices and screening of blood.

(b) Pollution and Its Control

(i) Sources, Types, Effects, and Methods of Control

Air Pollution

Sources: vehicle exhaust, industrial smoke, burning of fossil fuels.

Effects: respiratory diseases, global warming, acid rain.

Control: cleaner fuels, tree planting, emission control.

Water Pollution

Sources: sewage, oil spills, industrial effluents, agricultural chemicals.

Effects: spread of waterborne diseases, death of aquatic life.

Control: sewage treatment, proper waste disposal, avoiding oil spillage.

Land Pollution

Sources: dumping of refuse, plastics, pesticides, mining.

Effects: loss of soil fertility, death of soil organisms, land degradation.

Control: recycling, controlled use of chemicals, proper waste management.

Noise Pollution

Sources: loudspeakers, industries, traffic, airplanes.

Effects: hearing impairment, stress, reduced concentration.

Control: noise regulation laws, use of silencers, urban planning.

(ii) Sanitation and Sewage

Sanitation: Practices that maintain cleanliness and hygiene to prevent disease spread, e.g., proper disposal of refuse, provision of clean water, washing hands.

Sewage disposal: Methods include septic tanks, sewage treatment plants, pit latrines. Proper sewage management prevents contamination of water and the spread of diseases like cholera.

(c) Conservation of Natural Resources

Conservation involves the wise use and protection of natural resources to prevent their depletion.

Soil conservation: crop rotation, cover cropping, terracing.

Water conservation: dams, rainwater harvesting, controlled irrigation.

Forest conservation: afforestation, controlled logging.

Wildlife conservation: creation of game reserves and national parks.

(d) Game Reserves and National Parks

These are areas set aside for the protection of wildlife and biodiversity. They help conserve endangered species, provide opportunities for research, and promote tourism.

Examples in Nigeria:

Yankari Game Reserve (Bauchi State)

Kainji Lake National Park (Niger/Kwara States)

Old Oyo National Park (Oyo State)

Cross River National Park (Cross River State)

Gashaka-Gumti National Park (Taraba/Adamawa States)

Chad Basin National Park (Borno/Yobe States)

Okomu National Park (Edo State)

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Variation
notes.body:
## VARIATION

Variation refers to the differences that exist among individuals of the same species. These differences may be in physical appearance, physiology, or biochemical characteristics. Variations can be continuous (gradual, e.g. height) or discontinuous (distinct categories, e.g. blood groups).

(1) Variation in Population

(a) Morphological Variations (Physical Appearance)

These are visible differences in the outward body structure of individuals.

Size: Individuals vary in height, weight, and body build.

Colour: Variation in skin colour (fair, dark), eye colour (brown, blue, black), hair colour/texture (black, brown, curly, straight), and in animals (coat of dogs, feathers of birds, scales of fish).

Fingerprints: Unique to each individual, even identical twins have different fingerprint patterns.

(b) Physiological Variations (Body Functions)

These are differences in the functioning of body systems or ability to respond to stimuli.

Ability to roll the tongue: Some people can roll their tongues into a U-shape, while others cannot.

Ability to taste phenylthiocarbamide (PTC): Some individuals find PTC bitter, while others cannot taste it at all (due to genetic difference in taste buds).

Blood groups: Human beings can belong to A, B, AB, or O blood groups, with Rhesus factor (positive or negative). This is genetically controlled.

(c) Applications of Discontinuous Variation

Discontinuous variations (those that fall into clear categories, e.g. blood group, fingerprints, tongue rolling) have important uses in society:

Crime Detection: Fingerprints and sometimes DNA profiling are used to identify criminals since they are unique to individuals.

Blood Transfusion: Knowledge of blood groups ensures safe transfusion (e.g. group O is universal donor, group AB universal recipient).

Determination of Paternity: Blood group testing and DNA analysis can be used to determine the biological father of a child.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Heredity
notes.body:
## HEREDITY

Heredity is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to their offspring through genes. It explains why offspring resemble their parents and also why they differ.

(a) Inheritance of Characters in Organisms

(i) Heritable Characters

These are traits controlled by genes that can be passed from one generation to another.

Examples: height, eye colour, blood group, hair type, skin colour, ability to roll tongue, sickle cell trait, etc.

(ii) Non-Heritable Characters

These are traits acquired during the lifetime of an organism and cannot be inherited because they are not controlled by genes.

Examples: scars, tribal marks, body weight from diet, knowledge, pierced ear, language spoken.

(b) Chromosomes – The Basis of Heredity

(i) Structure of Chromosomes

Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of cells.

They are made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and proteins (histones).

DNA carries hereditary units called genes which determine traits.

In humans, there are 46 chromosomes (23 pairs):

22 pairs are autosomes (body chromosomes).

1 pair is sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).

(ii) Transmission of Hereditary Characters

During sexual reproduction, gametes (sperm and egg) carry half the chromosomes (haploid, n = 23 in humans).

At fertilization, gametes unite to restore the full number of chromosomes (diploid, 2n = 46).

Genes on chromosomes are thus passed from parents to offspring, controlling inherited traits.

(c) Probability in Genetics and Sex Determination

Probability in genetics is used to predict the chances of traits appearing in offspring, often with Punnett squares.

Sex determination:

The female provides an X chromosome (egg always carries X).

The male provides either X or Y chromosome in sperm.

If sperm with X fertilizes the egg → XX = Female.

If sperm with Y fertilizes the egg → XY = Male.

Thus, the male determines the sex of the child.

(d) Application of the Principles of Heredity

(i) In Agriculture

Selective breeding to improve crop yield and resistance.

Cross-breeding of animals for desirable traits (e.g. milk yield, disease resistance).

Production of hybrid crops (e.g. hybrid maize, cocoa).

Genetic engineering and biotechnology in modern farming.

(ii) In Medicine

Understanding hereditary diseases (sickle cell anemia, haemophilia).

Blood group testing for safe transfusion.

Genetic counseling to predict and prevent inherited disorders.

DNA testing in forensic medicine and paternity testing.

(e) Sex-linked Characters

These are traits controlled by genes located on the sex chromosomes, mostly on the X chromosome (since it is larger and carries more genes than Y).

Examples:

Baldness – a sex-influenced trait common in males.

Haemophilia – blood fails to clot properly, leading to excessive bleeding.

Colour blindness – inability to distinguish certain colours (commonly red and green).

Duchenne muscular dystrophy – progressive muscle weakness.

These conditions are more common in males because they have only one X chromosome (XY), while females (XX) need two copies of the defective gene to express the condition.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Biology: Evolution
notes.body:
## EVOLUTION

Evolution is the series of changes that takes place in an organism over a long period of time..

## TYPES

CONVERGENT: Coming from different ancestors and living together. e.g bat (mammal) and birds (both with wing), whale and shark

DIVERGENT: Deviating  from a common ancestor e.g Man and bat

COEVOLUTION: When both species who are dependent both evolute. e.g a flower and it insect pollinator

(a) Lamarck’s Theory (Theory of Use and Disuse)

Proposed by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744–1829).

Main idea: Organisms acquire traits during their lifetime and pass them to offspring.

Structures frequently used become stronger and more developed.

Structures not used gradually waste away.

Example:

The long neck of a giraffe evolved because ancestors stretched their necks to reach high leaves, and this longer neck was inherited by their offspring.

Weakness: Later disproved because acquired characters (like scars or tribal marks) are not inherited, since they do not affect the genes.

(b) Darwin’s Theory (Theory of Natural Selection)

Proposed by Charles Darwin (1809–1882).

Main idea: “Survival of the fittest.”

Within a species, individuals show variations (differences).

Organisms with favorable traits (adaptations) survive better and reproduce.

Offspring inherit these traits, leading to gradual change in the population.

Example:

Peppered moths in England: light-coloured moths survived before industrialization, but when soot darkened trees, dark moths had an advantage and survived better.

Strength: Widely accepted because it is supported by modern genetics.

(c) Organic Evolution Theory

This is the general concept that life originated from simple organisms and gradually developed into more complex forms over millions of years.

Suggests that all living organisms share common ancestors.

Supported by fossil records, genetics, comparative anatomy, and embryology.

2. Evidence of Evolution

Several lines of evidence support the theory of evolution:

Fossil Records

Remains of ancient organisms preserved in rocks show gradual changes over time.

Example: Fossils of extinct horses show transition from small, multi-toed ancestors to large, one-toed modern horses.

Comparative Anatomy

Homologous structures (same structure, different function) show common ancestry.

Example: Forelimbs of humans, bats, and whales.

Analogous structures (different structure, same function) show adaptation to environment.

Example: Wings of birds and insects.

Comparative Embryology

Embryos of vertebrates (fish, reptiles, birds, humans) look similar in early stages, suggesting common origin.

Molecular Evidence (Biochemistry & Genetics)

Similarities in DNA, RNA, and proteins across different species.

Example: Humans and chimpanzees share about 98–99% DNA similarity.

Geographical Distribution

Organisms in isolated areas show unique adaptations.

Example: Marsupials in Australia vs placental mammals elsewhere.

Observed Evolution in Action

Development of resistance by bacteria to antibiotics.

Development of resistance by mosquitoes to insecticides.

3. Modern Synthetic Theory of Evolution (Neo-Darwinism)

This theory combines Darwin’s Natural Selection with Mendelian Genetics and modern molecular biology.

It explains evolution in terms of changes in the genetic makeup of populations over time.

Key Points:

Variation arises from mutations

Mutation = sudden, permanent change in DNA.

Provides new traits (favourable or harmful).

Recombination and Sexual Reproduction

During meiosis and fertilization, crossing over, independent assortment, and random fusion of gametes increase variation.

Natural Selection acts on variation

Favorable traits ==> organisms survive, reproduce, and pass on genes.

Unfavourable traits ==> organisms die off or reproduce less.

Isolation leads to speciation

When groups of the same species are geographically or reproductively separated, they accumulate different mutations.

Over time, they become new species.

Population Genetics

Evolution is measured as a change in gene frequency in a population over generations.

Example of Neo-Darwinism in Action:

Development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Origin of new plant varieties through mutation + selective breeding.

Evolution of different species of finches in the Galápagos Islands, each adapted to different food sources.

✅ In summary:

Darwin’s Theory explains how evolution occurs (natural selection).

Mendelian Genetics + Molecular Biology explains why traits are inherited and how variation arises.

Neo-Darwinism = Darwin’s Natural Selection + Mendelian Genetics + Molecular Biology.

notes.subject: English Language
notes.title: English Language: Stress (Word and Emphatic)
notes.body:
In English, word stress generally falls on one syllable per word, and while there are many exceptions, some general rules apply.

Two-syllable nouns and adjectives usually stress the first syllable, while two-syllable verbs usually stress the second syllable.

## GENERAL RULES:

Two-Syllable Words:

Nouns: Stress the first syllable (e.g., TAble, MOther).

Adjectives: Stress the first syllable (e.g., SIlent, HAPpy).

Verbs: Stress the second syllable (e.g., beGIN, deCIDE).

Words Ending in "-ic," "-sion," "-tion":

Stress the second-to-last syllable (e.g., phoTOgraphy, deCISION, inFORmation).

Words Ending in "-cy," "-ty," "-phy," "-gy":

Stress the third-from-last syllable (e.g., deMOcracy, aBIlity, geOGraphy, TEchnology).

Other Important Considerations:

Compound Nouns: Stress the first word (e.g., GREENhouse, BLACKboard).

Compound Adjectives & Verbs: Stress the second word (e.g., old-FASHioned, bad-TEMpered).

Words that can be both Nouns and Verbs: The first syllable is stressed when used as a noun, and the second when used as a verb (e.g., CONflict vs. conFLICT).

Suffixes: Some suffixes like "-ade", "-ee", "-eer", "-ese", "-ette", "-ique", and "-oon" often carry the stress (e.g., lemoNADE, guaranTEE, JaPANese).

## 🔥💯 SURE SYNONYMS & ANTONYMS FOR JAMB 🎯🚀

A synonym is a word that has the same meaning as another word (or nearly the same meaning). For example, beautiful and attractive are synonyms of each other because they both refer to someone or something that looks good.

👇👇👇👇👇👇👇👇

*1.Recalcitrant – stubborn:* You are a very stubborn person.

*2. Magnify – expand* : He magnified their happiness like their pain.

3 *. Baffle – confuse, deceive:* The bad news he received consecutively confused him.

*4.Bossy – controlling, tyrannical:* You have a structure that likes to bossy.

5. *Hypocrisy – duplicity, falseness:* Everyone knows that they can never tolerate hypocrisy.

*6.Intelligence – smart, bright, brilliant, sharp:* We all know that you have unique intelligence.

7. _Introverted – shy, bashful, quiet, withdrawn:_ You already have an extroverted personality, we believe you will overcome all this.

*8. Kind – thoughtful, considerate, amiable, gracious:* We have always known you as a kind person, I could not make sense of all this.

*9. Lazy – idle, lackadaisical, lethargic, indolent:* When I met her teacher today, she told me that she was too lazy this year.

*10. Lucky – auspicious, fortunate:* How lucky you are! You won this game.

_11.  Mean – unfriendly, unpleasant, bad- tempered, difficult:_ I can’t figure out what this means most, please speak a little more.

*12. Old – antiquated, ancient, obsolete, extinct:* Today we will visit old aunts.

*13. Outgoing – friendly, sociable, warm, extroverted:* I think it has an extroverted structure.

*14. Pacify – appease, placate:* I came here to appease you.

*15. Positive – optimistic, cheerful, starry- eyed, sanguine:* I always recommend you to be positive.

*Types of figure of speech , meanings and examples*

👇🏻👇🏻👇🏻👇🏻👇🏻👇🏻👇🏻

## *⬛1. METAPHOR*

*This is a direct comparison between two things that are dissimilar in nature, by drawing imagery of the shared common characteristics or attributes, without the use of ‘like’ and ‘as’.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. The lady is a raging fire._

_b. The kidnappers are blood sucking devils._

_c. Nneoma, the beauty queen, is a rising star._📌

## *⬛2. SIMILE*

*While metaphor compares two things by stating that one thing is exactly the other, simile deploys direct comparison using ‘like’ and ‘as’.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. Mr. Oji, the hunter, is as brave as his father, Dinta._

_b. Echezona, the athlete, is like the deer._

_c. Madam Azuoma is as dark as the night._📌

## *⬛3. PERSONIFICATION*

*Personification is a figure of speech in which human attributes as well as the features of living things in general are assigned to non-living things or abstract phenomena.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. The ocean raved, sped and ate up the tourists at the beach._

_b. The famished sun yawned hungrily and sighed at the busy earth._

_c. The weary sun-scorched crops lay silently in the farm and beckoned for water._📌

## *⬛4. ONOMATOPIA*

*Onomatopia usually occurs in a situation in which an object is identified by means of the sound it produces.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. The thief scaled through the wall and landed on the ground with a resounding thud. (The ‘thud’ here suggests the sound of the feet)._

_b. The buzzing bee flew around to the irritation of the woman._

_c. The clatter of plates woke the sleeping baby._📌

## *⬛5. HYPERBOLE*

*Hyperbole is the use of exaggeration to create emphasis or draw attention to an intended message.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. The yams harvested from that piece of farmland are as big as large trunks of Mahogany tree._

_b. Mr Ngama worked so hard till he perspired blood._

_c. The woman warned the troublesome kid a million times._📌

## *⬛6. EUPHEMISM*

*Euphemism is a figure of speech which presents serious matters in a lighter manner to ameliorate the harsh effect of such information.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. Nwanyimma passed away last night. (died)_

_b. The manager told his employees that the company has to let her go. (sack her)_

_c. Adamma, the new bride, is under the weather. (unwell)_

## *⬛7. ALLITERATION*

*This is a figure of speech in which a given consonant sound begins each word in a roll and makes it musical. We say the sound alliterates.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

a. The butcher bought a basin. (‘b’ alliterates)

b. The excited girl skipped, swam and skied in the snow. (‘s’ alliterates)

c. The blind bird flew and fell on the floor. (‘b’ and ‘f’ alliterate) 📌

## *⬛8. ASSONANCE*

*This is a figure of speech in which an initial vowel sound is repeated in a string of words.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. Row, row, row your boat!._

_b. Arise, clap and dance._

_c. The drizzle dripped into the deep._📌

## *⬛9. OXYMORON*

*Oxymoron is a figure of speech which sets side by side two contrasting phenomenon for the purposes of emphasis.*

*Examples:*

_a. The young man who fell over heels in love with Chiona now hates her passionately._

_b. The elderly woman handed the sick child some sweet-bitter drugs._

_c. The quiet girl is the loudest fellow I have ever met📌_

## *10. PARADOX*

*THIS IS A FIGURE OF SPEECH IN WHICH A SEEMINGLY WITTY SELF-CONTRADICTING STATEMENT APPEARS TO BE THE TRUTH ON CLOSER ANALYSIS.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. Wealthy people are very frugal._

_b. Short routes are very far._

_c. The gossip has kept an open-secret._

## *⬛11. IRONY*

*IRONY IS A SUBTLE REPRESENTATION OF AN IDEA THE OPPOSITE WAY; DIFFERENT FROM THE LITERAL OR SURFACE MEANING, SUCH THAT THE INTENDED MESSAGE IS STRIKING AND CLEAR, EVEN WITHOUT BEING EXPLICITLY PRESENTED.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. What a tall man! (When the man referred to is actually a dwarf)_

_b. Mr Akpuzo is a giver; he could not offer even a cup of water to his guest._

_c. Madam Uze is very hospitable; she does not welcome strangers or even relatives into her house._📌

## *12. APOSTROPHE*

*THERE ARE TWO SIDES TO AN APOSTROPHE, ONE; AN APOSTROPHE ADDRESSES SOMEONE ABSENT OR DEAD AS THOUGH THEY WERE PRESENT AND SECONDLY, IT ADDRESSES INANIMATE OBJECTS AS THOUGH THEY HAVE LIFE.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. Oh powerless death, you are cruel!_

_b. Dear Martin Luther King Junior, take a look; your dream has come through!_

_c. Proud stars, shine on!_

*ALSO, NOTE THAT PERSONIFICATION AND APOSTROPHE ARE SOMEWHAT SIMILAR; WHEN PERSONIFICATION IS USED, INANIMATE OBJECTS ARE MADE TO CARRY OUT THE ACTIONS OF HUMAN BEINGS OR LIVING THINGS IN GENERAL, BUT WHEN IT IS APOSTROPHE, ATTRIBUTES OF HUMANS OR LIVING THINGS AS THOUGH THEY ARE ALIVE AND PRESENT, USUALLY HERALDED BY AN EXCLAMATION MARK.*📌

## *⬛13. CLIMAX*

*A CLIMAX IS A FIGURE OF SPEECH THAT PRESENTS AN IDEA IN AN ASCENDING ORDER; FROM THE SMALLEST TO THE GREATEST, IN SUCH A WAY THAT THERE IS A BEGINNING AND A PEAK; IT IS THE ZENITH OF AN EVENT WHICH BRINGS ABOUT A CATHARSIS.*

## *EXAMPLES:*

_a. The man became worried, got depressed and committed suicide._

_b. The boy stole sweets, ice cream, phones and ended a highway robber._

_c. Emeka took the first position in his termly examinations, passed his senior school_ certificate examination in flying colours and gained admission to study his dream course at the university of ibadan📌.

## *⬛14. ANT-CLIMAX*

*this is the opposite of climax. it is the arrangement of an idea from the most important ones to the less important ones.*

*examples:*

_a. madam ade gave his grandchild love, pencils and sweets._

_b. adeagoke failed his exams, could not study his books and played all day long._📌

## *⬛15.SYNECDOCHE*

*it is a figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole; the whole represents the part. the part is usually strongly associated with the whole.*

*examples:*

_a. the whole village came out to welcome the governor._

_b. aso rock has not issued any statement about the bloody attack._

_c. many hands make light work._

_d. the poor woman has six mouths to feed._

_e. which achebe are you reading this semester?_📌

"Where you are going is the heaven and haven of good things."

## *3. IMAGERY*

"Students, floating their spirited legs... fired by the Bata drum."

Vivid movement and sound depiction.

"Dozens of smartphone cameras joined the race..."

Appeals to sight, showing frantic capturing of a moment.

"Handkerchiefs of all shades..."

Colorful depiction of emotional farewell.

"Lagos traffic became a demon..."

Presents urgency and chaos.

"Jide one huge splash, ruffled Bepo’s jacket..."

Energetic airport scene.

"Some were pierced in their ears, lips, arms..."

Horrific depiction of torture.

## *4. PERSONIFICATION*

"The Bata drum fired."

Drum given action, enhancing energy.

"Smartphone cameras joined the race."

Technology portrayed with human intention.

"The hall erupted in applause."

Building given emotional response.

"Reality stared everyone."

Abstract idea becomes confrontational.

"The hard truth awaited every student."

Inevitable realization is personified.

"Lagos traffic became a demon."

Traffic characterized as a villain.

"The Oyingbo market never gets to find out..."

Market acting with human curiosity.

## *5. HYPERBOLE*

"100 p.m. to 2:00 p.m."

Exaggerated or erroneous time.

"Ten billion!"

Playful exaggeration of a gift value.

"Not less than $10,000—the highest..."

Emphasizing importance and generosity.

"No lateness, no penalty this time."

Overstated emphasis on punctuality.

"That will be taking on too much."

Overstatement to express reluctance.

"N50,000 boldly leaving him."

Dramatizing the value of the gift.

"Seven million!"

Emphasizing the vastness of the tragedy.

## *6. ALLITERATION*

"Students, floating their spirited legs."

Repetition of "s" creates rhythm.

"Stardom dreams! Together."

"D" sounds unify vision and hope.

"Sincere depths of appreciation."

Soft “s” sound enhances emotion.

"Very sure. Very sure."

Reinforces confidence.

"Jide said, jumping excitedly."

Energetic tone through "j".

"Slaves and their clobbered."

Harsh repetition reflects pain.

## *7. ONOMATOPOEIA*

"Noooo!"

Represents the raw sound of grief or rejection.

## *8. PROVERB*

"Oja Oyingbo ko mo p’ enikan o wa."

(Yoruba) — “The market doesn’t notice who is missing.”

Expresses indifference of the world or community.

## *9. SYMBOLISM*

"Okadas were the messiahs."

Represents salvation from traffic.

"The envelope..."

Symbol of gratitude and transition.

"Golden dreams / Stardom dreams."

Represent ideal futures and aspirations.

## *. ANAPHORA*

Anaphora is a rhetorical device in which a word or phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences. This literary technique is used to:

1. Emphasize a point

2. Create rhythm

3. Build momentum

4. Add emphasis

Examples:

Telegram Comprehension Lesson

## .✨ GENERAL TIP FOR JAMB COMPREHENSION

🟨 Read the questions before the passage.

This helps you know what kind of information to look out for. It saves time and keeps you focused.

🟨 Underline or mentally note key information as you read — such as names, dates, statistics, or strong opinions.

🟨 Don't assume! Always go back to the passage to confirm your answers. JAMB wants answers that are found directly or clearly implied in the passage, not your personal opinion.

🟨 Understand the question type:

Some questions ask for facts (What was said?)

Some ask for the writer’s opinion or tone (How does the writer feel?)

Some ask for implication (What is suggested but not directly stated?)

## EXAMPLE PASSAGE

In highlight, give a general tip for students preparing for JAMB Examination on how to answer comprehension questions accurately. Later, use the one below as an example Read this passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. PASSAGE I Time was when boys used to point toy guns and say 'Bang!'. Now, they aim real guns and shoot one another. Nearly 4,200 teenagers were killed by firearms in 1990. Only motor vehicle accidents kill more teenagers than firearms and the firearms figures are rising. The chance that a black male between the ages of 15 and 19 will be killed by a gun has almost tripled since 1985 and almost doubled for white males, according to the National Centre for Health Statistics. Who could disagree with Health and Human Services Secretary, Donna Shalala, when she pronounced these statistics 'frightening and intolerable?'In the shameful light of this 'waste of young lives' in Ms. Shalala's words, an often-asked question seems urgently due to be raised again: Would less violence on television – the surrounding environment for most children and young adults – make violence in actual life less normal, less accepted, less horrifying? It may be difficult to prove an exact correlation between the viewer of fantasized violence and the criminal who acts out violence after turning off the set. But if the premise of education is granted – that good models can influence the young – then it follows that bad models can have an equivalent harmful effect. This is the reasonable hypothesis held by 80 percent of the respondents to a recent Times Mirror poll who think that violent entertainment is 'harmful' to society. Witness enough mimed shootouts, see enough 'corpses' fall across the screen, and the taking of a human life seems no big deal. Even if a simple causal relationship cannot be established between watching violence and acting it out, is not this numbed sensitivity reason enough for cutting back on the overkill in films and TV? From The Christian Science Monitor, April 16 – 22, 1993, p. 20, CSPS, Boston, MA, USA. Questions Time was when boys used to point toy guns and say ‘Bang’. Now, they aim real guns and shoot one another. Nearly 4,200 teenagers were killed by firearms in 1990. Only motor vehicle accidents kill more teenagers than firearms and the firearms figures are rising. The chance that a black male between the ages of 15 and 19 will be killed by a gun has almost tripled since 1985 and almost doubled for white males, according to the National Centre for Health Statistics. Who could disagree with Health and Human Services Secretary, Donna Shalala, when she pronounced these statistics ‘frightening and intolerable'? In the shameful light of this ‘waste of young lives’ in Ms Shalala’s words, an often-asked question seems urgently due to be raised again. Would less violence on television, the surrounding environment for most children and young adults make violence in actual life less normal, less accepted, less horrifying? It may be difficult to prove an exact correlation between the viewer of fantasised violence and the criminal who acts out violence after turning off the set. But if the premise of education is granted-that good models can influence the young, then it follows that bad models can have an equivalent harmful effect. This is the reasonable hypothesis held, by 80 per cent of the respondents to a recent Time Mirror [poll who think that violent entertainment is ‘harmful’ to society. Witness enough mimed shootouts; see enough ‘corpses’ fall across the screen and the taking of a human life seems no big deal. Even if a simple causal relationship cannot be established between watching violence and acting it out, is not this numbed sensitivity reason enough for cutting back on the overkill in films and TV? The writer says 'the firearms figure are rising' because A. more teenagers are now getting killed by firearms than by motor vehicle accidents B. firearms now have figures that are terribly high C. more teenagers now carry firearm than used to be the case D. more teenagers are now getting killed by firearm than used to be the case In secretary Donna Shalala's view, the situation depicted by the statistics is A. tense and reassuring B. topical and intimidating C. alarming and unbearable D. disturbing and conductive Which of the following statements can be implied from the passage? A. people catch more colds in winter B. the origin of colds is inconclusive C. people catch more colds in warm weather D. people catch colds equally in warm and cold weather

🔍 General Tip for Answering Comprehension Questions in JAMB

Always read the questions first before reading the passage. This helps you know what information to look for as you read. When reading the passage, focus on main ideas, tone, supporting details, and the author's intent. Go back to the relevant portion of the passage when answering a question—never answer based on memory or assumption.

✅ Example Based on the Passage Provided

Question 1: The writer says "the firearms figures are rising" because—

Correct Option: D. more teenagers are now getting killed by firearms than used to be the case

Explanation:

The phrase directly links to the statistic that firearm deaths among teenagers have increased since 1985. Therefore, Option D captures the trend of increasing deaths compared to the past.

Question 2: In Secretary Donna Shalala's view, the situation depicted by the statistics is—

Correct Option: C. alarming and unbearable

Explanation:

Donna Shalala described the statistics as "frightening and intolerable." These words translate clearly to alarming and unbearable, making Option C the accurate match.

Question 3: Which of the following statements can be implied from the passage?

Correct Option: ❌ None of the options are supported by the passage

Explanation:

All the listed options talk about cold or weather, which were not discussed anywhere in the passage. This is a distractor question.

✅ Correct approach: Eliminate any answer unrelated to the content of the passage.

If you'd like, I can generate more sample questions from this passage or another one to help your students practice further.
